author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Women seek justice for Duterte drug war victims
content:
Trigger warning: details of violence and death


Seeing her son crying as she was about to leave for the market, she gave him a piece of candy. She later found him dead upon coming back home.


Emily Soriano was among the women whose loved ones were killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. They shared their accounts of the killings, highlighting their continuing struggle for justice with leaders of the World Council of Churches (WCC).


Members of Rise Up for Life and for Rights, a network of relatives of people killed during the anti-drug campaign, recounted their experiences during a dialogue

organized

 by the National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP).


The dialogue formed part of Thursdays in Black, a WCC campaign that seeks to end violence against women.


Aside from Soriano, Normita Lopez recounted how police shot her son despite his attempt to surrender. According to her, witnesses saw him raise both hands and plead with the police not to shoot but an officer pushed him down and shot him four times in the body and once in his right hand.


Challenges


For her part, Jane Lee said that people ignored their pleas for justice before the WCC facilitated her travel to bring the families’ stories to the United Nations.


Estrella Nonay said, “I didn’t know how to get justice, so I joined Rise Up because I believe that if one of us gets justice, it is also justice for my son.”


“We are sharing with you sacred stories. Now that you have heard them, you are witnesses. We invite the WCC to stand in solidarity with the families of the victims in their quest for justice,” Deaconess Norma Dollaga of Rise Up said.


Rev. Merlyn Hyde Riley, vice-moderator of the WCC Central Committee, said that the testimonies exposed deeper structural, political, economic, social, and spiritual issues behind the killings. “No human being deserves to be treated in the ways you have described your loved ones having been treated,” Hyde Riley said.


Rev. Dr. Karen Georgia Thompson, general minister and president of the United Church of Christ and president of the World Communion of Reformed Churches, also called on churches to confront state violence against poor and marginalized communities.


She said that poor and marginalized communities bear the brunt of programs designed to harm them and urged churches to uphold human rights and dignity.

(DAA)

Women seek justice for Duterte drug war victims

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Christian Ferrer: A Testimonial
content:
The World’s Grand Guffaw


Diego Sztulwark


Lobo Suelto

, 22/11/2026


The very recent death of Christian Ferrer deepens our affection for him and allows us to revisit a host of conversations, readings and moments with a sense of gratitude. It is not a bad place to start: the nobility of the sentiments from which one thinks and writes — his rejection of resentment and bad faith — was a decisive matter for him.


Like so many other students at the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Buenos Aires (UBA) in the 1990s, I first learnt of Christian through the magazine

El Ojo Mocho

. Those of us who were not studying Communication—and were therefore not his students—came into contact with him through his articles, rather than through that soft, measured tone with which he captivated endless cohorts of students. As a student activist in the mid-1990s, I did not have any particular fondness for him. Although I read his work with keen curiosity, I was drawn to that libertarian streak (please, let’s not get sidetracked by the infamous connotations of that little word; we’re being serious here) and his penchant for all manner of strange objects.


One summer in the second half of the 1990s – I can’t remember whether it was ’96 or ’97 – I bumped into

Horacio González

 and Christian on a lovely beach in Rocha, Uruguay: Punta del Diablo. I’d just started as a teaching assistant in

Rubén Dri

’s philosophy department, and I was racing against the clock, reading Hegel as much as I possibly could. One afternoon, Horacio and Christian, who were strolling along while arguing, came into the cabin where I was studying. One of the topics of their dispute was the university. Horacio, with a sardonic tone, was of the view that one should not consider the university in terms of admission or assessment criteria, and made mocking remarks such as “with anarchists, you always end up discussing order”. On one of those days, Christian advised me to abandon my utopian attempts to understand Kant and Hegel and to devote my efforts instead to reading Nietzsche. His work was more vital. It’s not a question, he said, of learning theoretical systems, but of having real conversations with genuinely provocative, powerful interlocutors. I tried to ignore him, but I failed.


In a sense, it was always like that with Christian. Whenever I tried to get closer to him, to share my concerns with him in militant language, I found myself faced with someone who, while listening, would lay down his own conditions: “Where you say “politics”, I hear “power””. He wasn’t interested in militant ideology, but he was interested in the country, Argentina, and history, the world. He could talk about that with great erudition, for hours on end. In that sense, listening to Christian was a learning experience. I tried to ignore his political anarchism, but – once again – I failed. Not because it made me change course, no. But it did create the conditions within me to become an attentive reader of his ideas. A reader, in the sense of needing to weigh up my own thoughts against his. A few days ago,

Santiago López Petit

 was in Buenos Aires, reminding us that it is one thing to “engage in politics”, and quite another to “lead a political life”. The essence of the critique, which I admired in Christian, ran from the latter to the former. The weight of that distinction does not create a political system, but it does create a certain—undoubtedly virtuous—way of being. Having read Osvaldo Bayer and Gilles Deleuze, I never had any doubts about the appeal of the great libertarian ethic, nor about the superiority of what some philosophers call “ontological anarchism”: constituent praxis, set against a backdrop of a non-hierarchical nature.


But with Christian, one could not talk about theory. On one occasion he invited me to write something for a faculty journal that he edited. I think it was around 2001. He said to me, mockingly: “Write about political theory; I know nothing about that”. It was not, of course, that he was ignorant of theory; the matter simply made him sarcastic. His readings of Schopenhauer, Benjamin, Debord, Foucault and Deleuze were more incisive than many of the systematisations of those theories that are in circulation (the repetition of the conceptual system must have seemed to him like a way of thinking that was alien, not his own). Quite simply, he had no interest—for radical, profound reasons—in that realm. His reasons were set out at …

author: Jonathan Pinckney
title: Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships
content:
This article

Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


What comes next for American democracy? Our research into authoritarian regimes reveals a striking pattern in how autocracies begin to fall apart — and democracy starts to regain ground.


The 2026 U.S. midterms revealed deep and growing frustration with the Trump administration, including among communities that

have traditionally

 supported Republicans. The secretary of the army, a Trump appointee,

resigned

 after disputes over military readiness and the Iran war. Small businesses

sued

 the administration over tariffs, while companies denounced ICE raids for gutting profits. The CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, a three-time Trump voter,

attacked the administration

 over ICE raids, saying that “South Texas will never be red again.” On Nov. 3, his prediction came true as Texas border counties

saw historic swings

 toward the Democratic party. These signs reveal widening cracks in alliances that have kept Trump in power.


This expanding circle of dissent evokes a common global pattern: When compliance with an authoritarian leader begins to break down, it can trigger a cascade of opposition that ultimately leads to regime collapse. Brazilian businesses that backed Jair Bolsonaro eventually denounced his anti-democratic behaviors, contributing to his electoral defeat. When parts of the Catholic Church removed support from the far-right Law and Justice Party in Poland, its governing coalition fragmented. And in Hungary, the electoral coalition that brought down Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was led by defectors from Orbán’s own party.  


When and why do people stop complying with dictators? We studied the behavior of thousands of key social groups whose compliance is critical for dictatorships to remain in power. These include businesses, unions, security forces and faith groups, key pillars whose political, economic and moral resources keep regimes standing. Looking at dictatorships and backsliding democracies in the post-Cold War era, one clear pattern stands out: Broad civic mobilization

and

 dense social ties between those complying with the regime and members of a pro-democracy opposition encourages non-compliance. Mass noncompliance is how autocracies fall. Indeed, the

chances of stopping democratic backsliding

 while relying only on institutional channels like litigation, legislation and voting is about 7.5 percent. The presence of a broad-based civil resistance increases the probability of success to around 53 percent.  


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Both broad mobilization and social connection are crucial because of the nature of compliance. While some people comply because of true ideological alignment, most do so for more ordinary reasons: to advance careers, protect business interests, show deference to authority, or out of simple psychological inertia. Others may for their safety. When people fear political retaliation, public support can mask private indifference or even opposition. For example, while farm bureaus across the U.S. may avoid publicly denouncing the administration, plenty of farmers and ranchers are

seething

. While big business has largely refrained from publicly criticizing the administration,

behind closed doors

 many CEOs are exasperated. A pro-democracy front should make room for people withdrawing their support for all of these reasons.  


Broad-based civic mobilization — where diverse groups use

protests

, marches,

boycotts

 and walkouts to push back — changes this picture. If people both see and believe that dissent is widespread, they are more likely to shift their behavior. Courage becomes contagious. 


Strong social ties between a regime’s pillars of support and its opponents can facilitate a cascade of dissent. If people only see those who are different from them protesting, their dissent is easy to dismiss as the actions of a radical few. Yet if those they know and trust begin to speak out, such actions are more difficult to discount. This helps explain why the

spread of protests

 into rural and traditionally conservative parts of the U.S. is noteworthy. In Tunisia’s “Jasmine Revolution,” the national labor union — initially a co-opted part of the Ben Ali dictatorship — shifted to supporting the revolution when local offices that had been regularly …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: Hitting the mark: “Grand Theft Capital”, by Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster
content:
REVIEWS


The Guardian

: “Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics” by

Aditya Chakrabortty


“…Over decades – through Reagan and Clinton, Bush and Obama – Republicans and Democrats have changed the tax code to reward ownership rather than earning, so the richest 400 households

now pay lower rates of tax

 than the bottom 50% of Americans. As the radical economists Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster show in their new book,

 Grand Theft Capital: What Workers Should Know About the Affordability Crisis

, the share of national income going to ordinary workers has slumped from 30% in the 1960s to 20% today. This is the destruction of working-class lives and dreams in which Republicans and Democrats colluded. This is the American carnage that in 2016 helped propel Trump into the White House. But the most glaring feature of this era of Trumponomics has been its shameless inequality….”

Read more

….

And you can see the A

dam Smith Institute’s miffed response

 to his piece, here…if you are interested in how weak it is.


Red Pepper

 picks: “

Botany, welfare, friendships, work and housing.

David Matthews

 picks six of the best new books for leftists

“


“Capitalism has been stagnating for decades, characterized by sluggish growth. Yet the wealthy continue to grow richer while the rest of us face declining wages and eroding living standards. Focusing on the United States yet deeply relevant to Britain and other capitalist countries, Magdoff and Bellamy Foster make clear that in a climate of economic decline, big business has deliberately and strategically targeted workers as a primary source of wealth extraction. Their conclusion is a call for mass action, from below…”


People’s Voice

(Canada):

“Succinct and accessible, this economic primer hits the mark for working people today”

, by Stéphane Doucet


“Magdoff and Foster have truly hit the mark with this short book…Interesting figures include the precipitous drop of work stoppages involving over 1000 workers, from over 330 per year in 1975 to less than 20 since the 2010’s; the corporate tax rate being more than halved since 1950; the CEO-to-worker pay ratio being multiplied by more than 10 times in 60 years; labour’s share of GDP dropping more than 10 percent since the 1960’s; and private sector workers with defined-benefit pensions dropping for 60 percent to 10 percent of the workforce. All these are very broad, clear, decisive and very powerful figures. The book provides many more, along with the necessary context…”

Read more

…


Counterpunch

: “

Why Working People Got the Blues

“, by Ron Jacobs


“The lack of affordability is the curse of the working class, whether its individual members are working or not. Politicians talk about it and some might even propose legislation to moderate it, but the cost of almost everything keeps going up more than wages and retirement benefits. The domination of the economy by monopolies and cartels–many of which are invested in the business of war and resource extraction–and by politicians at their service means the bills they rack up are going to be paid by us. When the ruling class tells us they can’t afford to continue providing social services, they’re lying. It’s not that they can’t, it’s that their priorities lie elsewhere, with consistently higher profits being near or at the forefront.”

Read more…

author: Franco Giandana Gigena
title: Nuestros datos, nuestras reglas: Gobernanza de datos para bienes comunes digitales en la era de la IA
content:
Esta pieza fue escrita por

Patricia Díaz

, coordinadora de la Alianza A2K Latinoamérica y Franco Giandana, analista de políticas públicas en América Latina y el Caribe para Access Now.


Desarrollar un sistema de inteligencia artificial requiere muchos datos, que los principales desarrolladores recopilan de la web, sin compensar ni reconocer a las personas y comunidades que los crean, organizan y custodian. Estos datos se emplean para entrenar sistemas de IA, es decir, para reconocer patrones o generar respuestas. Esta extracción masiva de datos es  una forma de explotación de los

bienes comunes

 del conocimiento y la cultura y una expresión del colonialismo digital, que afecta especialmente a la Mayoría Global. 


En Latinoamérica, las universidades, bibliotecas, archivos, museos, gobiernos, organizaciones sociales y comunidades indígenas poseen datos especialmente valiosos para el entrenamiento de estos sistemas, pues suelen estar organizados y provenir de fuentes confiables. Es ahí donde enfrentan el desafío de facilitar el uso de sus datos sin poner en riesgo la sostenibilidad de su misión. Sin embargo, la

concentración de poder

 de las empresas que desarrollan IA puede limitar el papel de estas instituciones al de simples proveedoras de datos y

consumidoras

 de productos construidos a partir de los conjuntos de datos que ellas mismas reúnen y custodian. 


Para los pueblos indígenas, este desafío es una preocupación de larga data. En 2004, el

Foro Permanente de las Naciones Unidas para las Cuestiones Indígenas

 advertía que la recolección de datos sobre estos pueblos generalmente no responde a sus intereses y, muchas veces, puede utilizarse para justificar medidas discriminatorias. En el contexto actual, los usos de estos datos para el desarrollo de la IA  plantean nuevos riesgos de colonización y hacen  aún más urgente la soberanía de sus propios datos. 


Los contenidos son libres, la infraestructura no


La IA modificó la escala y forma en la que se accede a los datos en internet. Mientras que los sitios web y repositorios digitales se diseñaron para consultas individuales, los sistemas de IA pueden recolectar colecciones completas de forma automatizada utilizando programas conocidos como “

bots

”. En esta publicación nos centraremos  en los “bots rastreadores”: programas informáticos que recorren páginas web para indexarlas en buscadores o para recopilar textos y datos para entrenar o inferir respuestas en sistemas de IA. 


Su uso masivo no solo aumenta la cantidad de datos descargados, sino también la demanda que generan en los servidores que los almacenan y disponibilizan. En 2024, el rastreo por bots representó el

51%

 del tráfico web mundial, superando por primera vez al tráfico humano y en 2025 alcanzó el

53%

. Además, una

encuesta que GLAM-E Lab

 encontró que 39 de 43 instituciones de patrimonio cultural registraron un aumento reciente del tráfico, y 27 lo atribuyeron a bots que recopilan datos para entrenar sistemas de IA. Esto obliga a preguntarse: ¿debería el acceso automatizado por bots tener las mismas condiciones que el generado por personas?


Algunas instituciones advierten el problema recién cuando sus colecciones quedaron fuera de línea debido a la sobrecarga de sus servidores. Para quienes sostienen estas infraestructuras, el volumen y la frecuencia de las solicitudes de los bots elevan los costos económicos y la complejidad técnica de su mantenimiento. Es que los bots

generan solicitudes

 en grandes cantidades y utilizan miles de

direcciones IP

 diferentes para dificultar su detección. La

Fundación Wikimedia

, constató que al menos el 65% del tráfico que más recursos demandaba para su infraestructura provenía de bots. Su respuesta fue categórica: “

nuestros contenidos son gratuitos, nuestra infraestructura no

”.


Las reglas de convivencia en internet están rotas


El uso de bots no es nuevo. Durante décadas, la convivencia entre los sitios web y estos programas se ordenó en torno a dos acuerdos. El primero es el

protocolo robots.txt

, un archivo con el que cada sitio indica a qué páginas pueden acceder los bots, aunque su cumplimiento es voluntario. El segundo acuerdo se estableció con los buscadores, como Google: los sitios permiten que sus bots los rastreen y, a cambio, aparecen en sus resultados de búsqueda y reciben visitas. 


Con el auge de los sistemas de IA generativa y la demanda de grandes volúmenes de datos para entrenar modelos, estos acuerdos …

author: Unknown
title: Kayyım atanan HalkTV'den nöbeti "Halk Televizyonu" devraldı
content:
Halk TV'ye 14 Ekim'de kayyım atanmasının ardından kanaldan ayrılan gazeteciler, Halk Televizyonu adıyla yeni bir yayın platformu kurdu. İlk canlı yayın, gazeteci Gökhan Kayış'ın sunumuyla 23 Kasım akşamı gerçekleştirildi.


Kayış, açılışta Uğur Dündar, Serhan Asker, Dinçer Gökçe ve avukat Seraf Özer'i ağırladı. Yayına gazeteciler, siyasetçiler ve meslek örgütü temsilcileri de canlı bağlantılarla katıldı.


Kayış, yeni yayın girişiminin nasıl ortaya çıktığını şu sözlerle anlattı:


“Kayyum atandıktan sonra dedik ki kardeşim bu memleketi bırakıp gidecek halimiz yok. Umutsuzluğa kapılacak halimiz de yok.”


Gazeteciliği sürdürebilecekleri yeni bir alan oluşturduklarını belirten Kayış, “Biz de bütün her şeye inat, bütün kayyum uygulamalarına inat Halk Televizyonunun macerasını başlattık” dedi.


Uğur Dündar: “Halkın gerçekleri öğrenme hakkına hizmet" 


Açılış yayınına katılan Uğur Dündar, gazeteciliğin temel işlevinin kamuoyunu bilgilendirmek olduğunu vurguladı:


“Gazeteciliği kaba anlamıyla tanımlarsak halkın gerçekleri öğrenme hakkına yapılan bir hizmettir gazetecilik mesleği.”


Dündar, iktidarların kamuoyunun gerçeklere ulaşmasını engellemeye çalışabildiğini belirterek araştırmacı gazeteciliğin karşılaştığı baskılara dikkat çekti.


“Görevimiz bu işi yaptığımız sürece doğruları, sadece doğruları, sonuna kadar doğruları söylemektir. Ve bunu yaparken de evrensel meslek ilkelerimize sıkı sıkıya bağlı kalmaktır.”


Dündar, yeni girişimin ekonomik dayanışma boyutuna da değindi. Halk TV'den ayrılan çalışanlar arasında ciddi geçim sıkıntısı yaşayanlar olduğunu belirterek YouTube gelirlerinin bu kişilere destek amacıyla kullanılabileceğini söyledi.


“Eğer bu kanal YouTube'dan para kazanırsa, ne kadar çok kazanırsa kazansın lütfen bana tek kuruş vermeyin. İhtiyacı olan arkadaşlarımıza dağıtın.”


TGC: “Basın hürdür, sansür edilemez”


Türkiye Gazeteciler Cemiyeti temsilcisi Sibel Güneş, canlı bağlantıyla katıldığı yayında medya kuruluşlarına yönelik kayyım uygulamalarını eleştirdi.


Güneş, son iki yılda çok sayıda televizyon kanalının yayınlarının sona erdiğini belirterek Halk TV, Tele1 ve Sözcü TV çalışanlarının karşılaştığı sorunlara dikkat çekti.


Anayasa'nın 28. ve 30. Maddelerini hatırlatan Güneş, şöyle konuştu:


“Anayasa 28. maddesi basın hürdür, sansür edilemez diyor. 30. madde de çok net basın araçlarının işletilmekten alıkonulamayacağını ifade ediyor.”


Güneş, Halk TV'ye yönelik soruşturmanın doğrudan yayın içerikleriyle ilgili olmadığını, buna rağmen yayınların durdurulduğunu söyledi.


“Biz haberin serbest dolaşımını istiyoruz ve sizler gibi değerli meslektaşlarımızın, üyelerimizin görevlerini yapabilir olmasını istiyoruz.”


“Bu yaptığınız şey bir yumruk sıkmaktır”


Yayına katılan gazeteci Zafer Arapkirli de yeni girişimi basın üzerindeki baskılara karşı bir dayanışma örneği olarak değerlendirdi.


“Bu yaptığınız şey bir yumruk sıkmaktır Gökhan. Yani baskıya karşı, istibdata karşı, faşizme karşı, bağımsız medyanın gırtlağını sıkmaya çalışan o kötü güçlere karşı bir yumruk sıkmaktır.”


Arapkirli, bağımsız haberciliğin farklı mecralarda sürdürülmesi gerektiğini belirterek şöyle devam etti:


“Bugün Halk Televizyonu, öbür gün başka bir kanal, başka bir gün başka bir kanal.”


Serhan Asker ise Halk TV'de yaptığı programların izleyicilerle kurduğu ilişkiye dikkat çekti. Kayyım sonrasında eski programlarının yayımlanmaya devam ettiğini, buna karşılık çalışanların iş ve sosyal haklarına ilişkin sorunların çözülemediğini söyledi.


“Yani işten çıktık, haklı fesihle ihtar gönderdik. Görüşelim, konuşalım diyoruz. Bir görüşme iklimi de bulamadık ne yazık ki.”


İlk yayında 100 bin abone


Açılış yayını sırasında kanalın YouTube abone sayısı hızla yükseldi. Yayının başlangıcında yaklaşık 39 bin olarak açıklanan sayı, programın üçüncü saatini geçmesinin ardından 100 bine ulaştı.


Kayış, yayın sırasında izleyicilere teşekkür ederken yeni platformun yalnızca bir gelir kaynağı olarak görülmemesi gerektiğini söyledi:


“Gerçekten vazgeçmememizin sebebi memleket meselesi. Sadece gelir kapısı olarak bakmıyoruz.”


Halk Televizyonu ekibi, haber ve programlarını YouTube ile sosyal medya hesapları üzerinden sürdürmeyi hedefliyor.


(AEK)

title: Soirée de soutien à A4 (rachat d'une ferme)
content:
Le Queer lieu de Saint-Denis et l'interchorale queer militante d'

IDF

 organisent une soirée de soutien avec cantine et transmission de chants au profit du projet d'implantation d'une ferme solidaire en Essonne. Le mardi 24 novembre de 19h à 22h à la Bourse du travail de Saint-Denis (9-11 rue Genin à Saint-Denis)


Soirée de soutien pour le projet finaliser le rachat d'une ferme en bio en Ile-de-France (Essonne)


L'association Ciwara (soutenue par A4) réunit actuellement les fonds manquants pour racheter le matériel agricole du maraîcher qui part à la retraite et transmet sa ferme de 17 ha, cultivés sans intrants ni irrigation.


Ciwara, pour quoi

 

?


Avec cette ferme c'est le rêve d'un lieu pour défendre l'agriculture paysanne et l'émancipation de tous et toutes, quelle que soit leur origine. Ce lieu, passerelle entre la ville et la campagne, permettrait l'implantation :


 D'une coopérative agricole de travail d'égal à égal : l'association Ciwara

 D'un espace de test et de préservation de semences paysannes

 D'un centre de formation et d'inclusion professionnelle

 D'un lieu de rencontre et de solidarité


Au programme de cette soirée (voir lien d'inscription plus bas) :


 19h : cantine préparée par l'équipe de Poésie culinaire sur fonds de chansons militantes

 20h : transmission de chants militants par l'interchorale queer militante d'Ile-de-France

title: Γαλλία: Χτίζοντας τον κόσμο που ονειρευόμαστε στις “κομμούνες” των Πανεπιστημίων
content:
Ανταπόκριση από Παρίσι. Ηρώ Σιαφλιάκη


Ένα μυστικό θαύμα συμβαίνει αυτήν την εποχή, στη σκιά της γνωστής γαλλικής εξέγερσης, όχι ως εξαίρεση αλλά ως συνέχεια, ως καρδιά θα μπορούσαμε να πούμε, παλιότερων εξεγέρσεων που η Ιστορία των γεγονότων συνήθως ξεχνά. Σε αρκετά πανεπιστήμια όπου οι φοιτητές υποστηρίζουν το κίνημα των μαθητών λυκείου (το ένα τέταρτο των Πανεπιστημίων τουλάχιστον έχουν αποκλειστεί ή διαταραχθεί από τις 6 Οκτώβρη) ο τρόπος δράσης έχει τελευταία αλλάξει. Τα αρχικά μπλόκα δίνουν τη θέση τους τώρα σε καταλήψεις, ως επανοικειοποίηση

των χώρων σπουδών κι

ομάδες φοιτητών οργανώνουν

 λ

αϊκά πανεπιστήμια

, σ

το Πανεπιστήμιο της

Nanterre

, στο

Creteil

 και στη Σορβόννη (

Sorbonne Nouvelle

), μεταξύ άλλων.


Από τους πρώτους, στην

É

cole normale sup

é

rieure d

’

Ulm

 στο Παρίσι οι φοιτητές έχουν μετατρέψει την κατάληψη που ξεκίνησε στις αρχές Οκτωβρίου :

«

σε ένα πανεπιστήμιο από τους φοιτητές και για τους φοιτητές, με στόχο να προσεγγίσει όσο το δυνατόν περισσότερο κόσμο. Η οργάνωση είναι πολύ οριζόντια, χωρίς ιεραρχία»,

υπογραμμίζει ο

Matthias

, φοιτητής μαθηματικών, με στόχο:

 «να αναπτύξουμε κριτική σκέψη». «Είναι εξαιρετικά συγκινητική αυτή η επιθυμία για γνώση και χειραφέτηση, που συνάδει με τα τρέχοντα γεγονότα»,


συνοψίζει

 ο

Arthur Jatteau

 στην

AFP

.


Οι φοιτητές δηλώνουν ως μία από τις πηγές έμπνευσής τους το Ελεύθερο Πειραματικό Πανεπιστήμιο της

Vincennes

 που ιδρύθηκε μετά τον Μάη του 1968. Όπως στη

Vincennes

 (που δεν απαιτούσαν καν απολυτήριο γυμνασίου, ώστε να έχουν τη δυνατότητα εγγραφής οι εργάτες) τα μαθήματα είναι ανοιχτά σε όλους και ποικίλα, ας πούμε στο πρόγραμμα μιας Τρίτης:

«Η ουτοπική πόλη στον κινηματογράφο»

 και μια διάλεξη του φιλόσοφου É

tienne Balibar

 ή

«Η ρητορική του Μακρόν: μας κοροϊδεύει;»

 μπορεί να ακολουθεί ένα μάθημα για την ιστορία της Παλαιστίνης, ή μάθημα τρομπέτας γι αρχάριους.


Απέναντι από το Πάνθεον, κοντά στη λεωφόρο

Saint

–

Germain

, το λαϊκό πανεπιστήμιο που διοργανώνουν φοιτητές του Πανεπιστημίου

Paris Cit

é

 πραγματοποιείται στο πεζοδρόμιο, κάτω από μπλε μουσαμάδες, μπροστά από τους κάδους απορριμμάτων που εξακολουθούν να φράζουν την είσοδο του κτιρίου στη οδό

Saint

–

P

è

res

. Οι ακροατές κάθονται πάνω σε παλέτες κι ακούνε τον

David Gaborieau

, καθηγητή κοινωνιολογίας, να κάνει μια προσπάθεια ανάλυσης του σημερινού νεανικού κινήματος κρατώντας έτσι μια σχέση με τους φοιτητές του ενώ συμμετέχει στο κίνημα.


*


«Κομμούνα του

Jussieu

».

Σχολή ανοιχτή για όλους,

 


ένας χώρος στην υπηρεσία της κινητοποίησης


Φωτό Φ.Κ.


Οι φοιτητές και το προσωπικό της πανεπιστημιούπολης του

Jussieu

 (

Sorbonne Universit

é)

 πέρασαν πάνω από δύο μήνες με την πανεπιστημιούπολη διοικητικά κλειστή,

 

μια μέθοδος που χρησιμοποιείται από τις πρυτανείες από την αρχή του κινήματος για να πνίξουν τις κινητοποιήσεις. Οι φοιτητές απάντησαν με ανακοινώσεις,

 

 υπενθυμίζοντας τον πολιτικό στόχο της δράσης τους:

 

να ανοίξουν τη σχολή για όλους και να την κάνουν έναν χώρο στην υπηρεσία της κινητοποίησης.

 


Σ

τις 4 Νοεμβρίου,

 

κατά τη διάρκεια μιας γενικής συνέλευσης 500 ατόμων,

 

ψηφίστηκε

η κατάληψη του χώρου,

 

η οποία ξεκίνησε το ίδιο βράδυ.

 

«Προκειμένου να ενθαρρυνθεί ο διάλογος και η συμμετοχή με το προσωπικό και τους/τις φοιτητές/φοιτήτριες που δεν συμμετέχουν στις κινητοποιήσεις, η ΓΣ ψήφισε λοιπόν το τέλος των μπλόκων και τη συνέχιση της κινητοποίησης με κατάληψη των χώρων.».


Το επόμενο βράδυ,

 

πραγματοποιήθηκε συγκέντρωση για να απαιτήσουν να ανοίξουν οι πύλες · η πρυτανεία,

 

η οποία είχε σπεύσει να καταδικάσει την κατάληψη σε ένα

email

,

 

κάλεσε την αστυνομία για να εκφοβίσει τους φοιτητές και να διαλύσει τη συγκέντρωση.

 

Παρά την τεράστια δύναμη καταστολής που αποτελούνταν από 400 αστυνομικούς των

CRS

 (ΜΑΤ) και της

BRAV

–

M

 (μοτοσυκλετιστές),

 

και πάνω από δεκαπέντε προσαγωγές,

 

η κατάληψη άντεξε και

άρχισε να οργανώνει

 ένα λαϊκό πανεπιστήμιο,

 

όπως σε πολλές άλλες σχολές.


Οι καθηγητές έκαναν μάθημα πίσω από τα κάγκελα και οι φοιτητές

τούς άκουγαν

 από την άλλη πλευρά,

 

στον δρόμο.

 Ένα συμβολικό μέτρο,

 

το οποίο όμως επέτρεψε να φανεί η αποφασιστικότητα του προσωπικού και των φοιτητών.

 

Και την Τρίτη 10 Νοεμβρίου,

 

η Γενική Συνέλευση του προσωπικού ψήφισε την ανοίξουν οι πύλες για την επόμενη Πέμπτη.


 

Στις 12 Νοέμβρη μια ανθρώπινη αλυσίδα, από τους φοιτητές κι αρκετά μέλη από το προσωπικό της πανεπιστημιούπολης,

τους επέτρεψε …

author: dev
title: La bataille du futur a commencé
content:
Un mois après le 17 octobre, force est de constater que la stupeur qui a saisi les gouvernants comme tout le commentariat politique s'est passablement dissipée. Le

Comité pour le maintien du dix-sept octobre

 nous a transmis ses analyses quant aux forces qui, selon lui, ont concouru à ce que nous ne quittions finalement pas l'époque contemporaine. Depuis là, il propose les pistes nécessaires à l'avènement d'un 18 octobre.


Le 17 octobre, nous sommes sortis de l'impuissance qui nous condamnait à attendre passivement la séquence électorale du printemps prochain. Contre toute attente et contrairement à ceux qui nous gouvernent ou y aspirent, nous avons tenu notre promesse : nous nous sommes levés et nous avons opposé à la terreur policière l'insurrection la plus joyeuse et la plus joueuse que ce pays ait connue. Ce jour-là, les monstres étaient en uniforme et les héros en déguisement.


Que se passe-t-il ?


Nous voilà jetés dans une bataille

existentielle

. Les revendications ne suffisent plus à exprimer la rage et le désir de

s'arracher à

 ce monde. Aucun programme ne semble à la hauteur de cette

fin d'époque contemporaine

, et si certains prétendent incarner la rupture par les urnes, d'autres ont cherché à la réaliser en actes pendant cet automne chaud. Ce n'est pas une lutte économique pour une meilleure répartition de la richesse, pour le droit d'accumuler et la garantie d'une survie un peu plus confortable que celle de son voisin. Nous avons dépassé la question de la quantité pour poser celle de la

qualité de la vie –

 vivre, pas survivre. Plus qu'une révolte contre la vie chère, une révolte pour la vie belle. C'est une lutte politique contre la répartition actuelle du pouvoir au sein de la société qui trouve ses symboles dans la Révolution française et qui prolonge sa haine du privilège et du mépris ; qui semble décidée à

prendre au mot

la vieille devise révolutionnaire pour en demander la réalisation

immédiate

. Sa devise (Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité – ou la mort) a survécu aux siècles et aux régimes monarchiques, impériaux et républicains. Elle semble désormais faire peser sur la démocratie moderne la menace de son propre dépassement. C'est cette menace qu'entend bien conjurer la contre-révolution préventive, par le renforcement d'une forme de républicanisme de guerre, compris comme synthèse des modes de gouvernement par l'assentiment – le réformisme, la division des pouvoirs, le recours au vote – et l'anéantissement – le fascisme, l'état d'exception, la guerre. Pour le dire simplement, ce républicanisme est l'aboutissement du sarkozysme, qui a trouvé dans le macronisme son digne héritier, jusqu'à sa mue en macro-lepénisme. Les forces qui espèrent encore pouvoir réformer la République se drapent d'illusions. Elles refusent de voir que la fille de la Révolution s'est muée en son ennemie la plus féroce. Le progressisme n'est jamais que l'aile gauche du conservatisme.


Il suffit de regarder de plus près le jeu auquel s'adonnent les organisations historiques du mouvement ouvrier, qui ont été critiquées

à raison

comme des forces de récupération et de neutralisation de la révolte ; si tenté qu'on puisse encore parler de « force » pour désigner ces organisations, marginalisées dans le monde du travail et dépourvues de réel pouvoir – tant de victoire réelle que de trahison consciente – dans ses tractations avec le gouvernement. Après la journée de grève du 29 septembre, l'intersyndicale a refusé d'appeler au 17 octobre – comme ce fut le cas pour le 10 septembre 2025 et, avant ça, pendant le mouvement des gilets jaunes. Elle a préféré donner rendez-vous le 5 novembre. Mais, confrontée à la résilience de la révolte et à sa reconduction quotidienne dans les lycées, les universités et dans la rue le samedi, elle n'a rien trouvé d'autre à proposer que la reconduction des cortèges attendus et encadrés, dernière proposition réelle encore

à sa hauteur

. Les 24 et 31 octobre, ces défilés se sont vus relégués aux boulevards des Maréchaux et à l'extérieur des centres-villes, sur des parcours

périphériques

 pour désarmer la masse de manifestants que le déploiement sécuritaire consécutif au soulèvement du 17 octobre n'avait pas convaincu de rentrer à la niche, et rendre invisible à nouveau la colère qui avait défiguré les centres-villes. Les syndicats ont cédé au chantage des Préfectures pour préserver leur rond de serviette à la table des négociations, bien qu'aucune chaise ne les y attende plus depuis …

title: Podcast: l’EZLN verso Città del Messico
content:
Sta per iniziare la “Gira por la vida” capitolo Messico, 4 anni dopo il viaggio in Europa.


Da Nodo Solidale


Più di 1500 delegat* zapatist* partiranno a breve in carovana dal Chiapas per arrivare a Città del Messico dove incontreranno decine di collettivi e le organizzazioni de las

Madres Buscadoras

. Un viaggio per abbracciare chi da troppo tempo sta lottando e cercando la verità verso una persona cara o un affetto scomparso, i e le

desaparecidas

, in quella che è la faccia più drammatica e odiosa della guerra contro la vita oggi in Messico.


Questo podcast è il primo contributo prodotto dal Nodo Solidale per iniziare a raccontare questo importantissimo evento che durerà più di un mese e che sta coinvolgendo nell’organizzazione una buona parte dei movimenti dal basso di tutta la capitale messicana e non solo.


Ps. Per leggere tutti i comunicati da parte dell’EZLN (alcuni tradotti anche in italiano) su questa importante e complessa iniziativa politica, potete andare su:

enlacezapatista.ezln.org.mx

author: Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise
title: Mit einem Lächeln kämpfen – Interview mit dem Kollektiv „Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise“
content:
Die französische Bewegung entfaltet eine enorme politische Kraft, dank derer – und das können wir ohne Übertreibung sagen – eine echte Perspektive für eine Neuordnung zwischen Teilen der Klasse entstanden ist, die einander oft misstrauisch gegenüberstehen und durch die rassistischen Mechanismen des Staates auf Distanz gehalten werden. Wenn der Konflikt dieses Ausmaß erreicht, ist eine politische und soziale Polarisierung unvermeidlich, und die liberale Demokratie offenbart ihr autoritäres Wesen. Diese sich abzeichnende Wiederannäherung wird vor allem von den Schülern der Oberschulen in den Vororten vorangetrieben, die die größte Kraft im Zusammenhang mit – im Übrigen – sehr radikalen Forderungen entfalten. Dies lässt sich aus diesem Interview ableiten, das zwar sicherlich parteiisch, aber wirklich wenig ideologisch ist und mit einer Gruppe von Oberstufenschüler aus Marseille geführt wurde, die sich ihrer Stärke so bewusst sind, dass sie keinen Bedarf haben, die Widersprüche und Schwachstellen der Bewegung zu verbergen. Die kleine, aber wichtige Erkenntnis, die man daraus ziehen kann, ist, dass es nicht stimmt, dass Konflikt und Konsens unvereinbare Alternativen sind. Im Gegenteil: Wenn es dem Konflikt gelingt, den materiellen Kern der sozialen Widersprüche radikal anzugehen, schafft er es auch, Konsens zu erzeugen.


Machina (Vorwort)


***


Antonio Alia: Wie kam es zur Mobilisierung in Marseille und was waren die wichtigsten Momente?


Jeunesse Antifa Marseillaise: In Marseille begann die Mobilisierung im vergangenen Jahr mit der Ankündigung von Haushaltskürzungen, der miserablen Verwaltung der Schulplanung und dem Abbau zahlreicher Lehrerstellen an öffentlichen Oberschulen. Die wichtigsten Momente waren die erste große Demonstration am 1. Oktober 2026, bei der es uns gelang, der Polizei die Stirn zu bieten, sowie die Demonstrationen am 17., 24. und 31. Oktober gemeinsam mit den Gelbwesten, auch wenn es bereits zuvor Demonstrationen und Blockaden gegeben hatte.


A.A.: Wie sieht die geografische Verteilung der Mobilisierung aus?


J.A.M.: Die am stärksten mobilisierten Gymnasien in Marseille: Saint-Charles, Montgrand, Thiers, Victor Hugo, Marie Curie (das stark unterdrückt wird), Rempart, Marseilleveyre, Daumier. Andere Gymnasien, die von den Forderungen weniger betroffen sind, wie beispielsweise das Henri IV, mobilisieren sich zur Unterstützung unserer Kämpfe. Alle Campusse der Universität Aix-Marseille (von Marseille und Aix bis nach Arles und Avignon) mobilisieren sich an unserer Seite, und umgekehrt unterstützen die Gymnasiasten die Studierenden. Außerhalb der Region ist die Mobilisierung ebenso bedeutend und hat denselben Umfang.


A.A.: Gibt es einen Unterschied in den Kampfformen zwischen der rassifizierten und der nicht rassifizierten Zusammensetzung der Studierenden?


J.A.M.: Es gibt keinen nennenswerten Unterschied zwischen den Kämpfen rassifizierter und nicht rassifizierter Menschen, aber es gibt einen Unterschied in der medialen Sichtbarkeit rassistischer Natur, der uns zutiefst empört und darauf abzielt, unsere Anliegen zu diskreditieren – was uns dazu antreibt, noch geeinter zu sein. Die Schüler, die Schulen in den Vororten besuchen, haben mit noch baufälligeren Gebäuden zu kämpfen als diejenigen im Stadtzentrum, doch ist ihr Zugang zu den Orten der Mobilisierung möglicherweise erschwert: An den Tagen der Mobilisierung wird der Nahverkehr mit der klaren Absicht eingestellt, die Zahl der Menschen zu verringern, die zu den Demonstrationszügen gelangen können.


A.A.: Wie sah das Leben der Schüler*innen vor der Mobilisierung aus und wie hat es sich danach verändert?


J.A.M.: Vor der Mobilisierung war der Alltag kaum zu ertragen. Überfüllte Klassenräume, abwesende Lehrkräfte, die nicht ersetzt wurden, ausgefallene Unterrichtsstunden wegen fehlender Räume oder Lehrkräfte und ein Klima, in dem man uns sagte, wir sollten den Mund halten und für „Parcoursup“ arbeiten, anstatt auf unsere Forderungen einzugehen. Die Beziehungen zu den Lehrkräften waren meist distanziert, da sie keinen Einfluss auf unsere Bedingungen haben und selbst überlastet sind. Einige unterstützten uns jedoch bereits und diskutierten mit uns über die Studien- und Lehrbedingungen, wenn sich während einer Unterrichtsstunde die Gelegenheit dazu bot – allerdings nie länger als ein paar Minuten. Seit Beginn der Mobilisierung hat sich alles verändert: Wir reden wirklich miteinander, halten gemeinsam Vollversammlungen ab, essen gemeinsam vor …

author: Acratosaurio rex
title: Contra el miedo
content:
O sea: un montón de gente va a votar porque tienen miedo. Miedo al fascismo, miedo a la ultraderecha, miedo a esa cantidad de gente de cientos de miles, o millones de personas, que van a votar de manera irracional y pasiva a unos criminales que son Canallas&Company. Una cerda no buscaría allí a sus hijos. Claro que no. 


Es el voto del miedo. Es ir a votar para que no salgan esos comemierdas que huelen a diarrea. Pero yo estoy a favor de la razón, a favor de reflexionar, y a favor de elegir según mi gustos y conveniencia. Eso me enseñaron mis padres. Y estoy en contra del miedo. Votar con miedo, "para que no salgan", es como comprar un jersey que no te gusta, para que no te regalen uno más feo. Al final seguro que vas hecho un adefesio. 


Pues yo no tengo miedo. ¿Sabéis por qué? Porque yo tengo mi sindicato. Tengo mis compañeros Y compañeras. Y allí están todo el puto año liados en la batalla. Allí me encuentro la conspiración permanente, y la gente que está en la pelea, no tiene miedo. En mi sindicato, mediante el conflicto, el cobarde se vuelve valiente, el insensato racional, y el tímido planta cara. Cómo una gata contra la pared, enseñando los dientes, afilando las garras, chas, un ojo menos.


He mencionado el sindicato, pero puede ser cualquier cosa en la que estés interviniendo. Un colectivo de lo que sea, que planta cara a unos cabrones de estercolero sin media hostia, es más complicado de manipular, que un votante solitario e inerme ante la urna. Porque ante una urna, uno elige lo que no quiere. Pasa siempre. ¿O no? Una persona acojonada, lo que hace es suplicar piedad. Se rinde. 


Pero en el combate, con tus colegas, o te tumban o repartes estopa hasta que derribas a ese imbécil y le quitas la risita y los dientes. Puede hacerse. Puedes hacerlo. Puedes perder el miedo.


Y si al final votas, hazlo sin miedo.

author: Unknown
title: Рассказ анархистки-трансдевушки, сбежавшей после вербовки ФСБ
content:
Это статья Ивана Асташина, вышедшая в октябре в The Insider.

Примечание редакции avtonom.org: Мы не рекомендуем подписывать какие-либо соглашения с силовиками, но считаем, что всегда следует действовать по обстоятельствам и допустимо спасать себя, если это можно сделать без причинения вреда окружающим.

В январе 2025 года сотрудники ФСБ пришли с обыском к 18-летней трансдевушке из Тюмени, нашли в ее телефоне переписку с «Боевой организацией анархо-коммунистов» (БОАК) и стали угрожать ей уголовным делом и многолетним сроком. Под давлением она согласилась на сотрудничество. Силовики поручили ей знакомиться с ЛГБТК-людьми, входить к ним в доверие и пытаться получить компрометирующую информацию. В разговоре с The Insider она рассказала, как выглядит вербовка, как ей удалось обмануть ФСБ и покинуть страну без связей, денег и загранпаспорта.

15 января 2025 года я проснулась от того, что на меня орет и дергает за плечо человек в маске. Я тогда жила у родителей, они открыли дверь сотрудникам ФСБ. Те пришли с ордером от прокурора и почему-то сказали, что ищут СВУ.

Мне толком никаких бумаг не дали рассмотреть: ордером помахали перед лицом и сразу убрали. Дома были два следователя, понятые и еще один фсб-шник в балаклаве и бронежилете. Изъяли компьютер, телефон и переносную камеру.

Когда я отказалась разблокировать телефон, фсб-шник в маске несколько раз ударил меня по спине. Бил и спрашивал: «Кашлять хочешь?» Я говорю: «Нет». Он снова бьет.

Потом мне натянули шапку на лицо, вывели в подъезд, посадили в машину и отвезли в городское управление ФСБ на Советской, 40. Это было часов в шесть утра. Там меня подняли на третий или четвертый этаж и почти до вечера опрашивали.

Здание ФСБ на Советской, 40 в Тюмени, URA.RU

Сначала спрашивали, не хочу ли я сама им что-нибудь рассказать. Потом унесли телефон в другой кабинет, а минут через пятнадцать принесли обратно — все пароли уже были сбиты.

Следователей было двое, причем они максимально тупо разыгрывали «злого» и «доброго». Один орал, угрожал и смотрел, что у меня в телефоне. Второй задавал вопросы по тому, что ему говорил первый о содержимом моего телефона.

Я решила: раз доступ к телефону у них все равно уже есть, то все, что они могут там найти о деятельности нашей инициативы, я возьму на себя. Сказала, что листовки клеила одна, граффити рисовала тоже одна.

Граффити, сделанных героиней материала с единомышленниками, Тюмень, август 2024 года

А потом вспомнила, что кое-что не успела удалить. Но было уже поздно: они нашли переписку с БОАК — Боевой организацией анархо-коммунистов. Мы переписывались по электронной почте. Там обсуждались инструкции по анонимным звонкам и то, как налаживать товарищеские контакты для инициативы. В одном из писем еще упоминалась «тачка фашистов».

Именно эту переписку они потом назвали основанием для дела об «обучении террористической деятельности». Когда они ее нашли, то сразу заулыбались и сказали: «Ну все, теперь тебе точно п***ец».

При этом они продолжали искать. Кроме фотографий листовок, моего маленького канала левой направленности человек на 30 и этой переписки, особо ничего не нашли. Пытались добиться, чтобы я призналась в чем-нибудь помимо листовок, граффити и переписки с БОАК.

Например, они почему-то считали, что я собиралась устроить акцию против главаря тюменской «Русской общины», направленную против его автомобиля. Я сказала, что максимум речь шла о том, чтобы порезать шины, а потом я вообще от этой идеи отказалась — вот машина и стоит целая.

Откуда силовики могли получить информацию

В самом управлении меня уже не били, там было в основном психологическое давление и неудобные условия. Например, я сидела не на стуле, а на системном блоке от своего компьютера. Они показывали на сейф в углу кабинета и рассказывали, что запихивают туда людей. Говорили, что одного человека якобы продержали там три дня и вообще не выпускали.

Они показывали на сейф в углу кабинета и рассказывали, что запихивают туда людей

Еще сказали, что если бы поймали меня не в Тюмени, а на оккупированных после полномасштабного вторжения территориях Украины, то вообще убили бы. Тот, который играл «злого», угрожал бросить меня в камеру, где меня будут насиловать пять человек.

Где-то к вечеру меня отвезли обратно домой и, можно сказать, передали отцу с рук на руки. Никаких документов опять не выдали. Формально никакого домашнего ареста не было, но устно сказали: из квартиры никуда не выходить, иначе меня заберут в СИЗО.

Телефон, компьютер и камера остались у них …

author: Keston K. Perry
title: The imperialism of progressive economics
content:
Progressive economics has an imperial problem. It is possible to denounce inequality, defend redistribution, and criticize neoliberalism while preserving a deeper hierarchy: the presumption that experts, often based in powerful institutions in the Global North, can determine what justice should mean for societies shaped by slavery, colonial extraction, and imperial rule. The issue is not simply whether their intentions are good or their proposals sufficiently radical. It is who has the power to define the problem, decide which histories count and prescribe solutions after short field visits or, worse, on conference calls, before those most affected have determined the terms of repair.

This contradiction is particularly visible in debates about reparations and climate finance. Universal basic income, public ownership, cheaper credit, and expanded development finance can all be useful demands. None, however, returns stolen land, reverses accumulated colonial wealth, repairs ecological destruction, or restores collective authority over political and economic life. Redistribution and reparations can reinforce one another; they are not interchangeable. When the former is offered as a substitute for the latter, progressive universalism becomes a way of setting aside historically specific claims.

I encountered this argument during a debate about reparations in 2020. A senior economist asked where reparative claims should begin and end, questioned the feasibility of identifying descendants of enslaved people, and suggested universal income or shared dividends funded by wealth taxes as more practicable responses. The framing exposes an asymmetry: Why must restitution meet an exceptional test of feasibility while universal redistribution is treated as a reasonable starting point? Who decides which demands are too complicated to count as politics?

The point is not to dismiss universal social provision. It is to insist that the injuries of empire cannot be reduced to unequal household incomes. Colonialism reorganized property, labor, public finance, land tenure, and the authority to govern. Repair must be capable of transforming those relationships, not merely compensating people for living within them.

At a conference on African economic sovereignty in Dakar in 2022, I heard related arguments from progressive economists who treated nationalization or the green developmental state as ready-made alternatives to reparations. State ownership and planning can be indispensable instruments of transformation. Yet our meeting in the Museum of Black Civilizations was a striking setting in which to overlook the intellectual traditions and struggles through which African peoples have articulated their own visions of sovereignty. A model developed in one context does not become universal because its advocates consider themselves anti-neoliberal. The question is who defines the political horizon, and whose knowledge is allowed to unsettle it.

A similar dilemma runs through the international sustainability industry. Island and African societies confronting climate disasters are surrounded by consultants, conveners, investment platforms, and intermediaries promising innovation. International collaboration is not inherently objectionable. What matters is who controls the agenda, data, networks, and resulting resources. When communities supply experiences while outsiders translate them into fundable or bankable projects, an old division of labor survives under the language of partnership.

The Bridgetown Initiative brings these contradictions into focus. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has rightly drawn attention to the global financial system’s unequal treatment of climate-vulnerable countries. The initiative has pushed sovereign debt, liquidity, Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development bank reform onto an international agenda that too often marginalizes small states. Yet recognition of an unjust financial architecture is not the same as transforming the relations of ownership and creditor power that sustain it. Expanded access to finance can leave the underlying distribution of wealth, risk, and power largely intact.

Consider what financial innovation means when disaster strikes. After Hurricane Beryl in 2024, Grenada activated a disaster clause that deferred debt-service payments. This created fiscal breathing room, but deferred payments were added to principal: relief in the timing of repayment, not cancellation of the …

author: WoMin
title: Practising solidarity economy: Women’s collective action and community finance in Memirlosho
content:
Conversations about economic development often portray rural women as people who need support, training, or assistance. Far less attention is paid to how women organise themselves to solve problems, manage resources, and build livelihoods together. During a recent visit to the

Memirlosho Women Cultural Village

 in Isiolo County, northern Kenya, we saw how Samburu women offer a powerful example of a community and solidarity economy in practice. The cultural village brings together four women’s groups (Narasha, Muruguti, Narupa, and Rapunye) that work as a collective to create opportunities, strengthen resilience, and improve livelihoods. Their lived experience demonstrates that solidarity economies are not solely theoretical concepts or future possibilities. They are already being built every day through cooperation, mutual support, and shared responsibility.


Collective organising as a condition for economic agency


The first foundation of Memirlosho’s economic model is collective organising. The women registered a Community Based Organisation (CBO) through which they transformed dispersed individual survival strategies into a legally recognised collective entity. This shift carries important economic and political implications as they gained greater visibility, legitimacy, and bargaining power. The umbrella structure allows the four groups to support one another while maintaining their own identities. Together, they can access external support, coordinate activities, and speak with a stronger collective voice.


More importantly, the organisation creates a sense of shared purpose. Members are no longer facing challenges alone, they have built a community that pools resources, shares risks, and works toward common goals.


Productive activities: turning livelihoods into collective assets


Memirlosho’s economic activities are rooted in skills and resources that already exist within the community. Hence, two productive activities form the backbone of the village. The first is beadwork. Women use their cultural knowledge and craftsmanship to produce traditional beadwork that can be sold for income. Working collectively allows them to purchase materials more efficiently, share information, and explore markets together.


Another important activity is goat rearing and trading. Through support from the

Samburu Women Trust

, the groups received forty goats, with ten goats allocated to each group. Rather than viewing these animals as a one-time gift, the women transformed them into a revolving community asset.


The goats are raised and later sold, with the proceeds used to purchase new livestock. In this way, the original investment continues to generate benefits over time. Instead of being consumed, the asset grows and supports future opportunities. This approach reflects one of the central principles of solidarity economies: resources are managed not only for individual gain but for the long-term benefit of the collective.


Financial solidarity: A savings system built around people’s needs


While productive activities constitute the foundation of

Memirlosho’s

 solidarity economy, the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) serves as its circulatory system. The VSLA operates as a community-owned financial institution managed according to principles of mutual support rather than external profit extraction. The system has three main characteristics:


a

) Socially oriented lending:

  Women can access loans for socially important needs especially school fees, respond to emergencies, or meet household needs. Interest collected on loans is not extracted by an outside institution. Instead, it returns to the group’s common fund, benefiting all members. This way, capital serves the community’s wellbeing and social reproduction rather than simply financial accumulation.


b) Inclusive flexibility:

 The savings model is also flexible. Members contribute according to their means and circumstances, recognising that income can fluctuate throughout the year, as a pastoral community. This allows participation even during difficult periods and helps ensure that nobody is excluded because they cannot meet rigid contribution requirements. It’s a system that prioritises participation and inclusion.


c) Community control over finance:

 The VSLA enables members to maintain ownership and control over their financial resources. By keeping financial decision-making within the community, the group reduces dependence on …

author: Carmen Esselink
title: Cape Verde’s Elections Were Loud. Its Voters Are Increasingly Silent
content:
On the 29th of October, before 10 o’clock in the morning, a car with speakers has already driven twice through my neighbourhood in Mindelo, the city of Cesária Évora and of Cape Verde’s best-known Carnival, blasting MpD (

Movimento para a Democracia,

Movement for Democracy) viewpoints and a jingle. I notice I’m immediately annoyed, because I’m trying to conduct an interview from home and the noise keeps interrupting the conversation. The same car passes twice more that day. Three days later, on Sunday 1 November, a whole procession of floats drives along the beach, honking, accompanied by Cape Verdean and PAICV (

Partido Africano da Independência de Cabo Verde

, African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde) flags, candidate headshots and more jingles, while my boyfriend and I are trying to get onto the road in the car. Election season in Cape Verde has begun: a very loud time, and a disruptive one. As an outsider, I wonder whether it has the desired effect, people voting for a certain party, or the opposite: abstention.


The noise is meant to bring people to the polls. In May’s parliamentary election, most of them stayed home. Just

46.5 percent of the 416,096 registered voters

 cast a ballot, down from 57.4 percent in 2021 and 66 percent in 2016. Yet Cape Verde is often held up as one of Africa’s most stable democracies, and in May the PAICV, which grew out of the independence movement, returned to power after ten years in opposition. It was the loudest election I’ve ever witnessed, with central roads closed for concerts and rallies, pickups with speakers crawling through town, and people handing out partisan t-shirts. Six months later, the country was campaigning again, this time for the presidential election on 15 November.


A concert stage goes up on Rua Lisboa in Mindelo ahead of the parliamentary elections of May 2026. Photo: Carmen Esselink


On 12 November at 8pm, the band

Corda do Sol

 plays on Rua Lisboa, ahead of a speech by President José Maria Neves, backed by the PAICV. At the same time, Joana Rosa, the MpD’s candidate and former justice minister, is holding a concert with the band Pendrive in Monte Sossego, another neighbourhood. While I’m standing in the crowd, I hear people behind me say: ‘Come on, the concert’s almost over and the speech starts after this. Let’s go to the other concert now.’ With street vendors with drinks and food around the corner as part of the rival political campaigns, it’s a night out for many people: they run into acquaintances and catch up over the music.


There are two kinds of people in the crowd. Some wear party t-shirts and make it very clear who they’re here for and who they’ll vote for. The others come for the music and would rather not talk about their political preference. They tell me they’re afraid of repercussions. ‘If I say I’m voting for this one and the other party gets wind of it, I’m afraid they’ll obstruct me in other matters,’ one person says. That fear isn’t unusual: in

a 2024 Afrobarometer survey

, more than one in five Cape Verdeans said it was likely that powerful people could find out how they voted, despite the secret ballot. A few people at the concert tell me they won’t vote. Others are still undecided, but say it matters to them to use their vote. A few more say they’ll cast a blank ballot.


The band Corda do Sol plays on Rua Lisboa in Mindelo ahead of a speech by President José Maria Neves, 12 November 2026. Photo: Carmen Esselink


When I asked António Tavares to describe election season, he started much further back, before independence. A choreographer, dancer and researcher, Tavares is the artistic director of the Mindelo Cultural Centre and a co-founder of Bombu Mininu, a cultural space in São Vicente. He was a child when Cape Verde gained independence in 1975, and he says he has never belonged to a political party. According to Tavares, music once carried the dream of independence. Musicians, poets and thinkers imagined the country through lyrics before it existed. ‘Music is the material,’ he says. ’It’s our way of communicating. We are a sonic entity. Why music? Because we knew we were going to leave here. If we had to leave, we had to come up with a Morse code.’


To this day, music is one of the main ways Cape Verdeans communicate. Cape Verde’s historic World Cup debut this year came with its own anthem,

Nôs Óra Dja Txiga

, bringing together artists from across the islands. While the World Cup gave Cape Verdeans a song …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Two men sentenced for Khayelitsha church sexual assault
content:
On Easter Sunday in 2023, two young men stormed the Showers of Blessings Christian Church in Zion, in Site C carrying a gun and a knife and robbed the women congregants before sexually assaulting and raping them. Yamkela Jobo and Okuhle Beya were found guilty on all 21 charges and were sentenced to 25 years in prison by the regional court in Khayelitsha today.


Thembinkosi Fati, the secretary of South African Zionist Churches, said they welcome the sentencing of the two. “The guilty verdict was a victory on its own, given how cases like this one just disappear into thin air. It might not be exactly what we wanted, but it shows that the investigating officers and the state did a good job,” he said.


According to Fati, Jobo and Beya took advantage of loadshedding, and the fact that the women and children were alone in the church hall where they were sleeping.


Nolukholo Jezile, one of the church leaders, said that they would sleep at the church during Easter. “It’s clear that they planned the attacks on us, because they waited until all the men were gone and they stormed the church,” she said.


She commended the courage of the women of the church for overcoming their trauma. “It was not easy at all; we could have easily given up,” but they are still not able to go to church alone.


Community-based organisations supported the church during the trial, including

Amadoda Aqotho

 and Sidima Sam Gentlemen’s Organisation.


Amadoda Aqotho supported the church members during the trial.


The prosecutors told the court that the pair ordered the congregants to strip naked, robbed 19 women of their cellphones, and sexually assaulted two of them before fleeing.


One of the mitigating circumstances offered by the defence lawyer was that the two young men were abandoned by their parents.


“Not having a parent does not give an excuse to be a thief and a rapist. Instead, it should teach you to be independent. I was not aware that they were this young. The women that the accused assaulted are old enough to be their mothers and grandparents,” said Sabelo Zekevu, the chairperson of Amadoda Aqotho. He called on men to stop abuse and report cases of gender-based violence when they witness them.

title: South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity
content:
South Africa, Palestine and the Urgency of Solidarity

Address at a public meeting hosted by Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa at the Ellen Melville Centre in Auckland on Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Comrades, thank you for inviting me to return to Aotearoa. I bring you greetings of solidarity from Abahlali baseMjondolo, the shack dwellers’ movement of South Africa, which was formed in Durban in 2005 and now has more than 200 000 members across South Africa.

It is fifteen years since I was last here, in 2011, when we commemorated the thirtieth anniversary of the great protests against the Springbok rugby tour of 1981. I want to begin by remembering that history, and by thanking all the people of this country who stood with us against apartheid. People marched, confronted the police, and sometimes faced arrest and violence. You refused to allow the apartheid state to present itself as a normal member of the international community.

This was an outstanding example of international solidarity, and an example that we should seek to emulate in our solidarity with the people of Palestine.

In our movement we speak of living solidarity. This means solidarity that exists in action, not just in words. It means solidarity between people who recognise one another as equals.

Settler colonialism in South Africa and Israel

South Africa and Palestine are both countries that have been oppressed by settler colonialism. This is part of the reason for the long solidarity with Palestine among South Africans.

But there are important differences between these two forms of settler colonialism. In South Africa, the colonial system was organised around the dispossession of Africans from their land, the theft of their cattle and the exploitation of their labour. The economy depended on African workers in the mines, on the farms, in the factories and in the homes of white people. The settlers wanted the land, but they also wanted the labour of the people they had dispossessed.

Huge numbers of people were forced from their homes and land as African people were pushed into ‘reserves’, based on the system used to oppress Native Americans, and later into the ‘Bantustans’, the so-called ‘homelands’. The Bantustans were not just used to confine the African people on tiny bits of land. They were also central to the migrant labour system that ensured cheap labour for white capital and for white families in their homes.

African workers were forced by economic necessity to leave their families and communities to find work in the mines and cities. Many were compelled to live in single-sex hostels, separated from their families. Africans were wanted as workers but rejected as citizens with equal rights. They were systematically dehumanised. This system was maintained through the police, the army, prisons, torture and killing. Those who resisted were treated as criminals and terrorists.

When we look at Palestine today, we recognise many of these methods of oppression. We see a fundamentally racist settler colonial system in which there is ongoing dispossession of people from their land by the Israeli state and settlers. We see homes being demolished. We see communities separated from one another by walls, checkpoints and military restrictions. We see people who stand up against oppression being called ‘terrorists’ and subject to mass imprisonment, torture and murder.

The struggles against racism and for land are central to the struggle for freedom, both in South Africa and in Palestine. But there are also differences between apartheid in South Africa and oppression in Palestine.

While Palestinians have been exploited as workers, the fundamental drive of settler colonialism in Israel is to remove or destroy the Palestinian people rather than to exploit them for their labour.

In South Africa, the apartheid system required the continued presence of a large and hyper-exploited African workforce, while seeking to control, segregate and impoverish it. In Palestine, the settler-colonial project has involved the destruction of Palestinian communities, the removal of Palestinians from their land and the attempt to establish and maintain territorial and political control through their displacement.

The Nakba of 1948 forced hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from their homes. Many became refugees in other countries, and they and their descendants remain unable to return. The occupation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967 has brought …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Thirty Years On, Intersex Africans Set Their Own Agenda for Rights and Belonging
content:
It was a rare energy, fueled by our shared trials nd triumphs, and by stories that stretched beyond these walls. We, intersex activists from across Africa, came together, gathering on the shoulders of those who paved the way, held together by a promise that our voices would carry us far. Seeing the adoption of the Nairobi Declaration reminded me that our voices are now influencing regional conversations, policies and demands for justice.


We have come a long way. Years ago, people would laugh at you for raising intersex issues in Ghana; today, journalists call us to make documentaries.


On 26 October, we marked thirty years of Intersex Awareness Day. The day commemorates a

1996 protest

 by intersex activists against unnecessary, irreversible surgeries on intersex children and their demand that we decide what happens to our own bodies. Thirty years on, that is still our demand: that we decide. Many gains since then have been won on this continent. South Africa’s equality law has recognised intersex status since 2005. Kenya became the first African country to

count intersex people in a census

 in 2019, and its

Children Act 2022

 recognised intersex children in law. In 2023, the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights adopted

Resolution 552

, calling on states to end non-consensual surgeries, infanticide and abandonment. This year, Zimbabwe’s Minister of Justice

convened a high-level meeting

 on legal recognition, and South Africa’s Human Rights Commission now

guides parents towards alternatives to invasive procedures

.


We are also building  and expanding our spaces.


From 30 September to 2 October, intersex Africans gathered in Nairobi for the first-ever Africa Intersex Movement conference. Activists came from East, Southern, North and West Afric

a.

For the first time, intersex activists, community members, scholars, cultural workers, and allies from across Africa came together.

We told our stories in our own words and s

et our own agenda and demands. It was a community in communion and a platform to press for rights, protection and dignity.


We left with the Nairobi Declaration, whose ten demands range from legal recognition and an end to infanticide and non-consensual surgeries to equal access to healthcare, education and work, and a real say in decisions that affect us, alongside a call for an African intersex rights framework. Meeting openly, as gatherings like ours are criminalised across the continent, was itself a statement.


It mattered that we met in Kenya, whose census showed why being counted matters. Who a state refuses to count, it can pretend does not exist. Yet this win must be built on, because Kenya’s

Intersex Persons Bill, 2024

 has yet to

become law

.


Who decides who we are, and which children are protected?


During the conference, one question kept coming up. Who gets to decide who is intersex? There are dozens of intersex variations, and many people never know until they are tested. Yet the first response is often, “What shows you are intersex?” Demanding medical proof leaves the power to define us with medical and state systems, not with intersex people ourselves.


I hear the question, “What are you?” most often in hospitals, from family members and communities, where people feel entitled to question bodies they do not understand. Often, these probing questions determine whether you receive medical care or can use services freely accessible to others. It creates shame, fear and self-doubt, turning spaces meant to offer care and belonging into places of rejection.


The cost of not fitting is real.

Policy guidance

 from the Africa Intersex Movement and the UN Development Programme documents these harms across the continent. In Ghana, we have witnessed the same infanticide and abandonment of babies seen as a curse, children operated on to make them fit, and adults hiding their identities from their own families.


In that room, we listened and held space for one another. Every variation is unique, yet people hold fixed expectations of what an intersex person looks like. Intersex people must define who we are.


In Ghana, an opening and its limits


In Ghana, intersex people lack legal recognition and protection. Last year, with support from traditional leaders (queen mothers) and lawyers, we urged

the Constitution Review Committee

 to ban non-consensual surgeries and infanticide and recognise intersex people. The president’s white paper supported …

author: ROAPE
title: Life after Museveni, or Uganda beyond fear?
content:
Yusuf Serunkuma’s recent article,

Life after Museveni

, is an honest expression of a particular political mood in Uganda today: exhaustion. It is the mood of a country that has watched opposition leaders imprisoned, activists disappeared, lawyers forced into exile, protests crushed, elections manipulated and every apparent avenue for change closed one after another. Serunkuma is right to describe the fear. He is right that Museveni has systematically destroyed competing centres of power. He is right that Uganda is facing a political transition. Where we part ways is what he makes of these conditions.


He looks at a defeated and frightened people and concludes that we should prepare ourselves for Muhoozi. He calls this realism, prudence and a search for a peaceful transition. But there is another name for this political position: reformism born from despair. It is the argument that because the forces of liberation have been defeated repeatedly, we should negotiate with the successor of the very system that defeated them. It is understandable. It is also precisely the kind of conclusion that every long dictatorship eventually produces in those who have become exhausted by the struggle.


The most troubling part of Serunkuma’s argument is that he presents Muhoozi not as someone Uganda should choose, but as someone Uganda must learn to accommodate because the alternatives have supposedly been defeated. This turns political defeat into political destiny. The fact that

Museveni has imprisoned, exiled, killed or neutralised his opponents

 does not mean that his son has therefore acquired a legitimate claim to succeed him. It means that the old methods of resistance have encountered a powerful system and must be reorganised. The defeat of individuals is not the defeat of a people. A movement is not finished because its leaders are in prison. A revolution does not die because its first generation is defeated.


History is full of moments when the people appeared to have lost everything. South Africa provides perhaps the clearest example. Apartheid was not defeated because the apartheid state suddenly became reasonable, nor because Black South Africans discovered that the safest option was to accommodate the successor of white minority rule. Decades of repression, imprisonment, exile and killing had exhausted the liberation movement. Yet the people continued to organise. They built underground structures, trade unions, community organisations,

student movements and mass campaigns

. They persisted when victory looked impossible. The eventual political settlement gave South Africans something enormous: political power and the formal end of apartheid. But the settlement also left the deeper economic structure largely intact. Land ownership, wealth and productive power remained overwhelmingly concentrated in white hands. The political liberation was real, but the material liberation remained unfinished.


That unfinished business is now returning in different forms, including the xenophobia that has repeatedly erupted against African migrants living in South Africa. Xenophobia is not caused simply by the presence of foreigners. It grows in conditions of economic deprivation, unemployment and competition over resources in a society where the majority were promised liberation but did not receive anything close to an equal share of the economic power. A settlement that secured political peace while leaving the material foundations of inequality substantially intact produced a contradiction that later generations inherited.


This is why Serunkuma’s proposal should concern us. He is effectively asking Ugandans to make a similar bargain. Accept Muhoozi as the vehicle for a peaceful transition. Accept continuity because a rupture may frighten the West. Accept the son because the father has defeated everyone else. Accept the architecture of the old regime because dismantling it might produce instability. But what exactly are Ugandans being asked to preserve in exchange for this peace? The military structure? The patronage networks? The neoliberal economic order? The land question? The corruption? The constitutional violations? The concentration of political power? The relationship between the military and the state? If these things remain substantially intact, then what exactly has transitioned?


There is an even deeper contradiction in Serunkuma’s argument. He acknowledges that Muhoozi is already part of the machinery of …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.
