author: Rose Nneoma Abba
title: Labors of liberation
content:
Ricci Shryock’s

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 is marketed as an account of the women who helped win the 11-year guerrilla war for independence from Portuguese colonial rule in Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Shryock’s book delivers on that promise with hyperrealistic scenes that drop you into mangrove forests where female teenagers and young adults shoot and dodge bullets, manage makeshift clinics, become mothers, devise new cooking technology, teach, gossip, and boil water for breakfast. 

It also exposes prejudice that women in the struggle faced at the hands of their fellow African men. A funny scene in the book exemplifies both the prejudice and the women’s handling of it. Shortly after Joana Gomes, a nurse and the book’s protagonist, joins a new base, the commander, who is also her distant cousin, threatens her that if she gets hurt, he will have to kill her. She replies that “as a nurse. . . .  even you, if you are injured and no-one can carry you I can give this medicine to you [to kill you].” As Carmen Pereira, a prominent guerrilla fighter with the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), nurse, and later acting head of state, famously observed: “In Guinea-Bissau, we say that women must fight against two colonialisms. One against the Portuguese, the other against men.”

But beyond illustrating women’s agency in the struggle, the book also offers timely provocations on our relationship with nature, the labor that sustains revolutions, elite-led movements, and the individual costs of collective struggle.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is its exploration of how the PAIGC’s vision of a future state manifested in practice long before victory was formally declared. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 to achieve independence for Guinea and Cape Verde from Portuguese colonial rule. For the party, building for the future state was just as vital as tearing down Portuguese colonial rule. 

This state-building effort is most visible in the book’s heartwarming scenes of education. We witness it when Joana’s father goes out of his way to secure teachers for his daughters. And again when 11-year-old Joana and her friends are instructed by Amílcar Cabral to teach the other teenagers on a boat trip from Guinea-Bissau to Guinea-Conakry. We learn that the PAIGC built 156 primary schools during the war across liberated territories compared to 11 created under Portuguese neglect. We also see the PAIGC send young Guineans to the Soviet Union and Cuba to master guerrilla combat tactics as well as medicine, engineering, agronomy, and teaching for the nation they were bringing into existence.

The book takes a firm stand: The success of a liberation struggle depends on the viable, egalitarian alternative structure you build to ground your sovereignty while you fight the oppressive power. As Shryock writes in the introduction, it is “a story worth knowing as a universal lesson in the undeniable courage it takes to imagine a new world, the way creation rather than destruction is integral to that new world.” Through Joana’s story, Shryock holds a steady lens on women’s central role in designing and executing that vital labor of building Guinean sovereignty from the ground up.

Shryock opens the book with a scene that haunts the entire reading experience: 22-year-old Joana inside a dry-season mangrove forest, where she had gone to retrieve a commander who was recovering from a lung infection. “Gnarly, bare mangrove branches protruding from the muddy riverbed stare back at [Joana],” setting the tone for the book from the very first page. 

The land, its trees, and its waters are alive. At times angry, at times hungry, mostly gracious, and systematically exploited by the Portuguese regime. And it was precisely this ecological exploitation that precipitated the revolution. Cabral, the founder of the PAIGC, was an agronomist by training, and his radicalization took root while he was conducting an agricultural census commissioned by the United Nations and the colonial Portuguese government. There, he saw firsthand how Portuguese land policies and price controls were squeezing the life out of both the land and the people tilling it.

As the Guineans fought for the land, the land protected them. Whether it is Joana tripping over an exposed root and narrowly dodging a bullet or people abandoning their towns to seek shelter in the forest, “besides the Soviets and the Cubans, the land [proved] to be the liberation …

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Regional leaders say future of Aurora College campuses remains unclear
content:
For the last two years, Dana Fergusson has been asking Aurora College the same questions.


As chair of Thebacha Leadership Council, she wants to know what academic programs will be offered at the college’s Fort Smith and Inuvik campuses as the institution works toward becoming a polytechnic university.


She also wants to know how decisions about program locations are being made, what progress the college has made toward its transformation and how much the process has cost.


“Where are the measurable outcomes on where they are with getting closer to this polytech?” Fergusson said in an interview with APTN News. “And then tell me where the money went.”


The Thebacha Leadership Council is governed by local leadership from Salt River First Nation, Tthebatthie Denesuline Nation, Fort Smith Métis Council and Town of Fort Smith.


On Nov. 18, the council sent a second open letter to Aurora College’s board of governors, the minister of Education, Culture and Employment and all members of the legislative assembly.


The letter asks the college to make clear commitments on regional program delivery, including transparent criteria for deciding where programs are offered, an assessment of campus infrastructure and utilization, and in-person engagement with communities.


It also calls for a public plan to maintain and renew student residences.


The letter follows a presentation the council made to the board on Oct. 2.


“We just received their response letter from that, and it really felt like a nothing letter,” she said. “It had nothing of substance in it.”


The letters signed by Fergusson on behalf of the Town of Fort Smith, along with the Fort Smith Métis Council, Salt River First Nation and Thebacha Denesųłiné Nation.


Fort Smith questions the future of its campus


The concern has a longer history. A 2018 foundational review found the school needed to evolve to better meet the need of northerners and it proposed moving the college’s headquarters to Yellowknife as part of its transformation into a polytechnic university.


The Thebacha Campus has classrooms, laboratories, a library, computer labs and student housing. Fergusson said much of that infrastructure is being underutilized.


“We have this huge regional campus here, big classrooms, library, labs, computer labs, all of these resources sitting here empty, vacant,” she said.


Fergusson has started making videos to show residents what is available at the campus, including its student housing.


“Why are we talking about centralizing something in another region, another community to build all this infrastructure when you have it already sitting here in Fort Smith?” she said.


Fergusson said Fort Smith has gradually lost access to programs that once brought students to the community, including teacher education, social work and early childhood education. She said some of those programs have been absent for about eight years.


The impact, she argued, reaches beyond the classroom. Fewer students living in Fort Smith also means fewer customers for local businesses.


The uncertainty is particularly difficult for young people trying to plan their education.


Fergusson said high school students have asked how they are supposed to prepare for post-secondary studies when they do not know where a program will be delivered.


“You don’t know where it’s going to be, so you can’t plan for the community,” she said. “How do you plan for where you’re going to live?”


Students may need to arrange housing, employment and financial assistance well before a program begins. Without knowing where a course of study will be offered, Fergusson says, those decisions become harder to make.


Inuvik wants more in-person diploma programs


The concerns are not limited to Fort Smith.


In Inuvik, Mayor Peter Clarkson said the town wants more in-person programming at the Aurora College campus.


Clarkson said there’s a notable decline in student enrolment. He puts the numbers at about 165 students at one point, compared with roughly 25 more recently, and just half of that number graduating last year.


Clarkson says office and business administration courses have been offered in Inuvik for decades, alongside some upgrading and online learning.


But he wants the college to introduce more diploma programs that respond to employment needs across the Beaufort Delta and the wider territory.


His suggestions include information technology, recreation leadership, northern natural resource …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Even Hegseth’s Former Chief of Staff Says It’s Time for Him to Be Ousted
content:
The secretary’s former top aide blasted the Iran war as a “shitshow.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s former chief of staff has said that the secretary should resign over his handling of the Iran war and internal Pentagon affairs, adding to calls for Hegseth’s ousting after he narrowly survived an impeachment attempt earlier this month.

In an interview with Politico, former top Hegseth aide Joe Kasper said that the secretary has become obsessed with his ego and image, as well as his mission to drastically remake the Pentagon in his violent, white supremacist image. Hegseth’s focus on boosting himself and his “showmanship” are getting in the way of his “ability to be effective,” Kasper said.

Kasper, who was Hegseth’s chief of staff for the first three months of President Donald Trump’s current term, rattled off a list of what he feels are Hegseth’s failures. For one, the U.S. war on Iran, in which the U.S. has killed thousands of civilians in Iran, has been a “shitshow,” he said — a popular view even among some Republicans in Congress and in the administration.

The Iran War was a major focus of Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Kentucky) impeachment attempt earlier this month. Massie’s articles accused Hegseth of violating the law in waging the war without Congress’s approval while violating civilian protection laws both in strikes on Iran and in the U.S.’s boat strike campaign.

Massie’s impeachment articles narrowly failed, after several Democrats missed the vote, but Democrats are preparing to target him again when they take over Congress.

Meanwhile, Kasper also criticized Hegseth for gutting top leadership at the Pentagon, seemingly specifically targeting senior Black and female figures in the military.

“At almost every high-profile position, or every senior leader position, there’s a vacancy,” he said.

Those fired included three top Pentagon officials who were dismissed last year, during Kasper’s time in the Pentagon, over supposed leaks to the media. Kasper said there was no evidence that those officials had ever leaked any information at all — and Hegseth recently subjected dozens of members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests in order to seek out more alleged leakers.

Interestingly, Kasper seems to have been personally involved in those three officials’ ousting, even though he now says that there was no evidence of leaks. Last year, Politico reported that Kasper was a major player in their dismissals, done in “an attempt to consolidate power.” Kasper denied that claim, which came from sources familiar with the matter.

Kasper departed the Pentagon shortly after those dismissals, without any public bad blood between him and Hegseth, who sang his praises after he left.

Kasper also criticized Hegseth for a recent incident in which Hegseth and his staff were reprimanded for laughing at a Veterans Day ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier; “distractions” like his testosterone testing and supplement initiative; and his inability to work with other figures on Capitol Hill, like those in Congress.

“He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill,” Kasper said. “He’s napalmed them.”

He predicted that Hegseth is going to be ousted in one way or the other. “He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Forensic psychiatrist testifies in 1st-degree murder trial
content:
A man who allegedly killed his wife was not “completely psychotic” at the time she was shot, a forensic psychiatrist told an Iqaluit courtroom Monday.


 Dr. Maryana Kravtsenyuk testified Monday during the

first-degree murder trial of Danny Paul Eyaituk, an Iqaluit man charged with first-degree murder in the death of

his wife Annie Tracy Oqaituq, 36, who was found dead in their Sanikiluaq home on April 19, 2024.


The trial began June 9 in Sanikiluaq and continued until June 25 but stopped while

Kravtsenyuk was on the stand

 due to witness, judge, counsel and courtroom availability, defence lawyer Alan Regel said in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


Canada’s Criminal Code says a person cannot be held responsible for a crime committed while suffering from a mental health disorder that makes them incapable of appreciating the nature of the act.


Regel had asked Kravtsenyuk to prepare a report to assess whether Eyaituk could be found not criminally responsible.


The report established that Eyaituk has suffered from mental illness, including paranoia, since childhood and that he was addicted to cannabis and cocaine at the time of the alleged incident.


Drug use can be a contributing factor in sudden changes in mental health, Kravtsenyuk said in the report. Eyaituk’s mental health breakdowns were exacerbated by substance use and stress from conflict in his marriage, she added.


Late Monday morning, Regel asked Kravtsenyuk about Eyaituk’s state of mind on the day Oqaituq died.


“He did not appear completely detached from reality or profoundly confused regarding the consequences of the alleged act,” she replied, quoting from her report.


Eyaituk appeared alert in court, wearing a blue sweatshirt with a crucifix around his neck. His hair was tied back in a short ponytail.


The first half of the proceeding lacked an Inuktitut interpreter, for which Justice Susan Cooper apologized.


She scheduled final submissions for Tuesday morning, as long as an interpreter could go over the morning’s proceedings with Eyaituk on Monday afternoon.

author: Valerie Anne
title: Liv Hewson Opens Up to Drew Barrymore About the Early Parts of Their Career
content:
feature image photo by The Drew Barrymore Show/Ash Bean via Getty Images

Yellowjackets star Liv Hewson reunited with their former Santa Clarita Diet co-star Drew Barrymore on Drew’s talk show this week.

In the interview, they discuss all sorts of topics, including but not limited to Yellowjackets, of course. Drew presents Liv with gifts for what she thought was their engagement, but Liv reveals that actually they got married already. (There are actually really cute pics that pop up behind them of the couple as well in the clip, so you should check it out.) Drew’s now-wedding gifts are two beautiful candlesticks Drew said represents the two of them living together in harmony.

Liv talks about meeting their now-spouse on the set of Yellowjackets when they were AD, and recounts seeing them for the first time and having a “who IS that” moment immediately.

Drew shows Liv a clip of another of their Santa Clarita Diet co-stars, Skyler Gisondo, asking Liv to share dating advice, and their advice boils down to the fact that people want to feel safe and that should be a priority in any relationship, not just romantic. (This is not really here nor there but I could listen to Liv talk for hours. They have such a calming presence and such a thoughtful way of speaking and you can tell, even just from little clips and interviews, that they are a deeply intelligent person, both intellectually and emotionally, and I just really love hearing them talk about pretty much anything.)

The pair also talks about Molly Ringwald coming on Yellowjackets to play Van’s mother, and Liv says they really hit the jackpot when it came to fictional moms, having now had two legends (Molly and Drew herself) play their mom on television.

Liv also talks about how they felt like they were living in a “defensive crouch” for a long time; they came to the US to work when they were 20 and felt like they had to go back in the closet as nonbinary when they started working in Hollywood, but that Drew and the cast of Santa Clarita Diet became a soft place for them to land and they are really grateful to her for that.

It’s a very sweet interview and as sad as I am to see Yellowjackets come to an end, I’m really excited to see what Liv will get up to next, mostly because they are extremely talented and should be cast in whatever the hell they want, but also because, selfishly, I want to watch them on more press tours.

author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Guardians of the Buffalo: New bison-care guide supports efforts to bring iconic species home
content:
The three authors behind a new bison-care manual,

Guardians of the Buffalo

, speak about their book at ‘Fort Qu’Appelle, Sask.’ in September during this year’s Treaty 4 Gathering. From left: the book’s photographer Johane Janelle, and co-writers Wes Olson and Cody Spencer.

 Photo by Brittany Boschman


Under the bright September sun, school buses arrived and departed from the valley as an announcer’s voice carried across the powwow grounds.


Youth chatted, learned and moved between tipis for hands-on demonstrations during the 40th Annual Treaty 4 Gathering in Fort Qu’Appelle, Saskatchewan.


Inside one of the canvas tipis, a Buffalo hide lay near the entrance, where co-authors Wes Olson and Cody Spencer sat with photographer Johane Janelle to introduce a new book on bison care.


The presentation was part of a September book tour for

Guardians of the Buffalo: The Essential Guide to Bison Care

, which offers practical guidance for Indigenous communities, farmers and others interested in restoring and caring for bison herds


Spencer himself was first introduced to bison — and inspired to work as a rancher and herd manager — thanks to Olson’s first book,

Portraits of the Bison

, which was co-written with Janelle, his spouse.


“I just caught the bug,” Spencer recalled, “and I just had to figure out ways to get involved with the species.”


He said the book grew out of the questions he and Olson have received from people interested in starting their own bison herds.


“One of the most frequent questions I’ve had during that time was from people who want to get into the industry: How do I start?” Olson said. “Where do I even begin?”


The Fort Qu’Appelle event took place on Sept. 17, during the

annual gathering

 to honour the 1874 treaty’s spirit and intent, bringing communities together to celebrate culture and share teachings with the next generations. Youth from surrounding communities attended the week-long gathering for its education days.


Decades of bison stewardship


Olson spent 32 years working in national parks, much of that time focused on bison management and establishing new wild populations. Spencer is a bison rancher from southwest Alberta who has managed several herds in Alberta and Texas.


“We’ve also been in the bison industry, raising bison in captivity for a long time,” Olson said. “Between us, I think we calculated 87 years of bison stewardship.”


Spencer grew up on a farm where his family raised grain and cattle. He said his lack of experience with bison initially allowed him to approach the animals without bringing assumptions about cattle management into his work.


“I didn’t have direct experience with bison, which can be a benefit for a lot of people,” Spencer said. “You’re not coming into management with preconceptions about how you need to be managing cattle and applying that to buffalo.”


He said his work has focused on finding management practices that benefit both the animals and the land.


READ MORE:


In Manitoba, a growing herd of bagwaji-bizhikiwag offers lessons in community


“We’re just always committed to finding out what are the best ways that we can manage these animals and caretake them for their own health,” Spencer said, “but also the health of the land.”


The book is intended to help readers understand the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd. Its opening chapter includes a questionnaire to help readers consider the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd.


“This is a manual,” Spencer said. “This is

the

 manual.”


The remaining chapters combine technical information about bison management with cultural, ecological and conservation perspectives. Topics include animal care, fencing, water systems, handling facilities, herd management and land restoration. 


“There’s a lot that you need to know, and so it’s all in the book,” Spencer said.


One section of the book compares the physical characteristics of wood and plains buffalo, helping readers understand how to tell the two types apart. It also explains why maintaining genetic integrity is important when establishing and managing herds.


Guardians of the Buffalo

 explains differences between wood and plains bison, including why preserving their genetic integrity is important.

Image courtesy International Buffalo Relations Institute

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Family Caregivers Month: The Economic Burden of Unpaid Care
content:
Every November, National Family Caregivers Month recognizes the millions of Americans who provide care to their loved ones. Caregivers are adult children, spouses, partners, and other loved ones who complete daily tasks and maintain their quality of life. While caregiving is often an expression of love and family responsibility, it also comes with high financial, physical, and emotional costs that frequently go unrecognized.

More than 63 million Americans provide ongoing care for adults or children with complex medical conditions or disabilities. Of these, 59 million care for adults. Around 10% of U.S. adults are caregivers for parents aged 65 or older, while another 3% care for an aging spouse or partner.

The financial burden is particularly pronounced among lower-income households. Among adults with an aging parent, spouse, or partner, 39% of those with lower incomes identify as caregivers, compared with 23% of middle-income adults and 16% of upper-income adults. For caregivers whose household income is less than $40,000, nearly one-third of their income goes toward out-of-pocket expenses related to their loved ones’ needs.

The financial demands of caregiving can be substantial. Every year, $1 trillion in family caregiving services goes unpaid. Housing and household needs account for the largest share of expenses, at 42%, with home modifications for safety making up 29%, and 37% going to insurance premiums, co-pays, and other medical expenses not covered by insurance.

Yet 65% of working caregivers experience work-related disruptions. These can include needing time off and finding extra work to cover these expenses. These disparities also vary dramatically across racial and ethnic minority groups and by region.

These financial burdens are not distributed equally across racial and ethnic groups. AAPI caregivers report an average cost of $16,716. Black caregivers spend a high share of their household income, averaging 52%, while Hispanic and Latinx communities report the greatest financial strain among the racial and ethnic groups surveyed by AARP. By comparison, White caregivers spend about 24% of their household income on caregiving.

Regionally, caregivers in the Mid-Atlantic spend twice as much on average as caregivers in the West North Central region, reflecting the cost-of-living crisis. However, costs are not the only issue to consider as we reflect on the holistic effort of caregiving.

Beyond these financial costs, caregiving remains a deeply gendered responsibility. Women are more likely than men to identify as caregivers. In the U.S., 28% of women with aging parents or spouses or partners consider themselves caregivers, compared with only 23% of men. Forty-seven percent of women, versus 30% of men, experience a negative impact on their emotional well-being, and 38% of women experience negative impacts on their health while serving as caregivers for their loved ones. Outside formal caregiving, women provide most informal caregiving, often becoming hands-on health providers, care managers, care advocates, companions, and decision-makers.

As we recognize National Family Caregivers Month, it is important to acknowledge not only the dedication of caregivers but also the financial sacrifices and inequalities they face. Caregiving is rooted in love, but it is also sacrificial. If you or anyone you know is serving as a caregiver, show them a little more love this month so they know they are cared for.

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: 6- Cuttings will regrow – Sitting-in for Grandmother Cottonwood
content:
On July 27th, 2026 the U.S. government and Fisher industries cut down three ancient cottonwood trees in a small town called Lochiel, Arizona in order to build not just one but two border walls. This area is the habitat of the endangered Mexican Wolf as well as jaguars, bears, foxes and many other bizarre, beautiful bugs and animals. It is also the home of the Tohono O’odham people, important to many indigenous tribes on both sides of the border. When the three grandmother cottonwoods were cut, one brave comrade stood in front of construction equipment, preventing the destruction of the last ancient tree and the construction of the border wall. In that last tree, we began our tree sit. With the support of hundreds of activists, the land owners, nearby towns and tribes, and even the local sheriff department, we halted construction of the walls for 75 days.

For 75 days, activists sat in the remaining cottonwood as ground support grew into a sprawling camp. It was the first tree sit to stop border wall construction and was briefly the first binational tree sit in history, with a sit erecting on the Mexican side for three days in August. During these 75 days, O:shad camp, jaguar in O’odham, held morning ceremony in the easement, the road which enforced the border. Ceremony frequently extended to effectively halt all construction vehicles for the day, or days at a time. People fell in love, they danced in the mud, cooked communal meals, all while defending the land. Utopia felt nearby.

Then, on October 5th, hundreds of border patrol officers, accompanied by turning point usa, invaded O:shad camp. They cut down the grandmother cottonwood and forcibly removed the tree sitter without a proper extraction team, risking her life. Activists on the ground circled the trunk to protect the tree and continue their resistance against the wall. More than 10 activists were arrested and many more brutalized. Though on private property and with no warrant, they ransacked the camp and destroyed our belongings.

Indigenous and non-white activists were singled out and beaten much worse than white comrades. Border Patrol violently pushed, pulled and dragged, but also kneeled on throats, punched eyes, pushed skin into barbed wire. They specifically targeted our medic (who is Indigenous) to be violently dragged, beaten, and arrested. They prevented our media team from capturing what happened, while escorting Turning Point USA to film the day in order to spread their right wing propaganda.

The next day, as Border Patrol expanded their boundaries further into private property to make way for the wall, five more of us were taken, and lawyers were unable to find them in the system while border patrol ignored calls from their lawyers, friends and family.

A day later, my comrade locked herself to a cement truck and stayed in a stress position without food or water for 7 hours while Border Patrol covered her with an emergency blanket despite the hot climate. One officer told her and the other officers that they should drive her to the middle of nowhere where no one would be able to hear her scream. They began to move the vehicle with her still above the tire; we all thought she would be killed. Two comrades who ran towards her, worried for her life, were tackled, brutalized, and arrested – one was sexually assaulted during her arrest. Finally they brought in an expert extractor who took her out of lockdown and she was taken to detention and then federal prison. She is now facing federal assault charges.

The rest of us were shot with pepper balls, tear gassed, leaving us vomiting, injured, bruised and emotionally exhausted. After the tree sitter was removed from the grandmother tree in Lochiel, a comrade reinstated the sit on the mexico side. Cut off from ground support by border patrol, she went over two days without food or water. When mexican firefighters and Fisher construction workers went to pull her out, she free climbed further up the tree. They destroyed her platform and life sustaining materials, leaving her to perch in the cottonwood branches without a platform or supplies. She suffered dehydration and starvation in high heat but still managed to keep a backpack on her, which she filled with clippings of the Abuela tree so that no matter what happened, the trees offspring could be replanted.

The following day the wall continued.

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.


Read our

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

author: Joshua Davis, Whitney K. Taylor
title: Federal Government Is Targeting Officials Who Are Trying to Hold ICE Accountable
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.


In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the

House Judiciary


Committee

 and the

Department of Justice

 (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.


House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent

report

 that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.


Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.


“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”


The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “

Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives

” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


The DOJ, in a June 18

press release

 announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”


Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.


Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”


These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s

Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors

 who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.

author: Christopher Read
title: Letters from 1914 reveal worry that Shoal Lake water rights would cripple Winnipeg aqueduct
content:
A century-old exchange of letters between senior government officials is at the heart of a $2 billion lawsuit alleging Indigenous water rights were sacrificed to ensure Winnipeg could draw its drinking water from

Shoal Lake

.


In 1914, Ontario deputy minister of lands, forests and mines Aubrey White warned federal Indian Affairs deputy superintendent general Duncan Campbell Scott that honouring existing legislative commitments to First Nations could “cripple” Winnipeg’s proposed aqueduct project.


The letters were uncovered by a historian hired by lawyer Julian Falconer’s firm.


“Completely out of sight of the First Nations, completely in secret, the deputy minister in a letter that we now have, says, if we follow through on this it would cripple, and that’s the word he used, cripple the Winnipeg water project,” says Falconer.


Falconer’s firm is representing Iskatewizaagegan (Shoal Lake) No. 39 Independent First Nation in litigation heading to trial against the City of Winnipeg and Ontario.


A statement of claim filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in 2024, alleges ecological, cultural and financial impacts resulting from Winnipeg’s aqueduct intake in Shoal Lake and seeks $2 billion in damages.


In a letter responding to White’s warning, Scott agrees that White has raised “important” points, but recommends that “we should say nothing about water or fisheries, but leave those questions to be decided as the cases arise.”


The following year, Ontario passed legislation that in effect eliminated the issue White had raised concerns about. The legislation governed reserve lands in Treaty 3 territory, and removed a provision from an 1894 agreement between Ontario and Canada that had recognized certain waters and lakebeds between projecting headlands as part of First Nations reserves.


Lawyer Julian Falconer at a presentation for Shoal Lake No.39 citizens. Photo: Christopher Read/APTN.


In its statement of defence, the city of Winnipeg denies Ontario altered the law for Winnipeg’s benefit, arguing the changes arose from a separate dispute.


The lawsuit also points to a provision in a 1913 Ontario Order in Council approving  Winnipeg’s Shoal Lake aqueduct that requires compensation be made to “all private parties whose lands or properties may be taken, injuriously affected or in any way interfered with.”


In 2019, before filing Shoal Lake 39’s lawsuit, Falconer asked the court for a ruling on whether the provision applied to the First Nation.


“We applied to a court to ask a simple question: Does Iskatewizaagegan number 39 constitute a private party for the purposes of this compensation provision? The court answered yes,” says Falconer.


The ruling did not determine whether Winnipeg is liable for the damages the First Nation alleges.


Winnipeg acknowledges the compensation provision exists but denies causing the damage alleged.


In its statement of defence, the city says other dams and overfishing are responsible for many of the environmental changes Shoal Lake 39 has identified.


Not so, says Shoal Lake 39 Chief Gerald Lewis.


According to Lewis, the aqueduct intake doesn’t just take in water.


“It also includes fish, and the fish eggs,” says Lewis.


Iskatewizaagegan litigation committee chair Rachel Green at the edge of Shoal Lake. Photo: Christopher Read/APTN.


For Iskatewizaagegan citizen Rachel Green, the lawsuit is also an opportunity to reclaim a history she believes has been largely told by others.


She’s the chair of her community’s litigation committee and a graduate student writing a master’s thesis at the University of Winnipeg. Her research is closely tied to Falconer’s team’s investigation into how Winnipeg’s aqueduct project came to be.


“My whole motivation for doing this research is because the Iskatewizaagegan water issue, our story, has only been told from the perspective of the government, a colonial perspective, and has never, ever been told from our perspective,” says Green.


Her concern about the issue is also rooted in deeply held beliefs about the water of Shoal Lake.


“When it comes to the water coming to Winnipeg from Shoal Lake, it’s used as a commodity, as a source to make revenue from,” says Green, “whereas us that are from Shoal Lake, having that spiritual bond and connection to the water, water is a relative.”


She is alluding to Winnipeg’s practice of diverting dividends generated by its water utility to subsidize the city’s general revenue.

author: Rizomatica
title: Seis en huelga en la cárcel, en sus casas un gran nudo en las gargantas
content:
Revisando hoy las redes sociales me entero de que seis de los dieciocho condenados por el caso Molino Grollmus iniciaron una huelga de hambre seca en la cárcel de Biobío. Uno de ellos es José Melgarejo Calbullanca, a quien represento. La noticia me golpea, porque de todo lo que he visto de la cárcel aplicada a los mapuche, lo más duro, sin duda, es la huelga. Duro para el preso y duro para su familia, porque no solo deja de alimentarse el huelguista: les aseguro que la garganta de sus mujeres y de sus madres difícilmente traga, de solo saber que allá adentro los suyos están dispuestos a morir por justicia.


Por:

Daniela Sierra

, Abogada.


Una huelga no es una medida de presión, ni una puesta en escena. Sin agua, el cuerpo empieza a apagarse en días, no en semanas. A eso no se llega por cálculo; se llega cuando ya no quedan puertas que golpear.


¿Qué piden? Lo primero, que se anule un juicio en que se condenó con testigos que nadie vio. Así de simple. En el caso de José, dos de los testigos con identidad reservada nunca pisaron la sala: la Fiscalía renunció a ellos, y lo que supuestamente dijeron lo contaron unos policías, de oídas. Los jueces no les vieron la cara, la defensa no pudo hacerles una sola pregunta, y con eso a José le dieron más de ochenta años de cárcel.


La Convención Americana garantiza a todo acusado el derecho a interrogar a quien lo acusa (art. 8.2 f), y el Código Procesal Penal obliga a condenar solo con la prueba rendida en el juicio (art. 340). La Corte Interamericana ya se lo dijo a Chile en 2014, y en un caso mapuche, Norín Catrimán: no se puede condenar únicamente o en grado decisivo con testigos de identidad reservada. Y eso era con testigos que al menos declararon. Aquí, ni eso.


Tampoco se pide impunidad, como tanto les gusta repetir. Si la Corte Suprema anula, la ley ordena un juicio nuevo (art. 386 del Código Procesal Penal), esta vez con las reglas del juego, y si la prueba no alcanza, la absolución. Eso se resuelve el jueves en la Corte Suprema, que es donde se tiene que resolver; no en La Moneda ni en ninguna reunión con ministros.


Lo segundo que piden huele, para algunos, a privilegio: un módulo para presos mapuche en Biobío, que puedan entrar la machi y el logko, comer su comida, vestir su ropa, hablar chedungun, tener trabajo y talleres. Privilegio, dicen, como si rezar, comer lo propio y hablar la lengua de la abuela fueran lujos de hotel.


Pero el Convenio 169 de la OIT, vigente en Chile desde 2009, obliga a proteger las prácticas espirituales de los pueblos indígenas (art. 5), a considerar su cultura cuando se les impone una pena (art. 10) y a darles una salud que respete su propia medicina (art. 25). Las Reglas Mandela de Naciones Unidas exigen respetar las creencias de cada preso, ofrecerle educación y trabajo, y permitirle practicar su fe con alguien de su propia tradición (reglas 2, 4, 65 y 66). Y el Reglamento de Establecimientos Penitenciarios dice algo que debería bastar: fuera de los derechos que la condena le quita, el preso conserva la misma condición jurídica que cualquier ciudadano libre (art. 2).


Lo más curioso es que nada de esto es nuevo. Gendarmería informó a la Corte de Apelaciones de Temuco que su módulo de comuneros tiene encomiendas con alimentación culturalmente pertinente, acceso a lawen, medicina tradicional y machi, y talleres de trabajo. Es decir, lo que se pide en Biobío ya existe en Temuco. Entonces la pregunta no es por qué regalarles un privilegio, sino por qué un mapuche pierde derechos según la cárcel a la que lo manden.


El Estado tiene a estos seis hombres bajo su custodia y responde por su vida. Pero la salida no está en sentarse a mirar cuánto aguanta el cuerpo. Está en que la Corte Suprema aplique el estándar que ya se le impuso a Chile.


Lo que piden es juicio justo, no impunidad. Lo mínimo, eso que la humanidad ya pagó con demasiada sangre. Y que, mientras tanto, allá afuera, sus mujeres, sus madres, puedan volver a respirar a la espera del futuro abrazo de los suyos.


*Enviado a la radio


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Ariadna Wdowiak
title: Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera, segunda edición
content:
Movilización de jubiladxs el 24 de septiembre del año 2025. Fotografía: Andrés Manrique (ANRed).


Muchas veces, el primer objetivo de la represión es inducir temor para desairar primero y después desarticular las resistencias populares. Contra ello, ANRed libera la segunda edición de

 “Primeros Auxilios en contexto de manifestación callejera”

, una recopilación de medidas y cuidados básicos a la hora de hacernos de las calles.


Saber de primeros auxilios en contextos donde predomina la violencia puede ser un aporte muy valioso, que tiene en sí mismo un efecto tranquilizador. Además, las personas que no recibieron entrenamiento en primeros auxilios suelen dudar al momento de actuar, o tienen miedo de ayudar por falta de seguridad para recordar las maniobras.


Si bien no frenará la decisión política de mutilar, intentamos generar conciencia sobre la importancia de cuidar nuestros cuerpos, con los que trabajamos y sostenemos nuestras vidas y las de otros, y enfatizamos en aquellas cosas que sí podemos hacer para cuidarnos. En particular, esta guía está orientada a la prevención.


Recordamos que los cuidados son siempre una tarea colectiva, históricamente menospreciada pero fundamental para cualquier resistencia. Este es nuestro aporte.


Estamos hace 32 años en las calles, practicando la comunicación alternativa, comunitaria y popular. Acompañando las luchas siempre, mostrando lo que otros omiten y silencian.

author: Natalia Viana
title: Mais mulheres ministras, menos orgias no Supremo
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Xeque na Democracia, enviada toda segunda-feira, 12h. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui.


“Cadê nossas norueguesas!? Rs”, “Vamos ter que mandar alguém lá buscar”, “Eu busco. Mande contato”. 


“Emprestei quarto do lado para ministro com 5 menina”. 


“Sobrou uma Ukraniana aqui. Gatinha. Vamos fazer a guerra no Brasil” “Eba. Nessa guerra tem que sobrar alguma refugiada pra mim”.


“Tipo gostosa! Vc conhece o q a gente gosta. Me manda as fotos. Tem q ser novidade.”


Todos esses diálogos foram proferidos por homens de poder da nossa República, ou seus assistentes mais fiéis. 


A primeira foi enviada pelo senador Irajá (PSD-TO), filho da ex-ministra da agricultura Kátia Abreu, logo depois de conhecer o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro pessoalmente, em 11 de outubro de 2024. Segundo

reportagem

 de Lauro Jardim, seguiram-se um convite para uma viagem a Dubai e um camarote para o jogo Brasil X Colômbia no estádio Mané Garrincha, uma festinha em um imóvel de luxo em Saint Tropez, na França, e muito lobby pela aprovação de um PL que libera jogos de azar no Brasil, incluindo cassinos, bingos e jogos do bicho (Irajá é o relator). 


A segunda, pelo mordomo do banqueiro, após uma noitada preparada por ele em um triplex no Itaim Bibi na noite de 28 de fevereiro de 2025 para o ministro do STF Kássio Nunes,

detalhada

 pela revista Piauí. Vorcaro alistou dois motoristas, um chefe de cozinha, um mordomo e uma faxineira para a festa privada. Pagou R$10 mil para uma das cinco meninas. Cinco dias antes, Nunes Marques havia desempatado na Segunda Turma do STF um julgamento que ameaçava uma carteira de precatórios no valor de mais de R$10 bilhões do Master, pertencentes à destilaria Alcídia. 


O terceiro diálogo demonstra como Vorcaro tratava as “agenciadas” pela empresa do qual foi sócio oculto, segundo excelente

reportagem

 de Natália Portinari, do Uol. As jovens – de 19 anos para frente – eram chamadas de “creche” e “escravas” e usadas para “confiança e surubinha privê” junto com políticos e juízes ou para “eventos de volume” maiores, cujos convidados eram invariavelmente homens de poder. O ano era 2024; havia dois anos que o país da refugiada urcaniana de 19 anos estava em guerra e naquele ano morreram pelo menos 67 mil pessoas no conflito. A menina fugiu durante 14 horas de ônibus para sair do país, enquanto a mãe enviava áudios de bombardeios na sua cidade natal e pedia que ela não retornasse. 


O quarto recado foi escrito pelo então sócio do senador da República Flávio Bolsonaro a uma agenciadora quando tentava marcar uma “outra festinha igual a do grand hyatt”, que contaria com a presença do ex-candidato à presidência – o sócio o chamava de “meu filho”. As festinhas registradas na reportagem do PlatôBR ocorreram no começo de 2022 em um dos quartos mais privativos, cuja diária chega a cerca de R$3 mil, com varanda e vista panorâmica para a Lagoa de Marapendi. Flávio Bolsonaro era, na época, filho do presidente da República. 


Ao longo dos últimos meses, quem acompanha notícias teve o desprazer de ler repetidos conteúdos de teor semelhante, provenientes do celular do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro ou de outros vazamentos, como o do ex-sócio de Flávio Bolsonaro.


A lambança do caso Master é tamanha – apenas na semana passada, relatórios da PF

detalharam

 relações do banqueiro com 4 ministros, 40% da corte – que a sua característica mais aberrante tem passado batido. Aquela que faz com que meu estômago embrulhe. 


Que faz com que 51,5% da população brasileira tenha nojo dos homens que nos governam.

 


Não exagero. Em grupos de discussão que participo, uma integrante mandou a seguinte proposição: “Eu tenho uma proposta de movimento cívico: nomear mulheres para o STF. Temos garantia que essa simples recomendação traria um retorno claro: diminuir as orgias envolvendo membros do Supremo.” A mensagem é absolutamente razoável, mas rendeu apenas alguns “kkk”s num grupo majoritariamente formado por homens; foi esquecida rapidamente. 


Ela vem do mesmo tipo de revolta que eu sinto, que muitas de nós sentimos durante este ciclo noticioso, ao perceber que, para os homens, o poder é associado a sexo, e sexo é associado a “ter”, “consumir” e “controlar” mulheres.

Não existe poder masculino, ainda hoje, dissociado do controle a corpos femininos. 


Mulher é propina. Buceta é propina. Buceta europeia é mais propina ainda.


E isso é tão …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado público de José Melgarejo Calbullanca, PPM del caso Grollmus en Huelga de Hambre
content:
Pu Machi, pu Lonko, pu Wuenen, pu Werken, pu Weichave, pu Kona.

Rekuluwaiñ ka yavuluwaiñ ni ta tuvachi weichan.

Inche José Melgarejo Calbullanca, tañi lov Lleu-lleu mapu, comunidad Nicolás Calbullanca, territorio lavkenche, Lago Lleu-lleu.

Doy a conocer mi situación como preso político mapuche, recluído en la cárcel CP Biobío, llevando ya 2 años y medio, de una condena de 7 años y medio y de otra por el llamado Caso del Molino Grollmus, por el cual fui juzgado por el Tribunal de Cañete y condenado a 86 años de prisión, juicio al que actualmente estamos apelando en la Corte Suprema, exigiendo su anulación y del cual me declaro, como lo he hecho anteriormente, inocente de los hechos que se me imputaron y por los que fuí condenado a esta altísima condena.

Por este motivo es que junto a otros ppm, hemos decidido iniciar una Huelga de Hambre de carácter indefinido, exigiendo 3 puntos principales:

Kiñe: Nulidad del juicio viciado y racista que nos condenó.

Epu: La creación de un módulo comuneros mapuche en el Cp Biobío.

Por esto hago un llamado a las comunidades, territorios, organizaciones, Hogares Mapuche, Estudiantes y a los demás prisioneros políticos, a que nos apoyen en este proceso. Estaremos eternamente agradecidos de su apoyo fraterno.

También aprovecho de agradecer a todas las personas que me han apoyado, a mi como a los demás ppm, todo este tiempo.

Desde acá me siento con alto newen para seguir luchando por nuestros justos derechos como pueblo nación Mapuche.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Comienza el juicio contra el policía que mató a un docente chofer de una aplicación de viajes
content:
A partir del próximo miércoles 25 de noviembre comenzará el debate oral ante el Tribunal en lo Criminal 1 de La Matanza, en San Justo, contra el policía Matías Alejandro Vizgarra Riveros, un efectivo de la Policía Bonaerense (UTOI), imputado por homicidio calificado criminis causa y robo calificado por el uso de armas del maestro Cristian Pereyra, ocurrido el 15 de marzo de este año. La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria (CPM) y el Centro de Profesionales por los Derechos Humanos (Ceprodh) participan del expediente como particulares damnificados en representación de la familia Pereyra. En los últimos días casi un centenar de organizaciones de derechos humanos, sociales y sindicales solicitaron ser tomados en la causa como amicus curiae, y que el juicio sea público, con garantía efectiva de la publicidad de todo el debate.


Pereyra era docente de una escuela técnica y como muchos de sus compañeros y compañeras no llegaba a fin de mes. La noche de su muerte estaba realizando viajes en la plataforma de Didi y fue así que subió a su auto el policía Vizgarra Riveros, que se hizo pasar por pasajero, le robó el auto y lo terminó asesinando de cinco disparos por la espalda, para luego irse a trabajar “como si nada hubiera pasado”. Con estas palabras, Brenda Pereyra había contado a ANDAR la secuencia en la cual este policía bonaerense mató a su hermano en la autopista Presidente Perón, mano a Ezeiza. “Lo hizo con su arma reglamentaria, aunque estaba fuera de servicio, por eso queremos saber cuál es la responsabilidad estatal en este caso”, agregó.


Las hermanas del maestro asesinado, Brenda y Victoria, consideran que aún falta develar la red de encubrimiento del caso. Como botón de muestra, exigen saber con quiénes se comunicó el policía que le quitó la vida a Cristian.


En el escrito de elevación a juicio el fiscal Adrián Arribas afirmó que “en cuanto al aspecto probatorio en concreto que, tanto la materialidad ilícita como la autoría, y participación del imputado, se encuentra debidamente acreditada con la certeza que este estadio procesal requiere, según resulta de mi sincera convicción y en base a los elementos probatorios”. En su dictamen, detalló los testimonios, las imágenes de cámaras de seguridad públicas y privadas, los informes de balística, de telefonía celular y de la aplicación Didi, y el resultado de la autopsia.


Vizcarra Riveros tiene 23 años y es integrante de la Unidad Táctica de Operaciones Inmediatas (UTOI). Para describir lo sucedido, el fiscal Arribas expresó que “en ejecución de un designio previamente orientado al desapoderamiento ilegítimo, el imputado generó las condiciones para consumar el ilícito patrimonial, abusando de la confianza de la víctima en la relación contractual temporaria previamente asumida por ambos. Fue entonces cuando, con pleno dominio de la situación y aprovechando esa relación que lo unía momentáneamente a Cristian Eduardo Pereyra, Vizgarra Riveros desplegó una conducta violenta de máxima intensidad, dirigiendo contra aquél una agresión letal”. La fiscalía considera que “el ataque, lejos de constituir un exceso o una reacción improvisada, se inscribió dentro de la lógica del plan criminal, teniendo por finalidad inmediata neutralizar cualquier resistencia y, de modo mediato, evitar la posterior identificación del autor”.


Familiares y compañeros del profesor se movilizaron junto al Suteba La Matanza hasta la Fiscalía que lleva la causa para realizar una serie de planteos. Las hermanas pidieron que sea investigado en profundidad el celular del policía. Ellas consideran que hay evidencia de que borró mensajes a un compañero del hospital Evita a las seis de la mañana y a las nueve, preguntando si había llegado un herido de bala, y luego ese mensaje no aparece.


Cristian Pereyra tenía 39 años, una hija de tres llamadas Olivia y daba clases en las escuelas 8 y 10 de La Matanza. Como el sueldo no le alcanzaba, comenzó a hacer viajes con su auto para la app Didi.


La lucha por el esclarecimiento del caso está acompañada por sindicatos docentes y partidos de izquierda, cuyos referentes señalan que el profesor se ha convertido en un emblema de la precarización salarial que afecta a los trabajadores y trabajadoras de la educación, así como del gatillo fácil que impera a manos de la Policía Bonaerense, y del todo el país. En los últimos días casi un centenar de organizaciones de derechos humanos, sociales y sindicales solicitaron ser tomados en la causa como amicus curiae …

author: Darío Aranda
title: Mapuches defienden el territorio, mientras la política de Estado es negar los derechos indígenas
content:
Por Susana Lara


Desde Río Negro


La ocupación tradicional indígena en tierras fiscales es una fuente permanente de conflictos en la provincia de Río Negro, a pesar de que tiene cuarenta años una ley específica que contempla la protección de la población rural originaria. En el centro de la provincia, en plena estepa, la cuarta generación de una familia mapuche fue despojada de la posesión de un campo de mil hectáreas por la Dirección Provincial de Tierras, órgano local que administra y adjudica las tierras fiscales, pero no resuelve sobre territorios indígenas, según la legislación vigente.


Todo en un contexto donde

el Senado Nacional aprobó la llamada "Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada"

, que mantiene límites para la compra de empresarios extranjeros pero

facilita los desalojos, donde comunidades indígenas y familias campesinas serán las más perjudicadas

.


Un siglo de presencia mapuche


Vicente Maliqueo y Francisca Coñohuepán se asentaron a principios del siglo XX en el paraje Guada Niyeu, a mitad de camino entre la ciudad de Fiske Menuco (General Roca), al norte, y Sierra Colorada, al sureste. Allí nacieron sus hijos y vivieron de la cría de animales. Con el tiempo levantaron una ruka (hogar) de adobe, crecieron los álamos y ampliaron las pircas (corrales de piedra), todo cerca de una vertiente de agua dulce. Su hijo Francisco Eufemio y su nieto Vicente sostuvieron la ocupación tradicional de esa fracción del territorio hasta el final de sus días, ocurridas en 2022 y 2021 respectivamente.


Ahora, el Estado provincial desconoció a sus descendientes y otorgó la tierra a un tercero ajeno al Pueblo Mapuche, un empleado público radicado en Cipolletti. En concreto, no permiten que la familia originaria ingrese a su territorio. La decisión es una práctica estatal históricamente ejercida en contra de la gente mapuche y los criollos pobres, en violación a la

Ley Integral del Indígena (2287)

 vigente desde 1988.


La parcela de mil hectáreas es parte de una fracción fiscal de 12.500 hectáreas, sin mensura ni planos aprobados todavía, según el catastro público oficial. Gran parte de esa tierra fiscal está dentro del área de permiso de exploración minera de GRG Resources Corp, proyecto de oro, cobre y plata como consta en la última versión del Catastro Minero e informa la propia empresa.


Foto: María e Hilda Maliqueo


La maquinaria administrativa


Eufemio Maliqueo nació en 1921 en Guada Niyeu. Formó familia con Matilde Ángel. Cuando ya tenían varios hijos, en 1960 se formalizó el inicio del trámite de reconocimiento de 1250 hectáreas ante la Dirección de Tierras y Colonias, según consta en la copia del expediente administrativo al que se accedió para esta nota. Con el correr de los años, se sumó a la petición su hijo Vicente.


Recién en 1984 la Provincia le otorgó un reconocimiento formal por mil hectáreas, cuando tanto él como su compañera tenían 64 años. En 2007 una inspección de Tierras vuelve a constatar la presencia del padre e hijo en el lugar, en un predio totalmente alambrado, con hacienda propia. Al año siguiente, la Provincia les otorgó el Permiso Precario de Ocupación (PPO), como si el anterior no existiera.


Luego del fallecimiento de su abuelo y su tío, en 2022, José Luis Llarenas Maliqueo se presentó formalmente ante las autoridades de la Dirección de Tierras para continuar la ocupación del campo conservando la marca y señal para los animales. El responsable del organismo le confirmó la recepción del pedido. Inmediatamente comenzó a hacer presentaciones en ese mismo expediente Pablo Melinguer, de Cipolletti, manifestando interés en el lugar argumentado sus trabajos hechos durante la esquila y asistencia personal a los ancianos durante sus últimos años. Una inspección de Tierras aseguró haber constatado la ocupación de Meliguer y dando por ciertos su presencia en una década. A la vez, denunció en la Comisaría a Llarenas y su familia por acceder al campo. En 2024, una nueva inspección certificó que ocupaba el lugar desde 2014, cuando todavía estaban con vida los ocupantes tradicionales. En ese mismo documento oficial consta que residía en Cipolletti donde presta servicios como enfermero del servicio penitenciario.


La tierra fiscal no está libre de ocupantes necesariamente. Más bien todo lo contrario. Sin embargo, en numerosas ocasiones el Estado provincial decide como si así fuera, desconociendo derechos de posesión ejercidos por décadas bajo la figura de “permisos precarios de …

author: Administrador
title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen. Teil 6: GESCHENKE
content:
Musik: „Es que yo te quiero a ti“, Kevin Kaarl Bilder, Schnitt und Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Ich glaube, es war im Juli, als Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés den Beginn der ersten Etappe der „Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko“ ankündigte. Ich glaube, er sagte damals in etwa, dass die suchenden Mütter wie unsere Mamas seien. Damit nahm das Problem seinen Anfang, wie es so schön heißt.

Denn wir alle aus der Truppe dachten: „Oha, das sind unsere Mamas, und wir werden sie besuchen. Auf keinen Fall können wir da ankommen und einfach sagen: ‚Bin da, Chefin, was gibt’s zu essen?‘“. Nein, wenn wir so ankommen, bekommen wir nur die Sandale, einen Klaps oder einen fiesen Kniff (denn nette gibt es ja auch) zu spüren. Denn die oder der Freund:in – na ja, das geht vorbei, dann ist es wieder gut und fertig. Aber wenn die Mamas sauer werden, lieber Gott im Himmel, da gibt’s kein Entkommen.

„Wir sollten ein Geschenk mitnehmen“, sagte einer. „Ja“, antwortete eine Insurgenta (*), „so wie wir Mutter Erde unsere ehrliche Arbeit schenken.“ Der Capitán meinte: „Ja, als vorbeugendes Geschenk. Also noch bevor die Standpauke losgeht, hast du das Geschenk schon parat, und wenn der Sturm losbricht, holst du das Geschenk raus, lächelst und machst ein Gesicht wie: ‚Mama, ich bin‘s, der kleine Marcos, und ich werde keinen Unfug anstellen.‘“

„Das glaubt dir doch kein Mensch“, mischt sich SubMoy ein und fügt hinzu: „Außerdem steht in allen sozialen Netzwerken, dass du keine Manieren, also keine Mutter hast.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter und alle einigten sich, dass es ein Geschenk geben solle. Aber dann gab es viel Wirbel darum, welches Geschenk das sein sollte. Vielleicht Blumen. „Nein, Compa, die sind schon verwelkt, wenn du in den Bus steigst.“ „Ein Gedicht“, schlägt eine andere Insurgenta vor. Darauf SubMoy: „Die Pueblos werden schon Briefe, Gedichte und Lieder schicken. Obwohl ich nicht weiß, ob die suchenden Mütter Hip-Hop und Rap und sowas mögen.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter. Und zog sich immer weiter hin. Und dann wurde es noch schlimmer, als ein Insurgente (**) vorschlug: „Schenken wir ihnen doch ein Andenken.“

Da kam es zum Tumult. Alle redeten durcheinander: Was für ein Andenken denn, wo sollen sie das hinstellen, das ist keine gute Idee, doch, ist es, denn die Erinnerung ist das Wichtigste, deshalb sind sie ja Sucherinnen. Wenn sie keine Erinnerung hätten, würden sie aufgeben, in Ohnmacht fallen.

Da sagten die Frauen – mit dieser schlechten Angewohnheit, die Frauen haben, Diskussionen zu beenden, gerade wenn es richtig spannend wird: Stickereien und Puppen. „Damit sie wissen und sich daran erinnern, dass sie hier Familien haben.“

Die Insurgentes, angeführt vom Capitán, widersprachen und argumentierten, dass Puppen und Stickereien was für kleine Mädchen seien, dass die suchenden Mütter doch schon groß seien, dass sie gar keine Zeit für Spielereien hätten, und dann noch Stickereien, dass das einfach nicht zu glauben wäre. Die Insurgentas wurden wütend und entgegneten, dass es nichts bringe, so zu denken, weil es sich um Erinnerungen handele, nicht um Spielzeug oder Schmuck.

Und die Diskussion geht weiter, aber jetzt ist alles durcheinander, weil dem Insurgente, der für die Verpflegung zuständig war, die Bohnen angebrannt waren – und das nur, weil er sich in das Gerede um das Geschenk eingemischt hatte. Und einen Moment lang machen Frauen und Männer gemeinsame Front, denn eine Sache ist, sozusagen, der Schlagabtausch, und eine andere sind die angebrannten Bohnen. Aber dann trösteten sich alle mit Tostadas und Reis nach vietnamesischer Art. Doch es war nur ein Waffenstillstand, so unbeständig wie das Temperament von Trump. Und so ging es, nachdem sie das Geschirr gespült und die Hunde und Kätzchen gefüttert hatten, weiter.

Da kam SubMoy hinzu: „Was streitet ihr denn so?“ Alle fingen quasi an, das Problem darzulegen. „Jetzt hört aber auf damit“, rief SubMoy. Es wurde ganz still. Die Männer hofften, dass sich der Sub auf die Solidarität unter Männern besinnen würde. Und die Frauen hofften auf sein gutes Urteilsvermögen.

SubMoy zündete sich eine Zigarette an und dachte nach. Nach einer Weile sagte er: „Macht eine Liste mit dem, was wir besorgen müssen.“

Die Insurgentas applaudierten. Die Insurgentes verzogen das Gesicht, sagten aber nichts, denn die Strafe bestand darin, die angebrannten Bohnen zu essen.

Also machten sich alle Insurgentes, gleich welcher Position, daran, Geschenke zu basteln. In aller Eile, denn bis …

author: Rizomatica
title: Comunicado inicio huelga de hambre Presos Políticos Mapuche del caso Grollmus
content:
«Comunicado inicio huelga de hambre ppm caso grollmus, 23/11/2026.


Marimari kom pu che, pu logko, pu werken, pu machi, pu weychabe, pu lob.


El día de hoy, nosotros, los abajo firmantes, venimos a informar a la opinión publica nacional e internacional, que tras largos procesos de discusión entre nosotros, prisioneros políticos mapuche lavkenche, y nuestros lov y comunidades, hemos tomado la decisión de iniciar una movilización consistente en una huelga de hambre de carácter seca e indefinida, esto como medio para exigir el petitorio que detallamos a continuación:


1) Nulidad y absolución para nosotros, los 18 Presos Políticos Mapuche recientemente condenados injustamente por el Caso Molino Grollmus. El tribunal de Cañete resolvió una pena ponderada de 1055 años, resolución judicial morbosa basada únicamente en 4 relatos de testigos protegidos y sin absolutamente ninguna prueba técnica o científica de corroboración.


2) Creación de un Modulo para Prisioneros Políticos Mapuche en el CP Biobio, para condenados e imputados, donde se garanticen no privilegios sino derechos internacional y nacionalmente consagrados.


• Este módulo garantizará espacio de cocina e ingreso tolerante y mayor de alimentos en la lista de providencias.


• Derecho a practicar ceremonias mapuche (acceso de pu machi, pu logko y pu werken )


• 100 cupos de enrolamiento por comuneros.


• Mayor encomienda, días de visita y venusterio.


• Garantía de usar vestimenta tradicional


• Acceso a Salud Intercultural (machi, lawentuchebe, ngutamchebe, pewmatube)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Church demands Pastor’s immediate release
content:
The police arrested a pastor of the United Church of Christ in the Philippines (UCCP) as he landed at Ninoy Aquino International Airport early Tuesday morning and is now detained in Calamba, Laguna.


Reverend Edwin Egar is undergoing arrest proceedings by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, UCCP said. Altermidya reported he is being accused of terrorism financing charges, a bailable offense.


The Church said its pastor is an active worker within the United Batangas Conference of its South Luzon Jurisdiction.


“His ministry has extended well beyond the confines of the church; he has been actively responsive to the calls and needs of the marginalized sectors in the region,” it said.


The Reverend was reportedly fresh from a missionary stint abroad.


The UCCP said Rev. Egar’s assistance to those suffering is not a crime but a living expression of faith. It called on authorities to ensure the reverend’s safety, respect his human rights and right to due process, and immediately clarify the legal basis for his arrest.


“Any deprivation of liberty or violation of an individual’s rights must be addressed with the utmost seriousness. The dignity, freedom, and rights of any person cannot be cast aside. As a Church and as people of faith, it is our duty to take a stand against injustice and to defend the oppressed,” UCCP added.


The UCCP said it demands its pastor’s immediate release. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)
