author: Unknown
title: Öcalan: Peace process must be strengthened through democratic law and free politics
content:
Abdullah Öcalan described the Peace and Democratic Society Process as a historic turning point and warned against attempts to obstruct political developments through provocations and anti-democratic interventions. In a new message, the Kurdish leader emphasized that the transition to a new phase can succeed only by strengthening democratic legal frameworks and ensuring freedom of political activity. He also underscored the importance of a Democratic Republic in which Kurds are legally recognized as an equal and constituent part of society.


The message was released following a visit by the Imrali delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) on Sunday and reads in full as follows:


"On November 22, 2026, we, the Imrali delegation, held a meeting with Mr. Abdullah Öcalan on Imrali Island. As was publicly announced last month, we were able to confirm that Mr. Öcalan had been transferred to a newly constructed section within the prison complex. This development is clearly a positive step in terms of his working and living conditions.


The next step is to establish the necessary channels of communication to enable Mr. Öcalan to personally present to the press and the public, in its entirety, the extensive work he has undertaken over the past two years on the historic bonds between Turks and Kurds and the pursuit of peace between them.


At the current stage of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the bodies envisaged under the framework legislation must begin their work, and the necessary legal foundations must be established. Mr. Öcalan is determined to further intensify his efforts during this phase in his capacity as coordinator for peace and political participation. Mr. Öcalan’s assessments during the meeting can be summarized as follows:


We stand at a threshold


“We stand at a threshold of great practical significance, one that will mark a turning point in the history of the Republic. Crossing this threshold and entering a new phase requires both intensive, multifaceted intellectual engagement and effort, as well as an awareness of the dangers that exist.


Politics in Turkey must not remain trapped in a cycle of pressure, provocation, and reaction. If this cycle obstructs the political sphere in Turkey, there is a serious risk of creating conditions in which anti-democratic forces can gain ground, as they have done throughout the history of the Republic. The primary targets of such forces are always those working for peace and democracy, particularly the Kurds. To this end, they seek to destroy the social and political space.


Since this process, which we are advancing with great care, holds far-reaching potential for fundamental change in the country and the region, various centers of power will repeatedly attempt to intervene with destructive plans. The most effective way to counter such attempts is to strengthen the process through democratic law and free politics.


The Kurdish question is a question of democracy


I regard the Kurdish question as a question of democracy. A historic initiative to resolve such a question serves the interests of all political and social groups in Turkey. It runs counter, however, to racist ideologies and aspirations for a coup.


Democratic politics cannot be conducted solely on the basis of day-to-day political developments and relationships. It requires a coherent program of principles and an approach grounded in shared values. The political sphere must demonstrate its capacity to foster democracy.


Justice, the rule of law, and democracy are not demands of the Kurds alone, but of the entire people of Turkey. The Kurds stand for peace and fraternity and are prepared to embrace the Republic without reservation.


The participation of Kurds in the Republic can be realized on a secure democratic foundation. Such a republic can flourish by recognizing all identities. Those who hold a narrow understanding of the Republic and object to this approach operate according to the logic: “Better to keep it small, as long as it belongs to me.” The Democratic Republic, by contrast, will strengthen Turkey and make it a model for others.


Rights violations in prisons are a provocation against the process


In light of these far-reaching goals, certain conditions that currently prevail can neither be explained nor justified. In particular, deaths in prisons, the obstruction of prisoners’ release, and the differing practices in correctional facilities …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Taichung Mayoral Debate Emphasizes International Prestige
content:
THE TAICHUNG MAYORAL debate was held on November 17th. The two primary candidates were Ho Hsin-chun of the DPP and Johnny Chiang of the KMT. Ho was first to speak, followed by Chiang.

Ho began by criticizing Chiang and outgoing KMT Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen for attempting to convince the public falsely that the DPP would end subsidies to the elderly. Ho then went on to point to Taichung’s growing role as Taiwan’s second-largest city, but that issues involving traffic jams and poor transportation infrastructure were increasingly visible. This included addressing congestion on highways, as well as finishing the MRT Blue Line, and increasing international links through the Taichung International Airport. Likewise, Ho stated that there needed to be more subsidies and government policy to assist young people and provide them with opportunities. Ho suggested that the KMT administration of Taichung had stalled progress, but that, in government, she would be able to allow for coordination between the central government and local government.

Johnny Chiang stressed his love of Taichung, as well as his successes in the past in winning international productions to visit Taichung to film. Chiang stated that he was motivated to improve Taichung in running for office, and that he hoped for Taichung to become an internationally esteemed city. This would allow local Taichung products to go abroad. Chiang, too, stated that Taichung must become a smart city through the incorporation of AI with automation. To this extent, Chiang also stated that he hoped to speed up commutes in Taichung, so that residents had more time, and that young people needed opportunities. Chiang stated that he hoped to allow young people to feel that having children was not a burden and that they did not have to make a choice between their work and having children, as a result of which he would seek to renovate education facilities in Taichung. Chiang claimed that he already had a blueprint for implementing changes.

When questioned by experts in the Q-and-A section about further developing Taichung, Ho stressed plans to expand venues for baseball and entertainment, so as to connect Taichung with international touring for large-scale performances. Chiang touted the accomplishments of his predecessor, Lu Shiow-yen, in terms of developing venues, as well as exercise centers. Chiang stated that such development would continue, as well as that he would continue Lu’s emphasis on sustainable development. When asked about priority policies, Ho again stressed transportation, while criticizing lack of progress and the waste of money due to slow progress on transportation infrastructure. Chiang, contrastingly, stressed urban safety and the health of the citizens, including a focus on boosting and allowing more access to vaccinations, as well as promoting exercise. Chiang also compared Taichung to LA in terms of development and suggested that the growth of the city would need to take patterns of urban development into account.

In closing statements, Ho stressed bipartisanship and that she would seek to help all residents of Taichung regardless of political views. Ho stated that she hoped Taichung could be a safe urban environment for children and the elderly, and that young people could find jobs they enjoyed and which could support themselves.

Chiang thanked supporters and stated that he hoped to build a better Taichung with them. Chiang stated that he hoped to see more hi-tech jobs in Taichung and that Taichung could become a place where young people would not have to leave the city for opportunities. Chiang, too, stated that he hoped to develop museums and cultural activities for young people.

One notes that between Ho and Chiang, both emphasized similar needs for the city. There was a large degree of overlap between the two’s policy proposals, though Chiang sometimes focused more on a vision for Taichung rather than specific proposals. Chiang also managed to cite the accomplishments of his predecessor, Lu Shiow-yen, without being reliant on appeals to her legacy. But Chiang was perhaps the better orator in the debate and, in many ways, the race is his to lose if he is able to coast off of Lu’s legacy.

title: Qehreman Osman: Em ê lobiyeke xurt ji bo her çar perçeyên Kurdistanê ava bikin
content:
Qehreman Osman, berpirsê Nivîsîngeha Şefa Barzanî, Serpereştyarê Giştî yê Revenda Kurdistanî li Baregeha Barzanî, di dema birêveçûna Sêyemîn Konferansa Kurdên Qefqazê li Tiflîsa, paytexta Gurcistanê de ragihand, armanca wan a sereke parastina ziman û çanda Kurdên diyasporayê ye ji bişaftinê û kar ji bo avakirina lobî û piştevaniyeke xurt ji bo her çar perçeyên Kurdistanê dikin, da ku revenda Kurdî li welatên cîhanê bibe hêzeke bibandor ji bo xizmeta doza neteweyî. Qehreman Osman, di dema beşdarbûna di gera nûçeyî ya Kurdistan TV de ragihand, di panelên konferansê de nûner û zanayên olî yên hemû pêkhateyên Mesîhî, Cihû, Misilman, Êzidî, Elewî û Yarsan beşdar bûn û bi awayekî şefaf û dûr ji tirsê gotûbêjên aştiyane û biratî pêk anîn. Her wiha amaje bi wê yekê kir ku beşdarên konferansê ji Amerîka, Kanada, Ewropa û her çar perçeyên Kurdistanê ve, ligel beşdarên Kurdistana Sor ku wekî perçeyê pêncem tê binavkirin, civiyan. Armanca sereke ya vê konferansê jî gihandina wê peyamê ye ku cudahiya ol û baweriyan divê nebe sedema çêbûna nakokiyan di pirsa neteweyî de, ji ber ku mirov dikare ola xwe biguherîne, lê nikare netewe û zimanê xwe biguherîne. Biryar e piştî bidawîbûna konferansê, pêşniyar û peyameke fermî ji aliyên olî û siyasî yên Kurdistanê re bê şandin. Di derbarê rola Konfederasyona Revenda Kurdistanî de, Qehreman Osman eşkere kir ku ji %80 zêdetir komele û rêxistinên bibandor ên revenda Kurdistanî yên li derveyî welat di çarçoveya federasyonên konfederasyonê de kom bûne. Armanca sereke jî parastina Kurdên diyasporayê ye ji bişaftinê, parastina ziman û çanda Kurdî, di heman demê de tevlîbûna wan a erênî bi civaka welatên mazûvan re, heta ku bigihîjin asteke bilind û bibin lobî û piştevaniyeke xurt ji bo her çar perçeyên Kurdistanê. Konfederasyona Revenda Kurdistanî bi destpêşxeriya Serok Barzanî ji bo komkirina Kurdistaniyên diyasporayê bi hemû reng, deng û olên cuda ve di bin sîwana Ala Kurdistanê de hatiye damezrandin. Di vê çarçoveyê de, Konferansa Kurdên Qefqazê sê sal e li pey hev li bajarê Tiflîsa, paytexta Gurcistanê tê lidarxistin û beşdarbûna Kurdistaniyan tê de sal bi sal zêde dibe. Li gorî gotina amadekarên konferansê, heta sê-çar sal berê Kurdên niştecî yên Gurcistanê ji aliyê neteweyî ve qut bûbûn û Ala Kurdistanê li wî welatî nedihate dîtin. Lê niha bi saya vekirina baregeha fermî ya Komeleya Ronahî ya ser bi Konfederasyona Revenda Kurdistanî ve û bilindkirina Ala Kurdistanê, rêbazeke zelal ji bo girêdana Kurdên wê herêmê bi ax û nasnameya wan a neteweyî ve hatiye avakirin.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Filipino migrant healthcare workers denounce ICE detention, deportation threats
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Filipino migrant healthcare workers condemned the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown while raising concerns over medical neglect inside US detention facilities.

Speaking at a press conference organized by Tanggol Migrante Movement USA on November 13, two Filipino healthcare workers called for humane treatment and due process for migrants, regardless of their immigration status or profession.

Mariae “LC” Nacu was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Phoenix, Arizona, on August 22.

The 22-year-old registered nurse had been working at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Phoenix and has a valid employment authorization.

She was held at the Eloy Detention Center for three weeks before her release on bond, according to Tanggol Migrante Movement USA.

The organization said that her bond was set at $17,000 (P1.08 million) on November 13.

Nacu also estimated that she spent around $300 weekly (P19,068) on commissary items and phone calls while detained.

More than two months after her detention, ICE continued to hold her identification documents, including her driver’s license, according to the organization.

“The difficult part was that I wasn’t there [in the detention center] as a nurse. I was another person in detention, locked in a cell, trying to get someone to listen,” Nacu said.

She recalled witnessing a medical emergency involving another detainee and struggling to get someone to listen to her concerns.

Nacu described the separation from loved ones, handcuffing, and transfers between detention facilities without knowing where she was going as “traumatizing and dehumanizing.”

Dr. Veronica Velasquez, a Filipino physical therapist and recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), faces the threat of being deported.

Co-chair of the Los Angeles Kalusugan Collective, Velasquez regularly visits detainees at the Adelanto Detention Center where she witnessed brutality and medical neglect.

Velasquez said that she has organized with Tanggol Migrante Movement USA for two years and continues to support detained migrants despite facing immigration-related uncertainty herself. “I am a healthcare worker who has seen firsthand the brutality inside detention centers. I, myself, am threatened with deportation and have experienced over 23 years of this immigrant injustice system. Even so, I’m here still fighting for my community while the community fights for me.”

She said that nearly 100 community members attended her first court hearing.

Both healthcare workers raised concerns about the treatment of migrants inside US detention facilities, particularly their access to medical attention.

Velasquez said that her experience in visiting detainees exposed her to cases of alleged brutality and medical neglect. “As healthcare workers, we are in a special position to shed light on these issues of migrants in detention […] You cannot deny us from saying that there is medical violence happening in these detention centers.”

Nacu’s account of witnessing another detainee’s medical emergency also underscored the difficulties people in detention face when seeking help.

Her testimony, however, does not independently establish the circumstances or outcome of the medical emergency.

Bulatlat previously reported the case of a Filipino detainee, Kuya G, who underwent a toe amputation after months of alleged medical neglect at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington.

Migrant rights advocates said that detention facility personnel failed to properly diagnose and address his condition.

The case adds to concerns raised by migrant organizations about the treatment and medical care available to people held in immigration detention.

Read: Filipino migrants face inhumane treatment at ICE detention centers

Velasquez raised concerns over the slow response and lack of accountability of Philippine consulates who are supposed to be assisting detained migrants. She cited one case where a consulate called the police on mothers of detainees who were seeking assistance.

Her remarks echo concerns raised by Filipino migrant organizations about the Philippine government’s response to the detention of Filipino nationals in the United States.

author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and …

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.


While building a network of such organisations, the network operated through collaborative research, education, organising, and advocacy. Activities involved …

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

Sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na kilos-protesta, iginiit ng mga progresibong …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Labor’s new ‘defence’ bill a threat to democracy
content:
The federal government's new “defence” bill shows the lengths to which Labor is prepared to serve its senior partners in AUKUS, particularly the United States.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026, which passed the Senate on November 19 with support of the Coalition, One Nation, Jacqui Lambie and Ralph Babet, hands “extraordinary new powers” to the defence minister, foreign militaries and private companies, Amnesty International said.

David Pocock, Lidia Thorpe, Fatima Payman and the nine Greens Senators opposed the bill in the Senate, and every crossbench MP backed the call for a longer inquiry.

The bill expands the defence minister’s power to establish “security zones”, which restrict public access to places it has designated to be areas of national security. The minister can authorise a senior public servant to simply declare any sea, land or airspace a “defence security zone”.

It allows the minister to override state and territory laws.

It introduces draconian penalties — including up to 15 years’ imprisonment — for “a person who commits an offence”. Activists, journalists and anyone else who stumbles anywhere near these security zones can be criminalised.

Amnesty said people could be detained even though they may not know the exact boundaries of the declared security zones.

Defence minister Richard Marles is trying to downplay the bill’s reach and significance. But he admits the bill is aimed at squaring Australian laws with the government’s commitment to the US and British war pact, known as AUKUS Pillar I and II. As he put it: “Australia’s strategic circumstances demand urgency.”

Labor has avoided taking the unpopular AUKUS deal to an election. It has also restricted parliamentary scrutiny on this controversial bill to just a few days.

The Point has listed six alarming aspects of this bill. They include giving the minister and certain public servants the power to make “capability declarations” which override state, territory and federal laws. These declarations do not have to be made publicly available. They can facilitate weapons testing — including by foreign militaries.

A public servant could “switch off” state laws so that a foreign military could test their weapons here. The bill does not specify which laws can be overridden, but as The Point notes, it will be the “inconvenient” ones such as environment or heritage protections.

The penalties for those wishing to protest are steep: fines range from about $4000 to more than $150,000; 37 of the offences appear to carry prison sentences, ranging from 12 months to 15 years.

“Most of those offences include ‘strict liability’ or ‘absolute liability’ for some elements. This means that prosecutors only need to prove that you did something, not that you meant to do it. It also means that very few defences are available.”

You can be “reasonably suspected” of committing an offence in relation to a defence zone and be detained, including by a weapons’ contractor for the Department of Defence.

Lawyer Rita Jabri Markwell has also pointed out that the bill dovetails with Labor’s ambition for artificial intelligence data centres and AI’s role in the Five Eyes’ surveillance work. She said the new law will make it “harder to hold universities to account for their complicity in developing technology that enables companies and forces to commit war crimes”.

It will also make it harder for Traditional Owners to stop weapons testing on Country; to stop the contamination of their land and water and for any of their Country to be used to store radioactive waste. The First Nations fact sheet makes clear that the Woomera Prohibited Area remains a military zone, despite local First Nations opposition.

The bill’s amendments affect 14 laws, including freedom of information laws, and laws relating to the National Anti-Corruption Commission and the Criminal Code.

Labor can ram its bill through the House of Representatives this week because it has Coalition and One Nation support. But it will only deepen and increase the anger over the AUKUS pact and Labor’s decision that, no matter the political and economic cost to the country, relations with Donald Trump’s administration remain sacrosanct.

Meanwhile, the US Congressional Budget Office’s report on the US Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan said its submarine industrial base is “currently struggling” to meet demand. It played down the prospect that it could increase …

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: The irrationality of the AI bubble is the irrationality of the market
content:
The AI investment boom is one of the largest bets in the history of capitalism. Money is pouring into the tech industry. Global AI spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $10 trillion cumulatively by 2032. The priorities of the system are obscene. Ending world hunger, according to the United Nations World Food Programme, would cost $40 billion per year. Amazon is spending over four times this on AI infrastructure this year.

In Australia alone, $150 billion is committed to building AI infrastructure over the next five years. That money could be life-changing for workers if it was used for almost anything else. Diverting the money from the data centre buildout could fund Australia’s health and Medicare budget for one year. Imagine the improvements we could make to an over-stretched and under-funded hospital system. With $150 billion, we could house the 200,000 households on the public housing waiting list at an average cost of just under half a million dollars and still have $50 billion left over. 

The $150 billion committed to data centres could also be used to pay for the Labor government’s aged care expansion package 38 times over. Or we could fund a significant chunk of the green transition needed to limit runaway climate change. The Australian Energy Market Operator places the cost of decarbonising the National Electricity Market by 2050 at $122 billion.

​Alas, the ever-rational invisible hand of the market has decided that we need more data centres to power Elon Musk’s Grok AI and its

 epic, vulgar roasts

.

​That the AI boom is socially destructive is irrelevant to investors. Data centres guzzle fossil fuels and water and are a significant source of noise pollution, emitting a constant low, droning hum. Most of the data centre buildout is happening in working-class and poorer communities in Western Sydney, not in Mosman or Toorak.

In recent weeks, the AI stock market boom has faced a sharp downturn. This is not because the world’s capitalists have taken notice of the socially and environmentally destructive nature of the industry, but because they are concerned that future windfall profits may not materialise.

​AI is now integrated into the militaries across the world, the result of an AI arms race. The results are terrifying. Take Russia’s

 

ZALA Lancet drone

, which uses AI to spot and dive bomb targets free from human oversight.

​Bosses are using AI as an excuse to sack workers. In the past few weeks alone, Qantas, NAB and Canva have announced over 4,000 redundancies cumulatively. Moreover, the data centre buildout is pushing inflation upwards, which the Reserve Bank is using as an excuse to raise interest rates, pushing unemployment higher. It is yet another way the AI boom is coming at the expense of the working class.

​The insanities of the AI boom are the insanities of the market. It is only in a capitalist society driven by profit and competition that it makes sense for trillions of dollars to be ploughed into AI while working-class needs are neglected. For anything that would benefit the working class, governments and capitalists across the world cry poor. Yet when there’s a share market boom, trillions find their way into it with no thought for what society actually needs. 

It’s not like people are crying out for data centres. In the US midterm elections, when data centres were on the ballot, voters rejected data centre expansion or approved local restrictions in 40 out of 41 ballot measures. AI data centres are unpopular yet continue to be imposed on ordinary people. Genuine democracy and the capitalist market are incompatible.

Under capitalism, production occurs to enrich the capitalist class, not to meet human needs. Karl Marx wrote in Capital: “Accumulate, accumulate! That is Moses and the prophets!” In a market economy, maximising shareholder value counts for more than the cries of hungry children or the plight of the homeless. 

​The AI boom is making many capitalists astronomically rich. Tech billionaires gained a combined $845 billion through the first nine months of this year. The stock market has reached record highs multiple times in 2026. The benefits of the AI bubble concentrate at the top, in the hands of corporate executives, financiers and the rich more generally. Workers, on the other hand, receive almost nothing. There is no boom in wages. Huge speculative wealth sits alongside stagnant or falling living standards.

​No boom, however, can last forever …

author: Gwenael Velge
title: Behind the myth of the green data centre
content:
A recent Guardian article provides a glimpse into what good practice looks like when it comes to data centres: The EcoDataCenter’s 80 MW facility in Falun Swede is built from timber, runs on hydro and wind power and pipes its waste heat into the town’s district heating.

Yet, the article concludes with a hollow cliché — there are better and worse ways to do data centres. This really means that there are better and worse ways to do capitalism.

How many data centres the world needs is largely a question of demand, we are told. “How much more AI do we require, and how much do the benefits offset the harms?,” the Guardian asked.

Which community, river or forest “demands” hyperscale data centres?

What is posed as a neutral given — supply and demand — is really a political choice set by capital looking for returns. The cost, however, eventually falls on people and ecosystems at the local and planetary level.

For this exact reason, the Falun project deserves attention. The local council there started the project in 2010, years before the AI boom. Suppliers were local, the power is renewable and the waste heat warms homes.

Falun’s origin shows that when a community plans infrastructure around its needs and resources, it can do it well. It does not show that hyperscale data centres are either necessary or “sustainable”.

The article provides us with useful ratios for Falun: A power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.15 against a European Union average of 1.36; a carbon usage effectiveness (CUE) of 1.17 grams per kilowatt-hour against 414 in the United States.

These numbers speak of efficiency per unit. But we are never provided with a total and that is what we must consider if we are to tackle global warming.

The primary question should be how much heat and emissions can we afford; how efficient each unit is comes second.

Getting it the wrong way around leads to a paradox in which efficiency feeds growth.

In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons pointed out that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal use; they increased it, because cheaper power found more uses.

The same logic applies to computing. Political economist Grace Blakeley points out that Morgan Stanley’s forecasts of US data centre power demand already include Nvidia’s next generation of far more efficient chips and still projects a shortfall of 107 gigawatts (GW) — 18 New Yorks worth of electricity — by 2029.

Efficient computing is cheaper, which expands demand, which requires more power, which generates more waste — heat, emissions, tailings and pollution.

Aren’t these “sustainable data centres” powered by renewables though?

The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz has shown that there has never been an energy transition; there has only ever been energy addition.

Coal did not replace wood: Britain used more timber to prop up its coal mines than its whole economy had burned as fuel a century earlier. Humanity burns more wood, coal, oil and gas today than at any point in history.

Under this historical-material lens, renewables are simply one more source of energy for accumulation, not a means towards energy transition.

In Thermal contradictions of electronic capital, Grégoire Chamayou traces a similar computing history. Each time chips hit a thermal wall, engineers find a fix: cooling fins, air conditioning, cooler chip designs and now immersion in liquid.

The engineering fix solves capital’s eternal problem — falling profitability — so that accumulation can resume and reach a higher peak. In effect, the engineering fix is to increase the speed at which the thermal cost can be externalised into the surrounding eco-social environment.

Data centres are a case in point; they are literally “hyperscaled heat machines”; all the energy that goes in comes out as heat.

In other words, accumulation is exponentially costly, it must find forever more efficient ways to externalise waste.

On a finite planet, this runaway waste accumulation eventually meets hard physical limits — planetary boundaries.

Under the accumulation paradigm “efficiency” and “sustainability” are themselves co-opted and become a means for further accumulation, whether materially via engineering fixes, or rhetorically as legitimating spin.

What the system refuses to acknowledge is the material absurdity of exponential growth.

The physicist Tom Murphy has calculated that even if we had a magic wand and solved carbon emissions today, yet kept growing at 2.3% a year …

author: Simon Upitis
title: Protesters Shut Down Bisalloy Steels - Again
content:
Hundreds of protesters shut down Bisalloy Steels on Sunday 15 November, preventing it from operating for 48 hours. This was the eleventh time Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFOP) had organised a picket of the company.

Bisalloy Steels produces armour plating used by the IDF and by West Bank settlers to oppress Palestinians. Steel plate produced by Bisalloy is used to retrofit civilian vehicles with armour plating, making them bulletproof and allowing them to be fitted with roof-mounted machine guns. Bisalloy is also set to benefit from Australia’s increased military spending via the AUKUS agreement. In July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy announced a $2 million contract would be awarded to Bisalloy to produce steel for US Virginia-class nuclear submarines. 

The picket had a lively atmosphere. A makeshift stage was set up at one entrance with DJs, live music and poetry readings. Free food and first aid were provided by volunteers. Dozens of activists camped overnight, ensuring that the company couldn't sneak workers through the picket in the early hours of the morning. Attendees came from far and wide, with many travelling down from Sydney. Palestine Action Bega Valley attended as a group. Other groups with an official presence included the NSW Socialists and the Illawarra Greens.

At the other entrance, political discussions were held in gazebos set up on the street, often involving dozens of attendees. One member of WFOP recently returned from the West Bank recounted their experiences defending Palestinian farms from settler violence. Nurses spoke against their regulatory agency’s adoption of a Zionist definition of antisemitism. There was debate about the type of movement required to free Palestine and the tactics and strategies needed to push the struggle forwards. NSW Socialists held a forum with the candidate for Wollongong in the state election, Ryan Chapman. The success of the various workshops and discussions prove the pickets can be a place for left-wing people to gather and discuss live political questions. 

This picket experienced much less police harassment and intimidation than the previous one. In June, the company planned to break through the picket line and bring a busload of workers into the site. We stopped them, but the police maintained a heavy presence on that occasion. One attendee was arrested. Another was violently thrown to the ground, and everyone else was subjected to their petty demands and often thuggish behaviour. Riot squad cops also came down from Sydney. 

This time, we heard on Sunday night that Bisalloy wouldn’t try to bring in workers until we left. Throughout the picket, there was a very minor police presence, normally a single cop car. This was a significant victory. It shows the company wasn’t confident enough to directly confront our community campaign.

Of course, we can’t be complacent. At some point, the company will get fed up with the disruptions and take a more combative and confrontational approach. In the meantime, the campaign remains committed to stopping Bisalloy profiting from genocide.

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

author: Kate Doherty
title: Reproductive rights under threat in Newcastle
content:
"Religion has no place in healthcare!" "You have the power to do something about this!" These words were shouted at Labor MP Jodie Harrison as she was booed offstage at a pro-choice rally on 8 November. Almost a thousand people filled Newcastle's Civic Park to protest against the imminent takeover of a local hospital by an organisation of Catholic bigots.

In May 2025, Healthscope, a nationwide for-profit hospital operator, collapsed. Its 32 hospitals were put up for sale, and 14 are set to be acquired by Calvary Health Care. Calvary is a Catholic organisation that enforces a "morality" code banning abortion, IVF and gender-affirming care, and

 

has even denied

 women urgent care for incomplete miscarriages.

The effects will be particularly devastating in Newcastle. Two of the city's private hospitals will come under Calvary's management at the end of November. One of these, Newcastle Private, is the only dedicated maternity hospital between Sydney and the Queensland border. More than 1,600 women give birth there every year, and it's a key provider of reproductive healthcare in the region.

Calvary has

 

already confirmed

 its "code of ethics" will be enforced at Newcastle Private, meaning even contraception won’t be offered. Labor health minister Ryan Park

 

defended the transfer, saying the state government had deemed Calvary fit to hold a license, and had no power to decide what services a private hospital would deliver.

Newcastle's public hospitals are in no condition to accept an influx of patients forced out by Calvary. The John Hunter Hospital is

 

overcrowded and understaffed

, experiencing bed shortages of 40 and 65 every day. The Mater Hospital up the road is

 

infested with lethal mould

—and already run by Calvary. If the sale goes ahead, women in Newcastle may be forced to travel to Sydney to access reproductive procedures.

This raises the question: why are women and LGBTI people so dependent on private healthcare in the first place?

The answer is neoliberalism. Both parties, Labor and Liberal, have spent the past forty years dismantling public healthcare and creating in its place a two-tier system. The logic given is that public hospitals are there for emergencies, so it's fine for "optional" elective procedures to be take care of in the private system. But not all urgent care is considered as such by our stretched public hospitals—even life-saving procedures for women are treated as though they were optional indulgences.

In NSW, less than 4 percent of abortions take place in public hospitals. Abortion was only decriminalised here in 2019, and only three of the state's public hospitals even routinely offer it. Most women are forced to "opt" for private care and pay

 

exorbitant costs

. Access to IVF through the public system is similarly limited by the appalling wait list of up to eighteen months. Women shunted onto the private system can suddenly lose access if their care isn't profitable enough, with ten private maternity wards

 

having closed

 over the past three years alone.

The effects of health privatisation on women are worsened by other aspects of our structural oppression. Because women in Australia are paid 71 cents for every dollar a man is paid, every expense is more financially onerous. Women are more likely to be financially dependent on a partner, imperilling their ability to access and make decisions about their reproductive health. Higher petrol prices increase the cost of long-distance travel. For a working-class woman in a regional area, reproductive freedom lies behind a gauntlet of financial barriers.

The NSW government should cancel the transfer of Newcastle Private to Calvary and instead take the hospital into public hands. The right of women and LGBTI people to access healthcare shouldn't hinge on their ability to pay, let alone on someone's twisted sense of morality. Socialists in Newcastle will keep fighting for a fully public healthcare system—one designed around the needs of all people, with no place for religious bigotry or the profit motive.

 

Kate Doherty 

is the NSW Socialists candidate for Newcastle’s Wallsend in the upcoming 2027 state election.

author: Juanita Spinelli
title: Ansell chair forced to respond to modern day slavery claims at AGM
content:
Ansell’s annual general meeting on November 9 at Park Hyatt should have been an opportunity for the company to show how well it has performed.

Instead, chair Nigel Garrard spent most of his address explaining why modern-day slavery in its supply chain was no longer a problem. Shareholders had sent him many questions over the past few weeks.

Garrard and the board said Ansell was concerned about the plight of the over 200 Bangladesh workers at ceramic mold maker MediCeram.

The workers had borrowed funds to work in Malaysia, only to have their passports withheld and, arguably, trafficked into forced labour. When they organised to complain about conditions, they were harassed and beaten by police, and eventually deported back to Bangladesh. They were not paid their wages.

Seventy of the workers have still not received their passports from the Malaysian government.

Community groups, including Socialist Alliance, Freedom Socialist Party, Community Defence Marshalling System and Trans-Feminists Unite, which had wanted to shut the AGM down, meant that security was out in force.

Ansell board members admitted they had failed to look into its supply chain with MediCeram. It claimed it had paid the Responsible Business Alliance, which had paid the workers’ recruitment costs and their involuntary repatriation costs.

Garrard was vague when asked, from the floor, if Ansell knew whether all the workers had received remediation payments and if welfare checks had been done.

For over an hour, the Ansell board faced questions on modern day slavery in its supply chain.

And as Stephen Mayne put it in his report on X: “Looking for relief from the questions from the floor pressure, Ansell chair’s Nigel Garrard went on the rarely used AGM telephone option. Hello from Bangladesh. There’s no escaping these supply chain issues at this AGM.”

For more than 10 months, on the last Friday, Ansell’s head office in Richmond has attracted community groups and unions, including the MUA, to show solidarity to the Bangladeshi workers, among other labour related issues.

The campaign “Ansell 100 Shareholders for Modern Slavery” refers to the number of shareholders needed to put forward resolutions at ASX listed companies’ AGMs.

Campaigners will continue to demand that the workers are paid their entitlements n the lead-up to Ansell’s 2027 AGM.

According to shareholder filings, market data and union campaigns, Australian industry superannuation funds hold significant stakes in Ansell Limited.

Unions’ industry super funds, combined, have around a 20% investment in Ansell: United Super — 5.0%; Hostplus — 6.2%; Australian Retirement Trust — 5.2%; Commonwealth Super Corp, 1.1%; Australia Super, 1-2%; and HESTA, 1.5%.

Shareholders of these funds should be asking Ansell to improve scrutiny over its supply chains and urge the company to stop wasting funds on lawyers and consultants.

Superannuation funds should not be profiting from the abuse of other workers trapped in the slave trade within Ansell’s supply chain or any other ASX-listed companies.

Meanwhile, after 2.5 years the Bangladeshi families are still suffering.

author: Aspen Ford
title: SpaceX Lab Workers Allegedly Dried Metal Part in Employee Breakroom Toaster Oven
content:
Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company is fighting Washington state over three health violations and a $6,000 fine.

Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company is fighting Washington state over three health violations and a $6,000 fine.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Elon Musk’s multitrillion-dollar company is fighting with Washington state over a $6,000 labor fine, fending off allegations of an unsafe workplace.

In November 2024, the Washington Department of Labor and Industries opened a chemical exposure investigation at the Redmond headquarters of Starlink, the division of SpaceX that makes satellites.

The state had received complaints stating the customer service department was connected to an engineering lab that didn’t have proper ventilations. Workers were experiencing eye irritation and headaches and dust was accumulating on their desks.

Unlike the lab workers, the customer service department didn’t wear protective equipment, according to a complaint. The two teams shared a breakroom.

The complaints weren’t news to SpaceX management. Customer service workers had filed dozens of internal complaints alleging chemical exposure symptoms that stemmed from an adjacent production lab. Management did not act until Labor and Industries opened its investigation, InvestigateWest reported.

The agency’s inspection took place in an unassuming office complex in Seattle-area suburbia. Tenants of the building included a pediatric clinic, a pediatric dentistry office, a “holistic” medical clinic, a mortgage lender and the Starlink customer service department, which adjoined two small Starlink labs.

After detecting a high level of lead on a work bench, the state issued SpaceX a violation and the $6,000 fine.

The department issued a second violation because SpaceX had not evaluated their employees’ potential exposure to chemicals. For that, there was no fine.

The third violation was unexpected.

In the middle of the investigation, a state compliance officer received multiple photos of a toaster oven. Cooking inside of it was a small piece of metal laying on top of aluminum foil. Workers feared anyone who used the toaster oven might have been exposed to harmful chemicals.

The officer issued a third violation for not keeping eating areas “safe and healthy.” No fine.

SpaceX is contesting all three violations. After Labor and Industries rejected the initial appeal, SpaceX appealed again.

The matter is now before a judge with the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals, a quasi-judicial agency independent of Labor and Industries. Potential outcomes range from affirming the fine and the three violations to vacating them, with numerous variations in between.

On Nov. 18 and 19, during a trial-like hearing conducted over Zoom, SpaceX attorney Skylar Sherwood and Assistant Attorney General Diane Cornell examined witnesses familiar with the investigation. Judge Magda Baker presided.

Haley Laing, former SpaceX environmental health and safety manager who was subpoenaed for testimony, described the layout of the customer service department as a “very open space” with two labs conducting lead-based work adjoining one side.

The labs were former conference rooms. They had windows and the doors were not airtight. SpaceX did not post signage to caution workers that toxic substances were used inside, Laing said.

The state compliance officer, Richard Caldwell, was not permitted to photograph inside the labs; SpaceX had a contract with “DARPA,” the federal government’s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, he said during testimony. To some employees, the labs were known as ‘Starshield,’ a type of satellite made for national security, InvestigateWest reported.

The labs’ proximity to the customer support department was supposed to be temporary; the compliance officer said he was told they would be moved to another site in 2025. It’s not clear whether that happened.

One lab was about the size of a storage closet, “probably 80 to 100 square feet,” Laing said. The other, “probably 250 square feet.” Inside, lab technicians cured parts in industrial ovens and assembled hardware onto circuit boards.

author: Kip Hedges
title: Interview: Repression of the Minnesota 15 is Part of a Larger Assault on Labor
content:
In June

the federal government arrested and indicted 15 people

, many of them union activists, on conspiracy charges over last winter’s protests and

massive strike

 against ICE in Minnesota. The “Minnesota 15” include union carpenters, electricians, teachers, university staff, and nursing home workers.

Donate here to support their legal defense.

Below is an interview with members of the Minnesota 15: Cal Robinet, a member of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 110, Alec Stewart, a member of the Minnesota Association of Professional Employees, and Isaac Sant, a member of SEIU Healthcare MN.—Editors.


Kip Hedges: Can you tell me a little about how you came to be so involved with the resistance to ICE during Operation Metro Surge?


Alec Stewart:

 For me it really began with the uprising after George Floyd was murdered by the Minneapolis Police Department. I got involved with Cop Watch efforts to monitor the activity of police, mutual aid to the community, and community patrols back in 2020. The people who plugged me in were active in the labor movement and I was a union member so I definitely had a strong orientation to the working-class movement.


Cal Robinet:

 I was part of a coalition, an organization called Workers Solidarity Circle. It is a group of union members and other workers that are looking to build real worker power. We knew that massive repression was coming with the election of Donald Trump, so we started to build up our capacity through mass meetings, speakers, skill shares, and fundraisers so that we could have mass community self defense once we found ourselves where we did. And we had been talking about the idea of a general strike as one of the most important ways we could push back. We talked with workers and unions about this for over a year before ICE got here.


Isaac Sant:

  I was opposed to the ethnic cleansing that ICE had done in Chicago and Los Angeles, and to what is really an attack on the entire working class by attacking the most vulnerable part of the class, which is immigrant workers. It became very personal to me when ICE abducted one of my co-workers, a Liberian grandmother, someone who was very well respected at work and in the West African community here. But I’ve been organizing in the labor movement for 16 years and immigrant workers have strengthened the workers’ movement in a big way. It’s in every worker’s best interest to defend immigrant workers, because if they can drive down and marginalize immigrant workers, it acts as a downward pressure on every worker.


What impact do you think Metro Surge had on the labor movement and on workers generally?


Isaac Sant:

 Some unions took really bold and decisive action in response to Metro Surge. A lot of credit has to go to SEIU Local 26, Minneapolis Federation of Educators Local 59, and St. Paul Federation of Educators Local 28. Local 26 has a ton of immigrant workers so they led the way, I think because so many of their members were suffering. Local 26 took a real risk in being at the front of the parade. The educators were out in front probably because so many of the kids and parents were under the gun from ICE and educators felt they had to step up to protect the kids that they care about.


My SEIU local, SEIU Healthcare, is much more conservative and my leadership didn’t step to the fore. In fact, they discouraged people from not going to work on January 23rd, the day of the mass strike, where more than 300,000 workers chose not to go to work. Of course a lot of my co-workers chose not to go to work anyway.


It’s also important to remember that the big majority of workers who didn’t go to work were not in any union. That day, January 23, the day of the march of 100,000 in the streets in minus 25 temperatures, also had a real multicultural, celebratory feel to it. Like, you’re not going to drive us down.


Cal Robinet:

 I think the whole idea that the labor movement should only deal with our own union contracts and stay away from so-called political issues has been a disaster for workers everywhere. It was the hundreds of thousands of working-class people involved in rapid response, mutual aid, and school defense that dragged the union leaders along. There were a lot of workers that figured out that they had to be the union, even where they didn’t have a union.


In my union, IBEW Local 110, a group of rank-and-file electricians fought to reinstate the idea that workers don’t have to work under unsafe working …

title: ¿Por qué no habrá papeleta de CNT en las elecciones sindicales del personal docente?
content:
Leer en

Castellano

Valencià


Castellano

¿Por qué no habrá papeleta de CNT en las elecciones sindicales del personal docente?


El próximo 3 de diciembre se celebran las elecciones sindicales en las juntas de personal docente no universitario de la Generalitat Valenciana. CNT no presenta candidatura y llama a la abstención. Apostamos por fortalecer la organización asamblearia que impulsamos en los centros antes de la huelga indefinida del curso pasado y que hemos mantenido viva durante la huelga y después de su suspensión.


Queremos seguir constituyendo secciones sindicales de CNT en cada centro. La huelga que empezamos el 11 de mayo la preparamos en los centros. Como docentes, nos reunimos en asamblea, debatimos las reivindicaciones, sostuvimos los paros y llenamos las calles. Desde CNT convocamos la huelga junto con CGT, COS y CSO para que confiábamos en nuestra capacidad de organizarnos desde abajo. Este noviembre hemos salido de nuevo a la calle con las asambleas docentes para exigir avances en las reivindicaciones pendientes.


Queremos continuar constituyendo secciones sindicales de CNT en cada centro


Qué vimos en la Mesa Sectorial


El 3 de diciembre se elige la representación en las juntas de personal. De esa representación electoral depende, en parte, qué sindicatos acceden a la Mesa Sectorial de Educación y con qué peso. En plena huelga vimos hasta dónde llegaba el peso de las mayorías. La Conselleria pactó las retribuciones con ANPE y CSIF, dos sindicatos con menor representación y no le importó la mayoría sindical de la Mesa.


Meses después de la suspensión de la huelga, seguimos movilizándonos para reducir los ratios, reforzar las plantillas, mejorar las infraestructuras, defender la enseñanza en valenciano y recuperar el poder adquisitivo. Hemos comprobado que la Mesa Sectorial es absolutamente inoperante y que las mejoras sólo se logran con lucha en la calle y organización en los centros.


Todo el poder para las asambleas y secciones sindicales


En plena campaña electoral, los sindicatos que se presentan nos piden el voto por ganar representación. ¿Pero esto es realmente útil? ¿Una nueva representatividad y correlación de fuerzas en la Mesa mejoraría nuestra situación? Sentimos afirmar que no.


Queremos continuar consolidando y fortaleciendo la Coordinadora de Asambleas Docentes del País Valenciano (CADPV) y extenderla a más centros y comarcas. Asimismo, queremos constituir más Secciones Sindicales de CNT, porque pensamos que esa red horizontal es el camino para ganar derechos. Para ello, necesitamos el apoyo y la afiliación del mayor número posible de docentes.


En CNT queremos mantener nuestra independencia. No necesitamos ni queremos las subvenciones ligadas a la representatividad electoral. A diferencia de otros, tampoco tenemos una estructura de liberadas y liberados sindicales que debamos mantener con los resultados de las elecciones y que tienen mucho miedo a perder. Nuestra fuerza sindical la construimos con la afiliación y la participación cotidiana en los centros.


El 3 de diciembre, abstención. A partir del 4, seguimos organizándonos. Hacemos un llamamiento a extender las asambleas y afiliarnos masivamente a CNT ya los sindicatos de base y asamblearios. Cuantas más compañeras y compañeros nos organizamos de forma estable, más fuerza tendremos para sostener las movilizaciones y arrancar en la Conselleria las mejoras que siguen pendientes.


Constituimos Secciones Sindicales de CNT en los centros. Habla con las compañeras y compañeros de tu centro y ponte en contacto con CNT para poner en marcha su sección sindical.


No te pedimos el voto ni queremos las subvenciones por representatividad. Te pedimos que te organices con tus compañeras y compañeros.


CNT Enseñanza


Valencià

Per què no hi haurà papereta de CNT a les eleccions sindicals del personal docent?


El pròxim 3 de desembre se celebren les eleccions sindicals a les juntes de personal docent no universitari de la Generalitat Valenciana. CNT no presenta candidatura i crida a l’abstenció.
