REVIEWS:


Morning Star

:

 “How did such a horror come to pass?” by Alex Hall


“

The Exterminating Empire

 began life as a Master’s thesis, nurtured into book form by Jason Hickel — the degrowth economist and author of The Divide, who contributes the foreword. The mentorship was well placed and De Ploeg has produced an impressively searing panorama of our global predicament…”


Counterpunch

, “

Resisting Annihilation: Reviewing “The Exterminating Empire”

, by Seth Sandronsky


“…de Ploeg, who does far more than compile lists of atrocities, draws parallels between the American holocaust of the native inhabitants’ relations with buffaloes and Israel’s genocide against Palestinians and their farming of olive trees. Land theft and separating those living on the land from it are nothing new. The author has skin in the game, given his family survived the Armenian genocide and Nazi holocaust…”


Counterpunch

, “

Capitalism is Waging War on Palestine While Creating a Burning Planet

” by Daniel Falcone:


Daniel Falcone:

What is the central argument of

The Exterminating Empire

 and how is the book structured? It looks as though the book serves as an intervention as well as an addition to current scholarship.  


Chris Kaspar de Ploeg:

 I open the book with some jarring facts that seem paradoxical at first sight. We need about 30 percent of our productive capacity to

give everyone on the planet a good life

. Not just the basics like housing, clothing and healthcare, but also modern appliances like refrigerators, laptops, access to the internet and more. At the same time, that standard of living is denied to about

80 percent of the world population

. Green energy has been cheaper than fossil fuels for years, yet climate breakdown is only accelerating. We could

solve world hunger

 with about 0.03 percent of global GDP, but hunger is only increasing.


That looks like an extraordinarily wasteful system, and it is. The point, however, is that under capitalism, these are not paradoxes at all. In fact, they are signs of capital’s success. Under our current economic system, the primary goal, ruthlessly pursued, is

profit maximization

. That profit maximization is reached through pushing down costs–and we are those costs, our labour, our environments, our lives–and by conquering markets, often through a mix of military and economic warfare. That essentially puts

capitalism on a warpath against life

. The system is working exactly as it is supposed to.


We see, for example, that profit rates are higher in the fossil fuel industry because it essentially

functions through monopolies

, despite the higher costs. We see that the military-industrial complex is growing exponentially, targeting any vestiges of resistance against

US-led global hegemony

, which globalized harsh budget cuts in social welfare, healthcare and education. These very conditions of

structural impoverishment

 then create the conditions of desperation necessary for people and countries to accept their status as sources for cheap labour, resources and land for global corporations, mostly centered in the Global North.


In the book I write about a dialectic between slavery and genocide, and between structural genocide and active genocide. A good way to understand that relationship is by going back to the

We Charge Genocide petition …

author: David Swanson
title: Defying Empire on the Ground: How Korean Citizens Stopped a U.S. Base Expansion!
content:
Sura Tidal Flat (수라갯벌): Of the Saemangeum reclaimed land, 16.5 million square meters of reserved land is intended for U.S. military base expansion.


By

Korea Update

, November 23, 2026


K’in ye’ k’in ye’


I used to hear this expression a lot when I was traveling through Central America—Mexico and Guatemala—during my good old graduate school days, when I was doing field research on undocumented farmworkers migrating to the U.S. Whenever I lamented the lack of progress in addressing grave problems related to the imperial subjugation of colonized and neocolonized subjects, descendants of the Maya in rural Mexico and Guatemala would tell me, “K’in ye’ k’in ye’” (a Mayan expression meaning “little by little,” “bit by bit,” or “gradually”).


This is the way I feel this morning as I share updates on great Korean citizens’ recent victory in stopping a U.S. war plan, as well as our fellow brothers and sisters in North Korea who are defying imperial coercion. This is a quick update and excerpts from selected news; I will follow up with references shortly. –Simone Chun


Reclaiming the Land: Grassroots Resistance and the Fight Against U.S. Militarization in Korea. Citizens Win at Sura Tidal Flat: Thwarting the Saemangeum Airport Plan


The spirit of resistance—refusing to allow South Korean land and infrastructure to be subordinated to U.S. military strategy—has proven decisive on the ground. In a major victory for grassroots organizing, South Korean citizens successfully thwarted plans to construct the Saemangeum New Airport, a project located just 1.35 kilometers from Gunsan U.S. Air Force Base that critics widely recognized as a de facto expansion of U.S. military infrastructure designed to project power and prepare for conflict against China. Despite institutional momentum, citizens rallied against both the geopolitical entanglement of unequal U.S.–ROK military relations and the grave ecological and safety hazards—including a bird-strike risk 610 times higher than at Muan Airport, the site of a catastrophic aviation disaster. Through relentless public opposition, environmental scrutiny, and legal challenges in the Administrative Court demanding the project’s cancellation, ordinary citizens forced accountability where the Ministry of Environment and state planners had faltered, proving that determined public action can halt the militarization of the Korean Peninsula.


This victory did not happen overnight. It is the hard-won result of years of dedication by those who stood on the frontlines to protect the Sura Tidal Flat, the plaintiffs and lawyers who painstakingly exposed the flaws in the development plans in court, those who studied and documented the ecology of the birds, and citizens who supported the struggle from afar and stood in solidarity. I extend my deepest respect and solidarity to all of them for their unwavering commitment and perseverance. Above all, I believe this is a victory made possible by the living creatures of the Sura Tidal Flat themselves. This ruling must not be the end, but the beginning. The victory in court must translate into the actual preservation of the tidal flats. The creatures of Sura Tidal Flat must once again be able to live in safety, and countless birds must continue to fly freely across its skies. May a struggle that began with the so-called crime of seeing beauty end in a victory that preserves that beauty.


“Opposition to the Saemangeum New Airport.


“The fact that the proposed new airport would be only 1.35 kilometers from Gunsan U.S. Air Force Base (now Gunsan Airport), the very place where I first came to understand the unequal nature of U.S.–ROK relations, convinced me that the project was essentially an expansion of the U.S. military base. Moreover, the risk of bird strikes is reportedly 610 times higher than at Muan Airport, where a catastrophic bird-strike accident occurred. Who can guarantee that another tragedy will not happen once the new airport is completed? I cannot be the only one aware of all these facts. The Ministry of Environment, which reviews environmental impact assessment reports, and the Administrative Court, which is hearing the lawsuit seeking cancellation of the Saemangeum New Airport project, must know them as well. If they intend to proceed with construction despite knowing all this, it is absolutely unacceptable.” Father Moon.


The birds have won. Those who fought to protect Sura Tidal Flat have won. And we have all won by refusing to give up …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Scientists study climate change impact on Baffin Bay ice
content:
An expedition aboard the Canadian Coast Guard research icebreaker Amundsen to study sea ice in Baffin Bay is nearly complete after departing from Iqaluit on Oct. 29.


Aboard the vessel with coast guard staff are 39 scientists from Canada, Switzerland, and France who are studying how climate change is altering the formation of sea ice in western Baffin Bay, said Dany Dumont, who is leading what’s being called the Cascades Expedition.


“We went up to 72 degrees north [latitude], chasing ice where it was forming,” Dumont said in an interview Thursday from the ship, sheltered off the coast of Brevoort Island.


The expedition also included visits to three other sites along Baffin Island’s east coast, located at 71, 74 and 75 degrees north, and will conclude Nov. 25 in Quebec City.


Dumont said it’s the first time the Canadian Coast Guard has allowed scientists to access the region this late in the season when sea ice freezes up, calling it a “one-of-a-kind expedition.”


He said the crew has mostly observed what he called “new ice” — ice that formed this season, as opposed to older ice that has lasted at least one summer or longer.


“Eventually, in a warmer climate — as it is the case in Antarctica for example — the old ice will likely disappear, and only new, first-year ice will be present,” said Dumont, who is also a professor at the University of Quebec at Rimouski’s oceanography department.


“This new ice is very vulnerable to melting, and that explains the warm temperatures and warm ocean that we see, and how little ice we see.”


Scientists used drones and small craft to study a number of variables from each site they visited, such as the temperature and salinity of the ocean’s surface, the characteristics of newer and older ice, and the formation of ocean waves, Dumont said.


Researchers also carried out sampling aimed at better understanding the relationship between sea ice and ocean ecosystems.


The second leg of the Cascades Expedition, taking place in November, represents a collaboration among the Institut nordique du Québec — a group of Quebec experts in the field of northern and Arctic research — the Swiss Polar Institute, and the French Polar Institute. In August, the same crew carried out a similar expedition from the icebreaker along the west coast of Greenland to study melting glaciers.


Jean-Éric Tremblay, the project leader for the expedition, said the release of freshwater from glaciers is important to study because it impacts the extent to which sea ice hardens in Baffin Bay.


The findings of the research will also aid scientists in making more accurate predictions about sea ice and climate change in the Arctic, Tremblay said. Those models are useful for governments and coastal communities who need forecasts about sea ice cover for use in navigation.


“We expect that with climate change, eventually all the glaciers will have receded on land, so in a way it provides us with a window into the future,” he said.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: We Need a Third Reconstruction: Bishop William Barber Pushes Democrats to Take Action After Midterms
content:
With Democrats preparing to take control of both houses of Congress in January, Bishop William Barber of Repairers of the Breach argues the coalition that delivered the Democrats their midterm victories must now hold the incoming Congress accountable and keep organizing from the ground up. He and other faith leaders are calling on members of the incoming Congress to join them outside the U.S. Capitol next month to sign “A Pledge for Moral Defiance” — a commitment to pass legislation that addresses the needs of poor and working people and other vulnerable communities. Barber is pushing for what he describes as a Third Reconstruction: a sweeping moral and political agenda that includes a living wage, universal healthcare, protecting voting rights, affordable housing, environmental justice and comprehensive immigration reform.


“This was a vote not for Democrats,” says Barber. “It was a vote to say, 'Will you use policy to answer the pain that we are experiencing in this country at this particular moment?'”

author: Unknown
title: Ecological destruction driven by profit in west, security in Kurdistan
content:
The environmental destruction caused by the climate crisis is deepening across Turkey. According to data from the Agriculture and Forestry Workers' Union (Tarım Orman-Iş), 257,000 hectares of forestland have been destroyed in Turkey over the past decade.


The drying up of numerous natural lakes and the transformation of Turkey into a dumping ground for waste are further disrupting the ecological balance. Seasonal differences are becoming less pronounced, temperatures are rising and drought is becoming increasingly widespread.


Academic Metin V. Bayrak, a member of the Climate Justice Coalition and a volunteer with the Peoples' Climate Summit, spoke to ANF about environmental destruction in Turkey and the consequences of the climate crisis.


Bayrak described the climate crisis as the visible manifestation of a crisis of civilisation in nature. He said that humanity's relationship with nature has historically been shaped by domination.


Bayrak said: "What we call the 'climate crisis' is actually the crisis of civilisation becoming visible in nature. Since the Industrial Revolution, we have understood humanity's relationship with nature in terms of domination. Since Francis Bacon, we have regarded knowledge as a tool for controlling nature and nature itself as a resource. This perspective emerged because humanity positioned itself outside nature. Yet we coexist with all living and non-living beings. We are fellow inhabitants of this planet.


We are now reaping the consequences of this way of thinking. We encounter these consequences in every aspect of our lives, from the air we breathe and the water we drink to our food and shelter. However, just as our contributions to creating this crisis are unequal, so too are the ways in which we experience its consequences. The climate crisis is therefore also a question of justice."


'We opened agricultural land to construction'


Bayrak said that Turkey faces environmental problems exacerbated by public policies, in addition to the effects of the global climate crisis: "The global causes of climate change and the problems Turkey has created through its own actions are different. Turkey is located in the Mediterranean basin, a region highly vulnerable to climate change. So what have public authorities done with this knowledge? For decades, we have reduced development to growth, and growth largely to construction, extraction, consumption and, so to speak, plunder. We opened agricultural land to construction, altered riverbeds, drained wetlands and opened forests to mining activities.


How rational is it to measure a country's wealth by the income it generates from consuming its own assets? We claim to create economic value by destroying forests. But is the value of the destroyed forest included in this 'accounting'? What we leave out of these calculations returns to us as ecological debt."


'Destruction in Kurdish regions is justified on security grounds'


Bayrak said that ecological destruction justified on economic grounds in western Turkey is carried out through security policies in Kurdish regions, drawing attention to forest clearing in Şırnak (Şirnex). He said that tree felling in Cudi, Gabar and Besta demonstrates the relationship between security policies and ecological destruction, adding that documents emerging during judicial proceedings also revealed requests for tree felling on security grounds.


Bayrak asked, "We need to question the very concept of 'security' here. Whose security are we talking about, and what are we trying to protect? Whose security are we ensuring by destroying the geography and living spaces of a people?" and added: "We are talking about a region where dams are being built on 'security' grounds, even though dams are known to cause permanent ecological destruction. Security cannot be used as a justification for removing public decisions from public scrutiny. Peace also has an ecological dimension. Can we establish social peace without repairing a people's relationship with the land they inhabit, for example, without reopening pastures?"


'People's relationship with the land has changed'


Bayrak said that the industrialisation of agriculture in Turkey has transformed people's relationship with the land: "With the industrialisation of agriculture, it is not only the mode of production that has changed, but also humanity's relationship with the soil. Farmers were once the bearers of knowledge about life passed down through generations …

author: winter oak
title: The island that broke free
content:
A book review by Paul Cudenec, who reads it

here


“Every word that comes from your speaking hole is a lie in some form”. [1]


“You, the self-designated Elite of this planet, brought to your position moreso by your own lack of what is understood in most places as morality and your willingness over millennia to steal and cheat and perform the most barbaric crimes… have betrayed your trust about as fully as any trust could be betrayed”. [2]


Dave Patterson does not mince his words in

Greenways

 – the first of two “

Green Island

” books – which although a work of fiction features a large amount of truth.


The basis of the novel is that Prince Edward Island in eastern Canada has partly broken away from the rest of the country after a surprise election result that ended the old two-party hold on power.


It has renamed itself Green Island and started organising society in a very different way to the previous status quo.


Now, the description of a stable and mainly happy society (not quite a Utopia, but heading that way) could have been as dull as ditchwater over the nearly 600 pages of Patterson’s work.


But he does a great job in making the book a lively read. For a start, his style (or styles, because he adopts many different registers according to who is speaking or writing) is one of anything but terse concision – ebullient eloquence would be nearer the mark and there is plenty of humour as well.


Neither is Patterson of the social realist school, as evidenced by the way that the island attracts the interest and presence of

Henry David Thoreau

, [3] Thomas More, Thomas Paine and Che Guevera and that the trial of the global elite featured in the opening citations is conducted by a divine presence called The One, accompanied by the blindfolded figure of Justice herself.


There are several distinct threads advancing through the pages, including chapters consisting of fragments and thought-provoking quotations from famous thinkers.


I will share a few of the latter to give you a flavour:


“Do not go where the path may lead; go instead where there is no path and leave a trail”. Ralph Waldo Emerson. [4]


“Whatever you do will seem insignificant, but it is very important to do it”.

Mohandas Gandhi

. [5]


“Justice is conscience, not a personal conscience but the conscience of the whole of humanity. Those who clearly recognize the voice of their own conscience usually recognize also the voice of justice”. Alexander Solzhenitsyn. [6]


“The trade of governing has always been monopolised by the most ignorant and the most rascally individuals of mankind”. Thomas Paine. [7]


“When plunder becomes a way of life for a group of men living in society, they create for themselves, in the course of time, a legal system that authorizes it and a moral code that glorifies it”. Frédéric Bastiat. [8]


But there is also plenty of wisdom in

Greenways

 to be found coming from the mouths, pens and keyboards of its various characters, all of which can of course be regarded as

Dave Patterson

 quotations. Here are some of them:


“Strength guided by a reptilian mind is not conducive to advanced civilization”. [9]


“At all times the power of a tiny point of Light is such that it will dissipate darkness all around, but the power of a tiny point of darkness in a place where there is Light is insignificant”. [10]


“I remember still when we had plenty and freedom in our village here, and happiness and security and a good life in our families, and no ruler… It was a simpler life, to be sure, but one I know most would joyfully return to, rather than what we have now”. [11]


“After a certain period of training, the people embrace their chains, they love their chains, they hate those who try to free them!” [12]


That last one reminds me of the multiple occasions when I would be using a day off work (Saturdays, usually) to make a stand for freedom, only for some chain-loving passer-by to angrily call out: “

Getta job!

“.


Only five years into their new era, the islanders’ world is still not too different from our own, although they are proud to be “turning back some of the less pleasant aspects of modern industrial society”. [13]


Traffic has been reduced because of “a good reliable public transport system” [14] and they enjoy permaculture and organic market gardens. [15]


Since Green Island is a real democracy I find myself hoping that they will reverse themselves yet further out of the industrial dead-end and collectively …

author: Kodao Productions
title: How to break the cycle of Indonesian forest fires?
content:
Stricter law enforcement, more frontline fire prevention, transboundary cooperation and slowing climate change can all play a part


Fidelis Eka Satriastanti


/

Dialogue Earth


The forest fires this year have damaged the health and finances of many Indonesians.


People in neighboring countries have not escaped the hazardous haze. Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines have, in the past few months, raised public health and safety alert levels to try to mitigate the impacts.


Though it made global headlines only about a month ago, Indonesia had already been in the thick of the haze by the summer, with

hotspots

 increasing in fire-prone islands like Sumatra and Borneo.


Between January and September, the fires

affected

 1.9 million hectares of land in the country, much of this in September, according to Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform. Meteorologists

note

 it was one of the driest Septembers in over three decades. Between then and November, one million more hectares

burned

, the platform told AFP.


Though the fires are the most intense in 11 years,

burning

 across six provinces in Sumatra and Kalimantan, Indonesia has been grappling with severe forest fires for over four decades.


The Great Fire of Borneo occurred in 1982, as a result of extreme drought and “slash-and-burn” clearing of vegetation to make room for agriculture, the Straits Times

noted

.


Large fires have been

recorded

 every few years since, but it was not until 15 years later that intense regional attention was focused on them. In that 1997 season, fires burned nearly 10 million hectares of land, predominantly in Sumatra and Kalimantan.


The haze spread to neighboring Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and Thailand, costing the region USD10 billion through impacts to transportation, crops, timber, tourism and healthcare, the World Resources Institute (WRI)

found

.


While regional action plans were put in place soon after, the fires kept coming back – in

2005

,

2006

,

2013

,

2014

,

2015

,

2019

,

2023

 and

this year

.


Such serious forest fires not only harm health and finances, they also strain diplomatic relations. What causes them and how can they be stopped?


Why have the fires been so severe?


This year’s fire season, like many in recent years, has been dominated by peat. Protected peatlands accounted for half of all burned area in Indonesia from January to September, Kompas

reported

.


Indonesia holds almost 36% of the world’s peatlands. Composed of organic matter drenched in water for centuries, they cover more than

24 million hectares

 in the country and are considered massive

carbon sinks

.


In their natural state, peatlands are waterlogged, making them fire-resistant in normal weather conditions. But when drained, degraded or dried out, peat becomes highly flammable.


Peatlands are typically razed to produce palm oil, timber and other export-oriented commodities.


Peat fires burn underground, enabling them to spread undetected, and making them hard to put out. They release stored carbon dioxide and spew hazardous haze.


People pass peatlands damaged by wildfires in Sekadau, West Kalimantan (Image: Tatan Syuflana / Associated Press / Alamy)


Almost all fires in Indonesia are caused by

human activities

, notes the WRI.


The 1997 fires were exacerbated by the Mega Rice Project which aimed to turn one million hectares of peat into rice paddies in Central Kalimantan.


The Suharto regime had launched the project the year before to feed the country’s growing population. Canals were dug to drain water so rice could be planted. Then, to clear the forest, farmers leaned on the cheap and fast slash-and-burn method.


Combined with the prolonged dry season triggered by an extreme El Niño that year, this burning practice created underground peat fires that spread uncontrollably.


Due to its persistent dried state, the ex-Mega Rice Project area has since become the

epicentre

 of regular fires in the province.


Fires ramp up in the dry season, from June to October, particularly during El Niño years.


Land clearing by burning was banned under Indonesian law in 2009. But in 2019, a government minister

told

 media that over 80% of the oil palm plantations in the country “do not meet applicable regulations”.


El Niño and global warming have worsened the forest fires. In November, scientists found that global heating driven by the burning of fossil fuels had raised temperatures by 1 …

author: Danilo Arao
title: Pagbabalik-tanaw
content:
Kayang kaya dahil kakayanin. May tagumpay dahil babakahin.

Sa nalalapit na pagtatapos ng 2026, mainam na balikan ang kalendaryong hindi na mabasa sa sobrang daming nakasulat.

Mula Enero hanggang Nobyembre, punong-puno ang iskedyul ng mga responsibilidad na kahit paano’y hinarap naman. Kahit ang susunod na buwan ng Disyembre, may mangilan-ngilan ding nakasulat kahit nakatakda itong panahon ng limitado pahinga. Opo, kailangan nang umupo’t humiga nang medyo matagal ang nakatatanda!

Kababalik lang mula sa sabbatical noong 2025, muling nagturo sa Unibersidad ng Pilipinas (UP) Diliman ngayong taon. Mas mataas na ang kumpiyansa sa gawaing pang-akademiko sa dalawang dahilan.

Una, natapos na ang doktoral na pag-aaral sa Alemanya noong 2024. Ikalawa, tumaas na ang posisyon at naging ganap na propesor (full professor) noong 2025, matapos ang 11 taon bilang kawaksing propesor (associate professor) at 11 pang taon bilang katuwang na propesor (assistant professor).

Sa wakas, nakamit din ang pang-akademikong “tagumpay” dahil sa tatlong letrang P, H at D na puwede nang ilagay sa dulo ng pangalan (at siyempre’y puwede na ring gamitin ang salitang “Doktor” kahit na hindi naman nagrereseta!).

Nagresulta ang bagong titulo’t ranggo sa mga bagong oportunidad. Matapos na maging ganap na kasapi (regular member) ng National Research Council of the Philippines (NRCP) noong Marso 2026, nakuha ang prestihiyosong NRCP Gabay Award para sa pananaliksik na may malaking pakinabang sa paghuhubog ng polisiya ng gobyerno.

Sa partikular, ito ay pagkilala sa ginawa ng Kontra Daya sa pagbubuo ng data set ng mga grupong partylist na tumakbo sa halalan noong 2025. Kahit na bagong miyembro pa lang, sinubukang magsumite ng dokumentasyon, lalo na ang paggamit ng iba’t ibang sangay ng gobyerno sa ginawang pananaliksik ng Kontra Daya, at pinalad namang kilalanin ng mga eksperto’t hurado ang kolektibong pinaghirapan ng grupo.

Sa mismong unibersidad, may ilang awards at grants na inaplayan at pinalad ring maaprubahan lahat. Sadyang nakakagulat ang 100% na approval rate pero nangyari talaga ito. Nagkaroon tuloy ng limitadong pondo para sa patuloy na pagtuturo, pananaliksik at gawaing ekstensiyon. Sa kabila ng patuloy na pagtaas ng presyo ng mga bilihin, nakayang bilhin ang mga kinakailangang gamit ngayong taon.

Dahil dito, mas maganda na ang kinakalabasan ng mga online na interbyu, pati na rin ang mga online na lektyur at talumpati sa loob at labas ng bansa. Pabirong hirit ng ilang kaibigan, kasama yata sa gastusin ang pagpaparetoke. Hindi po. Ilaw at kamera lang ang katapat ng bagong hilamos na mukha. (Huwag nang pag-usapan ang ilan pang bagong biniling gamit, salamat sa awards at grants.)

Sa taong ito, lumabas din ang tatlong librong inedit para sa isang dayuhang pabliser. Medyo mahal ito kung ibebenta sa mga kakilala sa Pilipinas kaya ginamit na lang ang bahagi ng pondo ng awards at grants para bilhin ang ilang kopya nito at ipamigay sa silid-aklatan ng mga piling unibersidad.

Kaya ngayon, libre itong mababasa ng maraming estudyanteng may panahong magpunta sa silid-aklatan. Nakakaintindi naman sila ng wikang Ingles kaya hindi malaking problema ang pagbabasa.

Pero kung nais ng nakasulat sa wikang Filipino, tinatayang lalabas sa Disyembre (sana lang!) ang ikapitong libro ng mga sanaysay. Matapos ang medyo mahabang panahon ng malalimang ebalwasyon at teknikal na pinalisasyon, mahahawakan na sa kamay ang ilang taong pinaghirapang buuin.

Kumpara sa mga naunang anim na libro, espesyal ang paparating na libro dahil tumulong ang mismong anak sa lettering ng pabalat ng libro. Siya rin ang gumawa ng ilustrasyon ng mga kabanata.

Sa madaling salita, awtor ang ama samantalang ilustrador ang anak. Siyempre’y may susing papel din ang asawang tinulungan ang anak sa gawain, bukod pa sa maraming suhestiyong parating sinusunod ng asawa sa usaping libro at buhay (o pabirong sabi sa wikang Ingles, “Yesband”).

Malapit nang matapos ang taong 2026. Nababawasan na ang mga nakasulat sa kalendaryo. Panahon nang maghabol para matapos ang kailangang matapos. Inaasahan ang limitadong pahinga sa mga natitira pang araw.

Kayang-kaya dahil kakayanin. May tagumpay dahil babakahin.

Para makipag-ugnayan sa awtor, pumunta sa https://risingsun.dannyarao.com

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Man shot by police said he was ‘sick of life,’ coroner’s inquest hears
content:
The jury in a coroner’s inquest into the death of a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man fatally shot by police in 2021 heard phone call recordings Monday in which the man said he was “sick of life” and wanted to end his life.


The recordings were from calls between Trey Angootealuk and Peter Crockford, the negotiator who called on the phone from Iqaluit in an attempt to de-escalate the situation.


In each call, Angootealuk swore at him before hanging up. In one call, he was heard saying that he wanted to die.


On Nov. 6, 2021, Angootealuk hijacked a truck and shot at officers in an area outside of town before he was fatally shot by police the next morning. The standoff lasted several hours.


The Ottawa Police Service, which investigated the shooting, later determined there were no grounds to believe any officer committed a crime.


The inquest by Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes will determine the circumstances surrounding Angootealuk’s death. It began Monday morning at the Siniktarvik Hotel and is scheduled to last until Friday.


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.


Cody Autet, who was acting corporal of the detachment at the time, was among the officers Angootealuk shot at.


Autet testified that he saw Angootealuk hijack the truck, heard him scream “I can’t take this,” and witnessed his death.


The inquest’s first witness, former RCMP constable Kyle Amsel, described calling on Angootealuk multiple times to drop his gun before he entered the truck but did not receive a response.


“It was freezing cold,” Amsel, who was among the two officers who initially responded to the call, told the jury. “We thought he was just going to get cold and give up.”


He then watched from afar as Angootealuk shot toward police.


He said he was not present at the time of the fatal shooting, because his shift had ended.


Sixteen witnesses are expected to testify at the inquest, Jessi Casebeer, counsel for the chief coroner, told the jury.


Among them are RCMP officers, emergency response team members, and the investigator from the Ottawa Police Service.


Family members may also provide testimony, Casebeer said.


The inquest is scheduled to resume Tuesday at 9:30 a.m. CT.

title: Indigenous Environmental Network urges Congress to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
content:
On Wednesday, in a shocking attack against Tribal sovereignty, Senate Democrats voted to move forward with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) (S. 5653), a bill steeped in environmental racism that would legally ensure the rapid buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure and AI data centers, while stripping away the federal-Tribal consultation process.

Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) are leading the effort, alongside far-right Republican colleagues Mike Lee (R-UT) and Shelley Capito (R-WV), to enact an aggressive attack on the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process. In addition to undermining Tribal consultation, the BAAJA erases protections under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act (CWA), and Endangered Species Act (ESA), paving the way to bring hyperscale data centers and natural gas projects online without critical guardrails for the land, water, and animals.

The Senate voted Wednesday 65-31 to invoke a cloture vote, which is a procedural vote that formally ends debate and allows the bill to move forward. Consideration of amendments is expected to begin Thursday, after which the bill will move into a final vote on passage before moving to the House. Despite the BAAJA being vastly opposed among climate justice groups, Tribal Nations, and Indigenous organizations, 14 Democrats voted to move forward with the bill; Chris Coons (DE), John Fetterman (PA), Ruben Gallego (AZ), Kirsten Gillibrand (NY), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (CO), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (NV), Brian Schatz (HI), Chuck Schumer (NY), Elissa Slotkin (MI), Mark Warner (VA), Raphael Warnock (GA), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI) all voted yes.

In perhaps the most egregious betrayal of all, the majority of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee–those Congress members charged with the highest responsibility to uphold the federal Treaty and Trust obligations–have continued to support stripping away Tribal consultation in the BAAJA. This includes Chairman Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Vice Chairman Brian Schatz (D-HI), as well as John Hoeven (R-ND), Steve Daines (R-MT), Jerry Moran (R-KS), and Alan Armstrong (R-OK).

Meanwhile, key Congressional environmental leaders and Tribal allies have strongly opposed the BAAJA and uplifted the concerns of Tribes and communities, including Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-AZ), and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI).

As an Indigenous organization representing grassroots Indigenous land protectors, the Indigenous Environmental Network stands with the hundreds of Tribal Nations, climate justice organizations, and community members strongly opposing this disaster bill. We encourage everyone to call your senators and representatives today to urge them to vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to preserve our land and sovereignty for future generations.

The BAAJA is a violation of the federal Treaty and Trust obligations.

The BAAJA proposes sweeping changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process that could effectively cut out Indigenous voices when determining whether a historically significant, sacred, or cultural site is worth protecting.

Congress and the federal government have a legally enforceable fiduciary obligation to protect Tribal Treaty rights, lands, assets, and resources, as contained in the framework of federal Indian law and legally binding Treaty-making. The Tribal consultation process is the basic function of this Treaty and Trust obligation, which has been codified since 1966 in the NHPA Section 106.

Under the BAAJA Sec. 2301, opportunities for Tribal input in permitting will be reduced and restricted in a way that reflects termination-era policy. Mandatory Section 106 Tribal consultation becomes optional, and agencies will no longer need to notify Tribal Nations before decisions are made that could impact sacred sites. The definitions of what agency actions require consultation and which cultural or historic properties qualify for protection is narrowed in such a way that cuts out a Tribe’s ability to define what is protected as sacred. Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (THPOs), often a Tribe’s greatest tool in preserving historic and cultural sites, will be under strict federal oversight with the risk of federal takeover. Along with State Historic Preservation Officers …

author: James Crump
title: Mamdani Launches Healthcare Scheme Directly for Taxi Drivers
content:
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has launched a new scheme to bring accessible and affordable health care directly to taxi drivers doing airport pickups.


The new scheme will see Driver Health Hubs set up at John F. Kennedy and LaGuardia airports, where taxis make about 34,000 pickups each day. Taxi drivers who cannot afford to take time off work will now have access to facilities at places they often frequent.


The Driver Health Hubs opened on Monday and will operate weekly to provide taxi drivers with preventative screenings, vaccinations, sexual health tests, same-day doctor appointments and insurance enrollment assistance, the mayor’s office

said in a statement

 about the scheme.


The city will also be deploying mobile services vans that will bring care directly to drivers working in high-density areas across the city.


In a statement, Mamdani said: “Today, New York City is letting its drivers know that we’re here for them too. No one should be forced to choose between earning a living and seeing a doctor. We’re bringing lifesaving health care directly to the places where drivers work, so they can easily access preventative care and stay healthy.”


Bhairavi Desai, executive director of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance, said: “Four New York City taxi drivers died on the job over the summer. All suffered from chronic health conditions but couldn’t afford to take unpaid time off for their care.” She added that onsite services are a “first step” in winning comprehensive healthcare for drivers. 


Last week, Mamdani

announced plans to disband

 the controversial New York City police unit, Strategic Response Group (SRG), known for using excessive force against protesters.


Mamdani said the SRG will be scrapped in favour of a “civilian-led approach” to policing protest that will put “communication, de-escalation” and “coordination” front and centre.


Under Mamdani’s reforms, the use of tear gas, rifles, painfully loud noises above 90 decibels and kettling – the surrounding and trapping of protesters, usually before mass arrest – will all be banned.

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: The Worst Impacts of GOP Medicaid Cuts Haven’t Hit Yet. Dems Must Take Action.
content:
In the wake of the blue wave, Democrats can restore Medicaid and move toward passing Medicare for All.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Millions of people in the U.S. are currently in danger of losing their health care as a result of Donald Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which was passed in 2025 with Trump in the White House and Republican majorities in both the Senate and the House.

The new bill tilted the economy evermore in favor of the wealthy, rolling back hundreds of billions of dollars of taxes and clawing back a portion of the lost revenue through extreme cuts to social safety net programs.

The biggest loser in the bill was Medicaid, which was coming off of more than a decade of expansion under provisions of the Affordable Care Act that allowed states to broaden eligibility for the program. Onerous new workfare requirements — requiring able-bodied recipients to prove 80 hours a month of work or community service — paired with more frequent eligibility checks, were crafted specifically to drive down the numbers enrolled in the health care program. Estimates of the impact range widely, but there is general agreement that somewhere between just under 5 million and just over 10 million people stand to lose their health care as a result of this bill.

Add in the millions being driven off of Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans by Congress’s refusal to extend tax credits as well as by rising premium costs, and there’s a real chance that, in coming years, America will revert to pre-ACA-era numbers of uninsured.

During the 2026 enrollment period, as deductibles and premium costs soared, the number of Americans in ACA-subsidized insurance plans dropped by more than one-fifth compared to the previous year; and, for those who stayed enrolled, many opted for far less comprehensive “bronze” plans rather than the increasingly unaffordable “silver” options that had previously attracted the most enrollees.

Astoundingly, according to the Commonwealth Fund, as of late 2026 nearly half of American adults under the age of 65 either have no health insurance, have experienced health coverage gaps at some point in the previous year, or are currently significantly under-insured.

Somehow the GOP thought it could dodge the issue by crafting the cuts to health care in a way that meant the worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the 2026 elections. Given the pain that people in the U.S. were already feeling around health care, it was a strategy doomed to failure.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, polls suggested that the U.S. public was deeply worried about access to health care. Economic issues, including the high costs associated with health care, topped voters’ anxiety lists — with democracy and corruption issues coming in next. Kaiser Family Foundation data indicates that 6 in 10 voters were “very concerned” about the cost of health care; and by a 20-point spread those voters believed that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to address this challenge.

The Kaiser Family Foundation analysis suggests that in swing states where health care was of most concern to residents, by a two-to-one margin voters worried about health care costs voted Democrat over Republican. In states such as Maine and Michigan, where Democratic candidates won on platforms that included a promise to push for Medicare for All, large majorities of the electorate told the pollsters that they wanted the government to play a larger role in securing access to affordable medical coverage for residents. In newly blue Texas, where more than 5 million residents currently lack health coverage, Democratic lawmakers have been lining up to propose legislation to expand Medicaid access in the state — almost daring the Republican majority in the state senate to block them and to then try to justify that action to voters.

Three-quarters of people in the U.S. now live in states with Democratic governors, many of them also with both state legislative bodies blue, meaning that state-level health care reforms will likely complement congressional efforts to bring more people under health coverage umbrellas.

Come January, Democrats have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape the health care landscape in the United States — or, at the very least, to lay out a set of policy reforms that they would enact were they able to get …

author: S.C.
title: Haldol First, Questions Later: My Psychiatric Detention
content:
T

his is not a post I wanted to write. I wanted to be able to go through my psychiatric admission patient file and affirm that healthcare providers definitively met their duty to the standard of care, and hewed as closely as possible to their Hippocratic oaths — within reason, of course. I wanted to be able to affirm that any initial feelings I had of betrayal and victimization were likely just figments of an overactive imagination, and potentially even evocative of a budding persecutory delusional disorder, and I should do my best to banish the thought.


But I can’t.


As the documents slowly trickled in from my family physician (because the hospital never provided any to me directly, despite my pleas), those feelings only deepened. Something monstrous really did happen to me in April of 2026. Doctors didn’t just breach the standard of care, but brazenly, maliciously, perhaps even gleefully continued to traumatize me, time and time again. This was not care. This was its evil twin: harm.


My first inkling that something might be amiss with my patient record was when I lay half-dead on the floor of a cold room, having been freshly injected with what I now understand to be a powerful antipsychotic drug, and my Form 42 (which informs a patient in writing that they are being detained at a psychiatric facility for a mandatory assessment) was carelessly tossed in by the doctor like some throwaway, rubber-stamp formality to be dispensed with without explanation


He checked two boxes where he indicated that he believed I was suffering from a mental disorder, and that I had:


1) shown a lack of competence to care for myself, and


2) this lack of competence would likely result in serious physical impairment of me.


That’s very odd, I thought. I had a good job, a lovely wife, two amazing daughters I saw off to school that morning, and I drove myself down to the emergency room asking for a sick note for work. Was I really among what the French call “les incompetents”?


And who exactly was he to judge, anyway? He never physically examined me. Actually, come to think of it, he never once

spoke

 to me. So, all of a sudden, I am being deprived of my freedom and drugged against my will because a physician who never once entered the same room as me believes I’m in such a degenerative mental state that I can’t eat, dress myself, or tend to my own wounds? No. That didn’t sound right. There must be some misunderstanding.


It’s worth noting that in the entire lead-up to my being hauled out of the psych room by six security guards and then administered Haldol on an emergency basis, no one once told me what particular ailment they believed I was suffering from. Sure, a mental health social worker shoved a pill in my face and told me to take it, but since she didn’t tell me what it was or what it did, I refused. It only became clear much later, when I reviewed my records, why everyone I encountered seemed so scared of me. I was deemed to be in “psychosis” (which apparently a lot of people seem to associate erroneously with the term “psycho” — thanks, Hitchcock).


I really didn’t understand how the physician made this assessment, so I resolved to get the ER consult note. When it eventually came from my GP (again), rather than being clear and elucidating, I found that note to drip with scorn, derision, and vague non-descriptive psychobabble that made it seem as if he had actually made a real investigation into my condition, when he clearly had not.


The title of his ER note? “Chief Complaint: Bizarre.” Okay. That’s a pretty good title… for a work of medical fiction. That’s supposed to be a space where the doctor writes what the patient was complaining about on that day — not a space to cheekily slander the patient’s presentation. I told triage that I was simply looking for a sick note for work. Once again, I found the doctor inverting the typical power dynamic that I had come to expect in the Canadian healthcare experience.


This had all started a few months earlier when I shared with my family doctor some traits of mine that I thought might be consistent with ADHD: traits like executive dysfunction, forgetfulness, and binge eating were just some of the classic indicators I felt underscored the need for more focus in my life. She largely agreed with the self-assessment, but instead of sending me to an occupational therapist or psychotherapist, she started me straight away on Vyvanse, 30 mg. For a while, it was great: I was more …

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release …

author: Freedom Editor
title: Bullshit Burnham’s war on the disabled
content:
Andy Burnham promised an end to forty years of neoliberalism. Instead, he’s embraced the persecution of its favourite scapegoats

The news that the Milburn Review is to recommend the end of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), and the health element of Universal Credit for most young people under the age of 25, is not a surprise to those of us in the disability rights community, but it is horrific all the same.

According to Labour, it’s for their own good; no-one, intones Andy solemnly, wants to be trapped in a cycle of dependency, do they? Of course, this is all bullshit. Intentions matter, and neither the Milburn Review into the number of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET) or the Timms Review into PIP itself, were commissioned for the benefit of the young or the disabled, but for the benefit of the government’s bank balance.

Put simply—and no-one is questioning this—the number of claimants has increased significantly since the pandemic. One million young people are not in work or education. And the government doesn’t want to spend money on the problem.

But the clue is in the chronology. Though COVID has been memory-holed by many, not least government, which has worked assiduously to prevent Long COVID being recognised as a disability, the UK as elsewhere went through a once-in-a-century pandemic a handful of years ago. Apart from the death toll, which the COVID Inquiry acknowledges was worsened by government policy, many were left disabled and chronically ill.

That’s not the whole story, but it’s a big part of it, and as with COVID more generally it’s one government simply pretends doesn’t exist. The Burnham/Milburn rhetoric on disability is one of sympathy, that this is a ‘moral’ choice by government, that these ‘changes’ are an opportunity for a generational reset for young people who have, by Burnham’s own admission, been failed by politicians.

On that last we can agree, but Burnham’s no break with that catalogue of failure. Like his predecessors Starmer and Reeves, Burnham’s characterised PIP as an out-of-work benefit, when it is isn’t – it’s paid to ensure folks can be independent (the clue is in the name) and meet the additional costs which are incurred by being disabled in an ableist society. This is a wilful play into right-wing ‘scrounger’ rhetoric.

Burnham’s not wrong to mention that austerity had an enormous impact on the young in the coalition years, but lest we forget this is a man who lost a previous chance at the Labour leadership primarily because he refused to vote against coalition welfare cuts in 2015, a decision which fuelled a grassroots revolt in the Labour Party and the ultimate election of Jeremy Corbyn.

Indeed, what’s proposed here is a massive real-terms saving to government dressed up as empowerment for its victims—which is the classic Labour play. But anyone with any critical faculty can read Burnham’s words and know they are bullshit.

His constant references to parity of esteem in the education sector could have been written by any government, Labour or Tory, for the last sixty years. As with everything with him, it is surface-level, hoping to play on common-sensical shibboleths that will encourage folks to look past (or not at all at) the actual policy.

The same weekend his op-ed was published, a TikTok found its way online from the Labour account with Andy saying “we used to have a laugh…talk about pub snacks” before the Union Jack came prominently into play. The more things change, the more they stay the same, as the Burnham revolution boils down to idiotic chat about pork scratchings and pints whilst the young have what precious little support they get taken from them.

Labour’s messaging this week is to say that what they propose is more humane than what the Tories want to do, that they are offering a jobs guarantee and hope. But like all Burnham’s promises it’s a mirage. Milburn has proposed a reduction in employer national insurance for young people, but not yet; young people will still be paid less for the same work too.

Young people still won’t be able to access the mental health care they need. They will supposedly be able to apply to ‘local funds’ for support, funds which don’t exist and if they ever did based on prior experience would be unlikely to be responsive. But this rhetoric is just to salve the consciences of those not directly affected.

Disabled people, and disabled young people in particular, are neoliberal capitalism’s …

author: Unknown
title: AKP ilçe başkanıyla görüşmeyen ilçe sağlık müdürüne "istifa" baskısı iddiası
content:
Rize – Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü görevinden alınan İ.Ö'nün, AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı Furkan Namlı’nın ziyaret talebini kabul etmediği gerekçesiyle geçen günlerde istifaya zorlandığı iddia edildi. Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, İ.Ö'nün görevine iadesini isteyerek, AKP yetkililerine “Kurum amirleri sizin hizmetkârınız değildir” dedi.

Edinilen bilgilere göre, 4 Ağustos 2026 tarihinde AKP Pazar İlçe Başkanı olan Furkan Namlı ve beraberindeki yönetim kurulu üyeleri, kurum ziyaretleri kapsamında Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nden telefonla randevu talep etti. İlçe Sağlık Müdürü Dr. İ.Ö’nün ilk talebin ardından müsait olmadığını belirttiği, ikinci telefon görüşmesinde ise 657 sayılı Devlet Memurları Kanunu’na tabi bir kamu görevlisi olduğunu ifade ederek siyasi parti ilçe başkanlarıyla makamında görüşmeyeceğini bildirdiği ileri sürüldü.

Rize'deki AKP yetkililerince bunun İl Sağlık Müdürü Prof. Dr. Gökhan Demiral’a ileterek Dr. İ.Ö’nün görevden alınmasını ya da istifa etmesinin istendiği, bunun ardından Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde telkinde bulunulduğu ancak ilçe sağlık müdürünün bunu kabul etmediği savunuldu.

Dr. İ.Ö. bir süre sonra ise İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alındı.

Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü çalışanları da Dr. İ.Ö’ye istifa etmesi yönünde baskı yapıldığını ifade etti.

Yeni Parti Rize İl Başkanı Saltuk Deniz, Dr. İ.Ö’nün Pazar İlçe Sağlık Müdürlüğü'nden alınmasına tepki gösterdi. Kamu kurumlarında görev yapan yöneticilerin siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetinde olmadığını vurgulayan Deniz, şu açıklamayı yaptı:

“Devlet kurumlarında çalışan görevlilerimiz siyasi parti temsilcilerinin hizmetkârı değillerdir. Kurum amirleri, hiçbir siyasi parti temsilcisi ile görevleri dışında görüşmek zorunda değildir. Daha önce de benzeri olaylar ilimizde yaşanmıştı. Rize İl Milli Eğitim Müdürü Halil İbrahim Akmeşe de İl Milli Eğitim Müdürlüğü görevine atanır atanmaz, daha koltuğuna oturmadan soluğu AKP İl Başkanlığı’nda aldı. Bunlar doğru şeyler değildir. Kurum amirleri sizlerin hizmetkârı değildir. Rahat bırakın çalışanları. Kurumlarda iş barışını bozmanın, amirleri ve memurları siyasal gücünüzü kullanarak görevlerinden almak ya da uzaklaştırmakla diğer kurum çalışanlarına gözdağı vermenin siyasi ahlakla da bağdaşmadığını düşünüyoruz. AKP sözcülerini ve İl Sağlık Müdürlüğü’nü bu konuyla ilgili açıklama yapmalarını, görevinden alınan doktorumuzun yeniden görevine iade edilmesini kamuoyu adına talep ediyoruz.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Sleshi Teshome Kehali
title: The Bone-Setters’ Ward: How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia’s Modern Healthcare Vacuum
content:
Reporting from Bahir Dar, Ethiopia


In a residential neighbourhood of Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia, patients visit the home of W/ro Birqe Yibre for help with injuries. Birqe, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, has practised for more than 20 years.


W/ro Birqe Yibre, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, sits in her residential courtyard in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. She says she has practised for more than two decades. (Photo: Sleshi Teshome)


One of her patients, Yidersal Mengistu, came with a painful right foot and a bruised big toe after kicking a stone while playing football.


“I didn’t go to the hospital. To be honest, I prefer the traditional way,” Mengistu said. He explained that he had visited Birqe before for heel pain and believed her treatment had helped him. He also said she had treated him without charge on that earlier occasion.


“If I recover fully this time, I will pay her,” he said.


For Birqe, payment depends partly on what patients can afford. She said people who have money typically pay between 150 and 200 Ethiopian birr, while she treats those who cannot pay without charging them.


“If someone has no money, I treat them and tell them, ‘Go on, go home,’” she said. “You cannot turn away poor people.”


A study of 836 people with a history of injury in Mecha district, published in

BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies

, found that 46.05 per cent had used traditional bone-setting services. Social acceptance was the most commonly reported reason for seeking this care. The findings reflect the study population in Mecha district and should not be taken as a national estimate.


For patients such as Mengistu, the decision is also shaped by personal experience and trust. But the treatment of fractures and other serious injuries can carry risks when patients delay seeking medical assessment.


Knowing When to Refer


Birqe said she distinguishes between injuries she believes she can treat and those that require hospital care.


“I handle muscle pulls and minor dislocations,” she said. “If someone comes with a serious, displaced bone or a deep fracture, I tell them plainly to go to the hospital. I don’t try to touch it.”


She said she was concerned about practitioners who accept serious cases despite lacking the necessary skills to manage them.


According to Birqe, some bone-setters bind injured limbs tightly with bamboo splints, locally known as Timaq, and continue treatment even when a patient’s condition worsens. She said some eventually advise patients to seek hospital care only after several visits.


“When parents bring me a child whose hand is already ruined, I tell them: ‘Run to the hospital, I won’t touch this,’” she said.


Her account highlights a distinction within traditional practice: while Birqe says she refers serious injuries, she believes other practitioners take on cases beyond their abilities. These claims describe her experience and observations; establishing how widespread such practices are would require further evidence.


A Crooked Arm


Thomas Habtamu, a student living in Bahir Dar, said a fall during a neighbourhood football match injured his left forearm. Because of his family’s financial difficulties, he did not go to a hospital and instead sought treatment from a local Wogesha.


“The healer kept massaging it week after week, telling me to be patient,” Habtamu recalled. He said the injury was close to the joint and that the treatment did not restore the arm to its normal position.


W/ro Birqe Yibre examines the injured foot and bruised big toe of Yidersal Mengistu in Bahir Dar. Mengistu said he injured his foot after kicking a stone while playing football and chose to seek traditional treatment. (Photo: Sleshi Teshome)


“He told me that if I ever fell down and hurt the arm again in the future, he might be able to reset it then,” Habtamu said.


Habtamu has never had the arm examined at a hospital. He said his forearm remains visibly bent and that he struggles with activities such as push-ups, lifting heavy objects and prolonged gym exercise.


He contrasted his experience with that of a friend who sustained a similar injury around the same time. According to Habtamu, his friend went to hospital, underwent an operation in which a metal plate was inserted, and recovered the use of his arm within about two months.


The two accounts illustrate the different experiences the men reported. Without medical records or an examination …

title: « L'émeute court plus vite que l'aliénation »
content:
Sommes-nous dans une situation pré-autoritaire ou pré-révolutionnaire ? L'insurrection est-elle un devoir en plus d'être un droit ? Faut-il articuler l'émeute au moment électoral ou pas du tout ? Nous nous posons ces questions avec Tristan Garcia (L'autorité est un chantage, 2026) et Patrice Maniglier (La terre ou le monde. Divergences cosmopolitiques. Avec Étienne Balibar. 2025).


À voir lundi 9 novembre :


Quand Marc Crépon affirme sur

C politique

 que l'incendie de la Mairie de Limoges le 17 octobre 2026 relève d'une « ivresse de la destruction » qui – d'une manière honnêtement

boomer

 – évoque pour lui la tarte à la crème du nihilisme des

Possédés

 de Dostoïevski, il ne se rend peut-être pas compte de l'hilarité universelle qu'il suscite chez à peu près tout le monde. Lorsque l'historien, professeur au collège de France, Patrick Boucheron, dans un entretien de Libération, le 31 octobre : dénonce ceux qui continuent de

« croire que la violence émeutière est toujours émancipatrice »

 et pose le constat que nous sommes en situation pré-autoritaire et pas prérévolutionnaire. Il ne se doute pas que nous rions tout autant.


Lundimatin

 n'a que faire des tautologies nihilistes et des dissociations sociales-démocrates. Notre position a toujours été celle de l'

Encyclopédie des émeutes

 : « Ce qui est intéressant dans l'émeute n'est pas une cause, mais un possible » (BE, II, 54). « Toute tentative des pauvres modernes pour organiser le débat sur le monde commence par une émeute : 1789, 1848, 1871, 1917, 1968, et en 1978 en Iran et au Nicaragua. » (BE, II, 55) C'est pourquoi l'émeute est pour nous « le début possible de la fin du monde » (55) et, en général, « un début de débat » sur cette fin (55). Toute émeute ne conduit pas à une insurrection ou une révolution, mais « il n'y a pas de révolution ni d'insurrection qui ne commencent par une émeute. » (55).


Nos invités ont peut-être d'autres idées sur la question, il faut néanmoins assumer que le débat sur le monde vient d'être relancé.

title: Das Recht auf sexuelle Selbstbestimmung
content:
Zwangssterilisation ist verboten. Dennoch erfahren Frauen mit Behinderungen häufig Druck von Angehörigen, Ärzt*innen oder Betreuer*innen, sich sterilisieren zu lassen.

Weißt du, wie viele Menschen ich begleitet habe, die darunter gelitten haben, dass sie sterilisiert wurden?“, fragte mich eine Beraterin am Telefon. Sie schult Menschen mit Behinderungen in Selbstbestimmung. Es war eines von hundert Gesprächen, die meine Kollegin Ramona Arzberger und ich geführt haben, um zur Verhütungspraxis bei Menschen mit Behinderungen zu recherchieren. Nach fast einem Jahr ist daraus der Film „Hauptsache, du kriegst kein Kind“ unseres Magazins „andererseits“ entstanden. Er begleitet mehrere Frauen in Deutschland und Österreich, die mit Lernschwierigkeiten leben und auf Unterstützung angewiesen sind. Drei von ihnen sind sterilisiert. Keine entschied allein. Elf Prozent der Frauen in deutschen Einrichtungen geben an, sterilisiert zu sein, so der Forschungsbericht zu Gewalt und Gewaltschutz in Einrichtungen der Behindertenhilfe des deutschen Bundesministeriums für Arbeit und Soziales von 2024. In Österreich waren es zuletzt 17 Prozent. In Deutschland habe fast die Hälfte der Betroffenen den Eingriff nicht von sich aus gewollt, heißt es in dem Bericht. In Österreich taucht in Befragungen dasselbe auf: Eltern, Ärzt*innen und Betreuer*innen hätten auf die Frauen eingewirkt. „Ich will auch mitmachen!“, platzte die Stimme von Hannelore Trtil ins Telefon, noch ehe meine Kollegin erfuhr, wer da sprach. Die 66-Jährige hatte unseren Flyer gesehen, der Betroffene erreichen sollte. In den 1980er-Jahren wurde sie in Wien „unterbunden“, ein anderes Wort für sterilisiert. „Die haben alle gesagt, man darf keine Kinder kriegen. Das habe ich nicht richtig gefunden. Und das habe ich nicht gewollt“, sagt sie im Film. Heute verbringt sie oft Zeit mit Kindern. Ihre OP-Akte hat das Krankenhaus vor etwa zehn Jahren vernichtet, nach Ablauf der Frist für Schadenersatz. Sie wird nie erfahren, welche Art von Sterilisation bei ihr gemacht wurde. Hannelore sagt auch, sie habe nie Sex gehabt, aus dem ein Kind hätte entstehen können. Diesen Satz haben wir in unseren Recherchen nicht nur von ihr gehört. Thea, die in Wirklichkeit anders heißt, wurde 2025 sterilisiert, in einem Alter, in dem manche noch nicht an Kinder denken. author: Tam Saavedra
title: WEI and UN Women Co-Launches Guide for Disability-Inclusive
content:
Across Asia and the Pacific, 350 million women and girls with disabilities navigate conflict, crisis, and climate instability. While they are frontline peacebuilders, community leaders, and human rights defenders, they remain systematically excluded from formal peace and security decision-making.

To break down these barriers, Women Enabled International (WEI) and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific have officially launched a landmark publication today: the Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive National Action Plans on Women, Peace and Security in Asia and the Pacific. Released ahead of the annual UN Security Council high-level debate in New York, this first-of-its-kind guide provides a practical, policy-oriented blueprint for governments, policymakers, and civil society.

Read the full Guidance Note on Disability-Inclusive NAPs on WPS in Asia and the Pacific

Historically, women with disabilities in peace policies have been viewed narrowly as victims or passive recipients of protection. Co-drafted through consultations with 26 women and gender-diverse people with disabilities, in collaboration with Women Enabled International and the UN Women Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, this guide directly challenges that narrative. It grounds its framework in a human rights model of disability and the core movement principle: “Nothing about us without us”.

As WEI Executive Director Maryangel García-Ramos Guadiana stated during the launch:

“The true value of this Guidance Note is that it exists, not as a siloed document, but as a means to ensure we, as feminist disabled change-makers, are not left out of the agenda, but we are the ones who get to set the agenda.”

UN Women Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, Christine Arab, added:

“National Action Plans on WPS that include everyone lead to peace that lasts.”

The publication was shaped by participatory research, drawing on focus groups and surveys with 26 grassroots leaders with diverse disabilities across the region. It addresses critical ground-level hurdles—including digital exclusion, inaccessible evacuation infrastructure, and ableism in mainstream spaces—ensuring that the voices of women, girls and gender-diverse people with disabilities form the foundation of the guidance.

The publication urges stakeholders to align National Action Plans (NAPs) with international standards—including the CRPD, CEDAW, and UN Security Council Resolution 2475—across all four WPS pillars:

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Participation: Reserve seats for organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs)—especially women-led OPDs—on NAP steering committees with full accessibility support.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Prevention: Recognize women and gender-diverse people with disabilities as active peacebuilders and integrate intersectional early-warning indicators.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Protection: Address unique forms of violence (such as caregiver abuse or institutionalization) and guarantee accessible shelters and evacuation procedures.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

Relief & Recovery: Ensure transitional justice mechanisms, reparations, and post-conflict upskilling actively include women with disabilities.

The guide also features a practical Disability-Inclusive WPS NAP Checklist to help stakeholders evaluate progress at every stage of policy implementation.

This Guidance Note was made possible with the generous support of the Government of the Republic of Korea (through the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family) as part of the project “Promoting Leadership of Future Generation Peacebuilders and Change-makers in Asia and the Pacific”, and of the Australian Government under the Regional Framework Towards Peaceful, Inclusive Societies (2023–2027).
