author: anonerror
title: El Mito Durruti
content:
EL MITO DURRUTI


 


Este 20 de noviembre se cumplirá el nonagésimo aniversario de la muerte de Buenaventura Durruti. La figura de Durruti, más que ninguna otra, ha llegado a encarnar durante décadas las virtudes y las aspiraciones revolucionarias del proletariado ibérico más allá del movimiento anarcosindicalista de donde surgió. Es más, a medida que el anarcosindicalismo retrocedía y perdía influencia mientras la memoria de las luchas obreras se oscurecía, el personaje Durruti tendía a imponerse sobre dicho movimiento hasta llegar a sustituirlo en el imaginario popular. Se puede decir que la decadencia creó el símbolo. La derrota de la revolución española del 36 transformó al sindicalista, al hombre de acción, al líder miliciano, en un mito orgánico. Las asombrosas peripecias de su militancia por el mundo facilitaron la operación mistificadora. El bagaje de esfuerzos por la causa, hazañas, cárceles, destierros y exilios, ya habían hecho de Durruti una leyenda en vida. Su presencia carismática en las giras de propaganda arrastraba a las multitudes deseosas de liberarse. Su apariencia imponía; su lenguaje tosco y directo penetraba en las conciencias de los oyentes mejor que el más riguroso de los razonamientos. La fama de hombre recto, espíritu fraterno, entregado al ideal y eterno rebelde incapaz de doblegarse, despertaba una gran adhesión sentimental que podía llegar a convertirse en fervor religioso. Por lo pronto, cuando empezaron las concesiones y los pasos atrás, Durruti llegó a personificar todo lo que el movimiento obrero representaba en la hora del triunfo, en las victorias milicianas, en fin, en “el corto verano de la anarquía”. Era un soldado de la revolución capaz de impulsar la movilización de los obreros libertarios en los distintos frentes: el económico, el político y el militar. Había dado ejemplo intentando liberar Zaragoza, incitando a la colectivización en primera línea, ayudando a formarse el Consejo de Aragón, protestando contra las intrigas de la retaguardia, rechazando la militarización y marchando con su columna a Madrid. Su muerte misteriosa en el sector de La Moncloa precipitó su mitificación. En los discursos de los jerarcas pronunciados en su mismo entierro quedó manifiestamente alterado su legado. El mito es el componente irracional de la lucha de clases; nace del culto al héroe, algo que en los momentos de estupor y debilidad abre una vía a la recuperación por el orden de antes. En tal caso, el mito obrero, a quien no le daban miedo las ruinas porque llevaba un mundo nuevo en el corazón, como dijo Durruti en la falsa entrevista de Van Passen, se transforma casi sin dificultad en un mito de aparato, valedor del Estado, reflejo de los intereses de la élite dirigente e inspirador de sus consignas.


 


Decía Max Horkheimer, pensador de la Escuela de Frankfurt, que “no existe ninguna concepción del mundo que sirva mejor a las finalidades de la clase dominante que la heroica.” La creencia en que el individuo salva el todo, luego el estatu quo, encajaba en las circunstancias de entonces, con cuatro ministros anarquistas en el gobierno y la revolución paralizada. Apenas muerto “por la causa antifascista”, Durruti fue convertido en “caudillo del pueblo”, defensor del progreso, de la “libertad hispánica” y, sobre todo, de la república “democrática”. La Oficina de Propaganda de la CNT-FAI lo elevó a “héroe de la independencia nacional”, y como tal, no fogueado en la herencia de miles de obreros anónimos, sino en la descendencia de Juan Martín “El Empecinado”, el patriota que combatió a las tropas francesas de Napoleón. Durruti había dejado de ser una figura típica del proletariado revolucionario; Federica Montseny lo justificó diciendo que “cuando un hombre adquiere la categoría de mito deja de ser un hombre representativo para convertirse en la representación genuina de toda una raza.” Así pues, el objetivo del combate durrutista no podía concretarse en una simple liberación de los trabajadores en un régimen comunista libertario; para Abad de Santillán se trataba de una lucha simbólica, idealista e incluso “cósmica”, que reivindicaba “las conquistas de la ciencia, las producciones del pensamiento, los avances de la civilización y dictaba las normas fundamentales del Derecho.” Ni más ni menos. Más directo al grano, García Oliver, en consonancia con los jefes estalinistas y las autoridades republicanas, describía a Durruti como un partidario acérrimo de la disciplina militar, del mando único y …

author: Unknown
title: Medikal Hospital çalışanları: Hakkımız olanı istiyoruz
content:
Elâzığ- Elâzığ’da faaliyet gösteren Özel Medikal Hospital çalışanları, 9 Kasım’da Kod 17 (iş yerinin kapanması) gerekçesiyle işten çıkarılmış ve bu nedenle eylem başlatmıştı. Eylemlerinin 13. gününde Postane Meydanı’nda bir araya gelen işçiler, patronu bir kez daha uyardı.

Çalışanlar adına PTT Meydanı’nda açıklama yapan Tuba Yalçın, şu ifadeleri kullandı: “Bugün burada, yıllarca alın teri dökerek çalıştığımız; Medical Park’tan devrolan Sonomed ve Medikal Hospital olarak bildiğiniz hastaneden çıkarılışımızın 13. gününde sesimizi duyurmak için toplandık. Hastanemizin kapanmasına sebep olan şirket sahipleri, geceleri rahat mısınız? 401 emekçinin ve onların omuzlarında yükselen yüzlerce ailenin ekmeğiyle oynamak bu kadar kolay mı? Unutmayın; bu insanların alın teri, gözyaşı ve kul hakkı her iki dünyada da boynunuzda olacaktır. Devam etmekte olan iş yerlerinizden, bizim gibi emekçilerin sırtından servetinize servet katarken bizler burada, her türlü şarta rağmen yılların emeği olan tazminat haklarımız için direniyoruz. Haklı mücadelemizin maddi tarafı için ‘Mahkemeye gidin’ diyen şirket sahipleri, bu sözleriyle korkmadan adalete meydan okumuştur.”

Yalçın, daha önce verilen sözlere ve ödenmeyen maaş ile özlük haklarına değinerek sözlerini şöyle sürdürdü: “Şimdiye kadar söyledikleriniz, samimi olmayan vaatlerinizin bir parçası mıydı yoksa günü kurtaran birer balon muydu? Taleplerimiz nettir: İşten çıkaran şirketin, çalışanların alamadığı tüm özlük haklarını hiçbir kesinti yapmadan ödemesi ve yeni açılacak hastanenin bir an önce faaliyete geçerek işsiz kalan tüm emekçilerin yeniden işe alınmasıdır. 13. gün bitti, 14. gün de gelir ama biz hakkımızı alana kadar susmayacağız, geri adım atmayacağız.”

Elâzığ halkından, kurum ve kuruluşlardan destek talep eden işçiler, hastane sahibinin Medikal patronunun kentte ikinci bir hastanesi ve eczanesi bulunduğunu hatırlatarak boykot çağrısında bulundu.

Eylem sırasında patronun sözlerini balona benzeten çalışanlar, şişirdikleri balonları patlattı. Halaylar çekip sloganlar atan işçiler, oturma eylemi de yaparak meydanda iki saati aşkın süre kaldı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: anred
title: Ya son cuatro los obreros muertos por la explosión y crece la responsabilidad empresarial y estatal
content:
La explosión ocurrida el 13 de noviembre en Remedios de Escalada se cobró otras dos vidas. Matías Leguizamón y Juan José Servín, trabajadores de la empresa tercerizada Exgadet, fallecieron como consecuencia de las graves heridas sufridas durante el estallido. Ya son cuatro los trabajadores muertos. Una tragedia que expone la precarización laboral, la tercerización de tareas estratégicas, la falta de controles y una política de desregulación que coloca las ganancias empresariales por encima de la vida. Por ANRed


La tragedia de Remedios de Escalada suma dos nuevas víctimas. Este sábado se confirmó el fallecimiento de Matías Leguizamón y Juan José Servín, ambos operarios de Exgadet, la empresa contratada por MetroGAS para realizar trabajos de renovación de la red de distribución de gas. Los dos permanecían internados desde la explosión del viernes 13 de noviembre.


Sus muertes se suman a las de Marcelo García, de 47 años, y Néstor Julián D’Alessandro, de 44, trabajadores de MetroGAS que también perdieron la vida como consecuencia del estallido. De esta manera, asciende a cuatro el número de obreros fallecidos en un siniestro que dejó además decenas de heridos, viviendas y comercios destruidos y familias que todavía no saben cuándo podrán regresar a sus hogares.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida de Agencia de Noticias Red Acción (@anredaccion)


No se trata de una fatalidad ni de un accidente inevitable. Lo ocurrido es un crimen social ligado al modelo de prestación de servicios públicos en el que las empresas concesionarias delegan tareas de riesgo en contratistas, fragmentan las responsabilidades y trasladan los costos de la reducción de gastos a quienes ponen el cuerpo en el trabajo y a las comunidades que viven alrededor de las obras.


La tercerización como negocio y como riesgo


La investigación deberá determinar las responsabilidades penales y técnicas, pero hay elementos que ya permiten dimensionar la gravedad de lo ocurrido. La explosión se produjo durante trabajos con una tuneladora que habría perforado una cañería de gas. La máquina pertenecía a Exgadet, contratista de MetroGAS.


Uno de los puntos centrales es qué sucedió después de la rotura. Según la propia presentación de MetroGAS ante la Justicia, un inspector de la distribuidora informó sobre el daño de la cañería a las 9:44, y reiteró el aviso a las 9:51. A las 10:06, una vecina también alertó sobre la pérdida de gas. La explosión y el incendio se produjeron posteriormente.


La Justicia investiga si se incumplieron los protocolos de emergencia y secuestró la máquina perforadora para realizar peritajes. Hasta el momento, la investigación busca establecer las responsabilidades de las empresas y de quienes intervinieron en las tareas.


La tercerización no es un detalle administrativo. Es una modalidad empresarial que permite reducir costos, fragmentar responsabilidades y precarizar las condiciones de trabajo en actividades que requieren experiencia, capacitación y controles permanentes. En este caso, cuatro trabajadores terminaron muertos.


La Asociación del Personal Jerárquico de la Industria del Gas (APJ GAS) había advertido sobre estos problemas incluso antes de que se conociera la magnitud de la tragedia. En un comunicado del 14 de noviembre denunció que la tercerización sistemática profundiza la precarización, fragmenta los controles, dificulta la aplicación de normas de seguridad y debilita la capacitación continua de los trabajadores.


El sindicato también señaló que había denunciado anteriormente las irregularidades y los métodos de trabajo de empresas contratistas como Exgadet, que presta servicios para MetroGAS y Naturgy Ban. Según la organización, ni las concesionarias ni el Estado escucharon esas advertencias.


Desregulación: el Estado que se retira y las empresas que avanzan


Lo sucedido en Remedios de Escalada tampoco puede separarse del contexto político y económico. El gobierno de Javier Milei impulsa una política de desregulación, flexibilización laboral y reducción de los controles estatales que presenta como una condición para favorecer las inversiones y liberar las fuerzas del mercado.


La reforma laboral promovida por el Gobierno, el debilitamiento de los organismos de control y la transferencia de responsabilidades hacia el sector privado forman parte de una misma orientación política: garantizar mejores condiciones para la rentabilidad empresarial, aun cuando eso implique deteriorar …

author: Unknown
title: Jiyan Tosun: State rhetoric of violence fuels social violence
content:
Individual gun ownership and incidents of violence involving firearms are steadily increasing in Turkey. According to data from the Umut Foundation, approximately 70 percent of violent incidents and murders committed in the country over the course of a year involve firearms. The majority of these weapons are unlicensed.


It is reported that 80 to 90 percent of the weapons used in firearm attacks and murders are unlicensed. Data from the Ministry of Interior also reveal the widespread prevalence of unlicensed firearms in Turkey.


According to the ministry, operations carried out throughout 2025 resulted in the seizure of 110,104 unlicensed weapons, including 50,216 handguns, 35,724 shotguns, 22,669 blank-firing pistols and 1,492 long-barrelled firearms.


Figures released by the Ministry of Interior for the first three months of 2026 show that the proliferation of firearms has continued. According to the data, 25,580 unlicensed weapons were seized during the first quarter of the year.


Demand for unlicensed firearms has increased


The proliferation of unlicensed firearms is raising concerns about individual gun ownership and firearm-related violence. In Turkey, where the activities of criminal gangs have also become a prominent issue, public trust in security institutions and the extent to which individuals feel safe have come under scrutiny.


According to a survey conducted by ASAL Research in July 2025, one in four people in Turkey said they did not trust any institution. The police ranked third in the trust survey, with a rate of 10 percent.


Concerns about personal safety are among the factors driving individuals to seek their own means of protection. One significant factor behind the growing demand for unlicensed firearms is that these weapons remain outside registration and oversight mechanisms.


Social media platforms, messaging applications and sales networks established by criminal organisations are reportedly playing a role in the supply of firearms. Weapons are reportedly traded through closed online groups, while correspondence and screenshots included in court files concerning certain criminal organisations have also exposed these networks.


How are unlicensed firearms obtained?


Social media and messaging applications have increasingly become prominent channels in the illegal firearms trade. In sales conducted through closed groups, membership is reportedly obtained through referrals, while information about the characteristics and prices of weapons is shared among members.


Firearms are also reportedly traded through open groups. Some groups resembling the accounts of officially registered firearms dealers allegedly direct people who make contact with unlicensed weapons.


Beyond online trading, weapons held by criminal organisations are reportedly circulated through unregistered sales networks. These transactions involve direct, in-person delivery, while some businesses allegedly facilitate the networks under the guise of legitimate commercial activity.


How are unlicensed firearms classified?


In the unlicensed firearms trade, weapons are classified into different categories according to their characteristics and history. Whether a weapon has previously been used, whether it has been linked to a crime and how it was manufactured are determining factors in these classifications.


Terms used in the trade include "original", "clean", "dirty", "homemade" and "converted from blank-firing weapons". These descriptions are used to determine the commercial value of firearms.


The conversion of blank-firing weapons into live firearms is a particularly concerning aspect of the unlicensed firearms market. The technical characteristics and reliability of such weapons vary, while their circulation outside official registration systems creates serious security risks.


A report prepared by the Umut Foundation in 2025 stated that the number of unlicensed firearms in Turkey had exceeded 30 million. Easier access to weapons and the spread of individual gun ownership remain major concerns for public safety not only in Turkey but also in Kurdistan.


 


'Violence is being normalised through the media'


Jiyan Tosun, Co-Chair of the Istanbul Branch of the Human Rights Association (IHD), said that one of the main reasons for the increase in individual gun ownership is the authorities' tolerance of firearms entering Turkey. title: First Kurdish Film Festival continues in Zurich
content:
The first

Kurdish Film Festival

, organised in Zurich, kicked off on 19 November. Running until tomorrow, Sunday, the festival is presenting feature films, documentaries, short films, discussions with directors and various cultural events.


The festival is organised by the Kurdish Film Festival Zurich Association, established at the end of December 2025. The association, which aims to bring Kurdish cinema and Kurdish cultural and artistic producers together in Switzerland, describes the festival as a meeting space where diverse cinematic works about Kurdish life and stories can gain visibility.


Aiming to introduce the diversity of Kurdish cinema to international audiences, the festival also seeks to promote cultural exchange and dialogue through film.


A diversity of stories


The festival opened on Thursday, 19 November, with a screening of

Singing Wings

, a documentary by director Hemen Khaledi. Set in a Kurdish village in Rojhilat, the documentary tells the story of 78-year-old Khadijeh, who, while caring for her ill husband, tries to nurse an injured stork back to health and persuade her daughter, who wants to immigrate to England, to abandon her plans.


The programme on Friday, 20 November, featured four films exploring different aspects of the Kurdish people's historical memory, cultural identity, experiences of migration and social life.


The documentary

Kî me Ez?

 (Who Am I?), directed by Esin Akgül, explores the life and literary work of Kurdish poet and intellectual Cegerxwîn, as well as his place in Kurdish cultural memory. Drawing on archival footage, historical documents and testimonies from family members, the documentary sheds light on an important period in Kurdish literature through Cegerxwîn's life.


The film

Nachbarn

 (Neighbours), directed by Mano Khalil, tells the story of six-year-old Sero, who lives in a Kurdish village on the Syrian-Turkish border during the 1980s. Set under the rule of Hafez al-Assad, the film examines repression targeting Kurdish identity, relationships between people of different faiths and the social realities of the period through the eyes of a child.


My Uncle Jens

, directed by Brwa Vahabpour, tells the story of a young Kurdish literature teacher living in Oslo, Norway, and his experiences with his uncle, who arrives from Kurdistan. Using humour, the film explores family relationships, generational differences and the impact of European migration policies on Kurdish families.


The final screening of the day was

One of Those Days When Hemme Died

, directed by Murat Fıratoğlu. The film follows Eyüp, who returns from Izmir to his hometown of Siverek and works in a tomato field. Through the conflict he experiences over unpaid wages, the film explores labour exploitation, poverty and the contradictions of everyday life.


Kurdish cinema from Rojava to Rojhilat


Today's programme (Saturday, 21 November) features films addressing war, migration, women's struggle and the lives of Kurdish people across different geographical regions.


The first screening of the day, at 14:00, will be Xavier Koller’s 1990 film

Reise der Hoffnung

 (Journey of Hope). Based on a true story, the film depicts the arduous migration journey of a Kurdish family attempting to reach Switzerland in the hope of finding a better life.


Hasan Oswald's documentary

Mediha

 will be screened at 16:30. It tells the story of a young Yazidi woman who was abducted during ISIS attacks against the Yazidis in 2014 and her struggle to rebuild her life and find her missing family after escaping captivity.


The documentary

Arzela from Amed

, directed by Elif Yiğit and Johannes Paech, will be screened at 18:00, followed by

Dream's Gate

, directed by Negin Ahmadi, at 18:30.


Dream's Gate

 follows a young woman filmmaker travelling from Rojhilat to Rojava, where she witnesses the lives of women fighters resisting ISIS and explores women's search for freedom.


At 20:00, Arash Rakhsha's documentary

All the Mountains Give

 will focus on the story of two Kurdish friends who make their living as kolbers, carrying goods across the Iran-Iraq border.


The programme will continue with screenings of Mehmet Ali Konar's

When the Walnut Leaves Turn Yellow

 and Rosida Koyuncu's

Rêya Penaber

.


The festival also features a discussion about the Rojava Film Commune, meetings with directors, an acting workshop for children and various cultural events.

title: PUK and KDP hold talks in Hewlêr
content:
Representatives of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) met for talks in Hewlêr (Erbil). The meeting took place at the PUK Politburo headquarters, with senior political representatives from both parties in attendance. The talks come amid the ongoing political crisis in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI), which has intensified further since the KDP unilaterally filled the parliamentary presidency in early November.


The PUK was represented at the meeting by Rêwaz Fayîq and Yusif Goran, while the KDP delegation consisted of Piştîwan Sadiq and Mehmûd Mihemed. According to information obtained by the Roj News agency, the meeting has since concluded. Neither the PUK nor the KDP initially commented on the talks or any possible outcomes.


Dispute over parliamentary presidency escalates


The latest dispute began with a session of the KRI parliament on November 4. The KDP had unilaterally convened the first supplementary session and filled the positions in the parliamentary presidency. The PUK protested the move and questioned its legality.


In a video message released afterward, PUK President Bafel Talabani announced, on behalf of his party’s Presidential Council, its withdrawal from the KRI’s caretaker government. He also warned against further unilateral appointments by the KDP. If the KDP independently appointed the regional president, prime minister, or ministers, the PUK would make corresponding appointments in Sulaymaniyah, he stated.


Legal dispute before Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court


On November 10, the PUK and the New Generation Movement (Nifşê Nû) filed a complaint with Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court, seeking to annul the disputed parliamentary session and temporarily suspend parliamentary activities. On November 15, the court rejected the request for an interim injunction to suspend parliamentary proceedings. However, the substantive complaint challenging the session remains pending.

title: HPG announces identities of eight fallen guerrilla fighters from Selmas
content:
The People’s Defense Forces (HPG) released the identity information of eight guerrillas from Selmas in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat) who lost their lives between 2007 and 2018. In a statement, the HPG Press Center paid tribute to their efforts and reaffirmed its commitment to continuing their struggle.


The statement by HPG Press Center reads as follows:


“We commemorate our comrades Serhildan Selmas, Rodî Gabar, Rojhat Selmas, Cûdî Şikakî, Şêrîf Stêrk, Cegerxwîn Zagros, Şînya Cûdî, and Welat Özgür, the courageous sons and daughters of Eastern Kurdistan and self-sacrificing militants of the Apoist movement, with respect, love, and gratitude.


Our comrades were convinced that the PKK embodied the hope for freedom for the Kurdish people and joined our struggle with great determination. They embraced the Apoist philosophy and reshaped their personalities on the basis of freedom. Drawing on the extensive experience of our guerrilla forces, they developed into determined militants and insisted on being deployed to the most challenging areas of struggle. Through their spirit of Apoist self-sacrifice, their determination, and their unwavering will, they became outstanding representatives of Kurdistan’s revolutionary tradition.


Our comrades stood on the front lines of resistance in numerous regions of Kurdistan against attacks aimed at annihilating our people. They fought fearlessly to protect the existence of our people. Devoting all their strength, they played a leading role in the struggle for our existence and freedom.


Despite all the hardships and difficulties, our comrades never compromised their commitment to the Apoist spirit of self-sacrifice. Through their struggle, they became historic figures whose memory will endure. Their efforts gave hope to the oppressed and exploited Kurdish people. With their deaths, they left their comrades and our people another reason to continue the struggle and joined the ranks of the immortals.


We extend our condolences in particular to the esteemed families of our fallen comrades and to the entire patriotic people of Kurdistan. We pledge to carry forward the banner of struggle passed on to us by our martyrs, conscious of our responsibility toward all those who have fallen, to fulfill their goals without fail, and to keep their memory alive forever.”

title: Final declaration of the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women meeting in Sulaymaniyah
content:
The Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women held a meeting in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. The meeting brought together political figures, activists, and representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan. Participants exchanged views on women’s issues, recent developments, and the political situation in the region. Efforts to strengthen national unity among Kurdish women and preparations for the Third Kurdish Women’s National Congress were also key items on the agenda.


‘Unity is the only way to a solution’


The meeting’s final declaration outlined the following positions and proposals:


“We support the preservation of the constitutional status of the Federal Kurdistan Region and are working to promote unity among the Kurdish people, dialogue, and a return to the ballot box as the only way to resolve internal problems and crises.


We will under no circumstances be party to the division of the Kurdistan Region. On the contrary, we support the establishment of a broad-based, united, and democratic government founded on genuine partnership and the right to citizenship.


As a platform, we support the preservation and strengthening of the Democratic Autonomous Administration system in Rojava (Western Kurdistan) to guarantee the rights of all peoples and communities.


‘The peace and democratic society process must be supported’


We support initiatives for democratic solutions in all parts and regions of Kurdistan and efforts to address the demands of the Kurdish people. We call on democratic society and all political forces and parties to support the peace process in Bakur (Northern Kurdistan).


Our position on the situation in Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan) is clear and unwavering. More than 700 people have been arrested and executed across Iran this year. We therefore demand that the platform take a clear and urgent stance to halt these penalties and protect their lives.


We emphasize the importance of coordination and joint efforts with political parties, groups, and organizations to unite efforts and bring positions closer together.


We firmly oppose femicide, self-immolation, and all forms of violence. We will under no circumstances accept women’s rights being sacrificed to political crises. On the contrary, we are working to strengthen the position of women and ensure the continuity of their achievements in all parts and regions of Kurdistan under the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ (Woman, Life, Freedom).


‘Act with historical responsibility and take practical steps’


As Kurdish women, we declare to the participants and platforms that we support the process of democratic integration in our struggle to protect our rights and achievements.


At this meeting, the importance of mutual support and solidarity among all parts of Kurdistan at every stage was highlighted.


Visiting all political parties and organizations to promote Kurdish unity and organizing a meeting with broad participation.


Making preparations to organize a culture and arts festival across Kurdistan.


Organizing a series of large-scale and comprehensive actions to protect the achievements of the women’s revolution.


Intensifying efforts and the struggle for Kurdish unity, particularly in Bashur (Southern Kurdistan).


Working toward the preparation and organization of a Kurdish Conference.


Supporting a common discourse in the media and publishing sector under the slogan ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî.’


Protecting the legal rights of Yazidi women and ensuring justice by recognizing the crimes committed against them as genocide, punishing the perpetrators, and providing survivors with legal, medical, and psychological support and compensation. At the same time, combating sexual and physical violence, eliminating social stigma, and guaranteeing their security and active political participation in Shengal.


Finally, we reiterate that unity and joint efforts among Kurdish political forces and parties are the fundamental guarantee for safeguarding achievements and attaining peace, freedom, and democracy. We hope that all parties will embrace these proposals with a sense of historical responsibility and take practical steps to implement them.”

title: Hatimoğulları: Treatment of sick prisoners amounts to torture
content:
The vigil demanding the release of seriously ill prisoners outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice in Ankara continues. On the fifth day, Tülay Hatimoğulları, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), described the state’s treatment of sick prisoners as torture. She stated that prisoners were being denied timely medical treatment and prevented from being released despite suffering from life-threatening illnesses. The government must put an end to this practice, she said, referring to the ongoing peace and democratization process.


Relatives of prisoners Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın, and Selim Çiftçi were among those taking part in the vigil organized by the Federation of Legal and Solidarity Associations of Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED). The Co-Chairs of MED TUHAD-FED, Pınar Sakık Tekin and Kerem Canpolat, as well as representatives of various civil society organizations, also attended the vigil. Carrying banners and chanting slogans, the demonstrators demanded the release of sick prisoners, including Newroz Bozkurt and Evin Zapsu.


Criticism of forensic medical reports


Hatimoğulları accused the Turkish Forensic Medicine Institute of refusing to issue the medical reports needed by seriously ill prisoners, thereby preventing their release. “Everyone in Turkey now knows that the institute is incapable of issuing the necessary reports for sick prisoners. It remains an institution that fails to uphold the obligations of the Hippocratic Oath.”


The DEM Party politician addressed the medical professionals responsible directly: “You are doctors! Your duty is to keep people alive.” Even when prisoners obtained a medical report stating that they could no longer remain in detention, prison administrations often failed to act on it. This is another injustice that we cannot accept,” she said.


As an example of the consequences of delayed medical care, Hatimoğulları recalled political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam, who died recently after a long denial of treatment. “If families are holding a vigil outside the Ministry of Justice today, it is because they want to prevent another coffin from being carried out of prison. Correctional facilities have become places where prisoners are left to perish. From here, the families are calling out: Do not let prisons become morgues.”


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/fc17a848_20261121134205_2026-11-21-ankara-tulay-hatimogullari-dem-parti-es-genel-baskani-adalet-bakanligi-eylem-1.mp4


“Can you take responsibility for this?”


Hatimoğulları gave a particularly harrowing account of the situation of Evin Zapsu, who has been imprisoned for nine years. Zapsu, who is being held in Kayseri Women’s Prison, was diagnosed with stage-four cancer, yet the necessary treatment has not been initiated, she said. “Everyone has heard her daughter’s desperate cry. Evin Zapsu has been in prison for nearly ten years. Her daughters chose to study at Istanbul University so they could visit their mother. The burden falls not only on prisoners but also on their families. Transfers to prisons far from home make family visits even more difficult. Many families are already living in severe poverty.” Addressing the Turkish Minister of Justice, Hatimoğulları asked: “What conscience, what religion, what faith can justify knowingly leaving sick prisoners to die? Can you take responsibility for this?”


Delayed medical treatment of Newroz Bozkurt


Hatimoğulları also addressed the situation of seriously ill prisoner Newroz Bozkurt. During a visit to Sincan Women’s Prison, the women incarcerated there had given her detailed accounts of prison conditions and mistreatment. “We have repeatedly spoken with the Ministry of Justice to ensure that Newroz Bozkurt receives medical treatment. Our lawyers have worked day and night on this. Nevertheless, she has not received adequate treatment. It has been postponed again and again, repeatedly. The families’ desperation has now reached an unbearable level. When mothers say they will set themselves on fire if necessary unless their children are released, it shows just how hopeless they feel their situation has become. Our mothers are holding this vigil in tears. Enough is enough.”


“How do they intend to make peace under these conditions?”


Hatimoğulları directly linked the situation in prisons to the Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stated that the DEM Party was repeatedly confronted with the same question at public gatherings …

title: Saturday Mothers demand answers about the fate of Hayrettin Eren, missing for 46 years
content:
At their 1,130th vigil in Galatasaray Square in Istanbul, the Saturday Mothers once again demanded that the fate of people who disappeared in state custody be clarified. This week’s protest focused on Hayrettin Eren, who was detained by police on November 21, 1980, and has been missing ever since. Exactly 46 years later, his relatives demanded that those responsible be brought to justice and that legislation be introduced to ensure such crimes are not subject to statutes of limitations.


The participants gathered in the square in Istanbul’s Beyoğlu district, carrying carnations and portraits of the disappeared. The joint statement was read by Ümit Tekay Dişli of the Istanbul branch of the Human Rights Association’s (IHD) Commission on the Disappeared.


Detained and erased from police records


Hayrettin Eren was 26 years old when he came under scrutiny by the security authorities following the military coup of September 12, 1980. He had been active in the youth movement during the 1970s. After the coup, an arrest warrant was issued for him. On November 21, 1980, Eren met a friend at the Haşim Işcan Passage in Istanbul’s Saraçhane district. Both were detained there and initially taken to the Karagümrük police station. Eren was subsequently transferred, along with eight other detainees, to the Political Department of the Gayrettepe Police Directorate.


When his mother, Elmas Eren, went looking for him, she initially found clear evidence of his detention. “Elmas Eren went to the Karagümrük police station and saw Hayrettin’s name in the custody register. She was told that her son had been taken to Gayrettepe,” Dişli said. On the premises of the police directorate, his mother spotted her husband’s car, bearing the license plate 34 F 6798, which Hayrettin had been using at the time of his arrest. However, the officers denied that he was being held there.


“When she asked about her son, the police officers replied: ‘No such person is in custody.’ Elmas Eren then returned to the Karagümrük police station. This time, she discovered that the page of the custody register containing Hayrettin’s name had been torn out.”


Witness testimonies have been available for decades


According to the IHD, eight people detained during the same police operation confirmed that they had seen Hayrettin Eren both at the Karagümrük police station and at the Gayrettepe Police Directorate. A criminal complaint was filed on the basis of these witness statements. Nevertheless, Eren’s fate remains unknown to this day, and no one has been held accountable for his disappearance.


“The state’s obligation to investigate the crime of enforced disappearance, uncover the truth, and punish those responsible remains in force,” Dişli stated. He noted that the Saturday Mothers are therefore demanding a renewed and effective investigation into the case, taking into account all available evidence and witness testimonies. “We want Hayrettin Eren’s fate and whereabouts to be established, and those responsible for his disappearance to be identified and brought to justice.”


“The state is making itself an accomplice”


Hayrettin Eren’s sister, Ikbal Eren, then took the floor. She recalled that 46 years ago, she had personally seen her brother’s car on the premises of the Gayrettepe Police Directorate. “Our loved ones were detained and murdered by state officials. By failing to bring these people to justice today, the state is making itself an accomplice to the crime,” Eren stated.


She particularly opposed the application of statutes of limitations in cases of enforced disappearance: “Crimes against humanity must not be subject to statutes of limitations. Abolish these limitations through legislation and bring those responsible to justice. For decades, the families have been denied their right to a judicial investigation. Many of the mothers who began their protest in Galatasaray Square 31 years ago have since died without ever learning the fate of their children. Nevertheless, our struggle would continue.”


“We will never leave unfinished the struggle of the mothers who sat down in this square 31 years ago to demand justice and died without learning the fate of their loved ones,” Ikbal Eren said. In closing, she reaffirmed that restrictions on their protests would not deter the families from continuing their struggle: “Whether you open this square to us or not, we will be here until the last of our disappeared loved ones is found, no matter which generation …

title: Uğur and Ahmet Kaymaz commemorated on 22nd anniversary of their deaths
content:
“My son and my husband were people who would never have harmed anyone. Yet they were killed in front of our home without even being questioned.” With these words, Makbule Kaymaz commemorated her son Uğur and her husband Ahmet on Saturday. Both were shot dead by Turkish police officers on November 21, 2004, in Kızıltepe district, in the province of Mardin. Uğur was twelve years old at the time. He was struck by 13 bullets. Even 22 years later, no one has been held criminally accountable for the fatal shootings.


To mark the anniversary, family members and representatives of political parties and civil society organizations gathered at the graves of the two victims. The commemoration was organized by MEBYA-DER, an association that supports the families of people who have lost their lives as a result of the war in Kurdistan.


A twelve-year-old child branded a “terrorist”


The case of Uğur Kaymaz remains emblematic of the deadly violence perpetrated by uniformed state personnel against the Kurdish people and the subsequent impunity. DEM Party MP Beritan Güneş Altın recalled that the authorities had portrayed the twelve-year-old as a “terrorist” after his death.


“A twelve-year-old child was killed in front of his own home and subsequently branded a ‘terrorist.’ This historic disgrace has persisted for 22 years,” the MP stated, also recalling other Kurdish children killed in police and military attacks.


“What children need most urgently is peace”


 


Beritan Güneş Altın linked the commemoration to the question of what conditions must be met for lasting peace. “The place where peace holds the greatest significance today is the grave of Uğur Kaymaz. What children need most urgently is peace – the opportunity to grow up in peace.”


The MP stressed that this was not merely about ending violence, but also about social and political equality. “A system in which a child is killed in front of their home, in which a child cannot receive education in their mother tongue, and in which a child does not have equal opportunities because they are Kurdish or not Turkish can never bring about peace.”


Salih Kuday, Co-Chair of MEBYA-DER in Mardin, stressed that the significance of the case extends far beyond the fate of the Kaymaz family. “If those responsible for Uğur Kaymaz’s death had been punished, perhaps many other Kurdish children would not have been killed,” he said and underlined that impunity had paved the way for further acts of violence. “The current political process must therefore also allow for a judicial reckoning with crimes committed by the state,” he added.


Kuday also pointed to the responsibility of state institutions in the current peace and democratization process. He underlined that the decades-long practice of impunity must end, and those responsible for the killings of Uğur and Ahmet Kaymaz must be brought to justice.

title: Press and Digital Commune established in Geneva in memory of journalist Seyit Evran
content:
Kurds and their supporters gathered in Geneva, Switzerland, to announce the establishment of the Geneva Martyr Seyit Evran Press and Digital Commune. The statement announcing the commune’s establishment was presented to the public by reporter Veysel Kuşkanadı.


Emphasizing that protecting the language, culture, history, identity, and social values of the Kurdish people is a shared responsibility, Kuşkanadı stated that the initiative was undertaken to strengthen organized community life in the diaspora, foster social solidarity, and pass on cultural values to future generations.


https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/52fd77b2_20261121150622_2026-11-21-cenevre-sehid-seyid-evran-anisina-basin-dijital-komunu-kuruldu-1.mp4


Preserving collective memory and cultural values


Among the main areas of work of the Geneva Martyr Seyit Evran Press and Digital Commune is raising the visibility of the activities undertaken by the Kurdish community in the city in the fields of culture, art, literature, history, and social life.


The commune aims to record, document, archive, and share these activities with the public, while also strengthening communication and solidarity among community initiatives in the diaspora.


Kuşkanadı emphasized that the role of the press and digital media goes beyond simply sharing news, as they also bear an important responsibility for preserving society’s collective memory and passing its cultural heritage on to future generations.


Seyit Evran left behind a journalistic legacy spanning more than 30 years


Kuşkanadı stated that the commune was dedicated to the memory of journalist and writer Seyit Evran, who lost his life on September 22, 2023. He noted that throughout his journalistic career spanning more than 30 years, Evran worked under the most difficult conditions in all four parts of Kurdistan, using his pen and camera to bring the realities experienced by the Kurdish people to the attention of the world.


Describing Seyit Evran as an important figure in the free press tradition, Kuşkanadı emphasized that he had left behind a substantial body of journalistic work, written publications, and an extensive archive. He recalled that Evran regarded journalism not merely as a profession, but as a responsibility to preserve collective memory and document the truth.


Kuşkanadı also recalled the words from Evran’s final message: “I was Kurdish, and my people deserved to be free. That is why I used my pen and camera until my last breath and spoke my truth.”


Seyit Evran’s legacy to be passed on to future generations


The statement emphasized that Seyit Evran’s memory would be carried into the future not merely through words, but through efforts in journalism, culture, art, documentation, archiving, and the preservation of collective memory.


Kuşkanadı called on the Kurdish community in Geneva, young people, women, artists, intellectuals, media workers, and supporters to contribute to the commune’s activities.


Highlighting the importance of pooling information, documents, photographs, and archives, Veysel Kuşkanadı reiterated his call for collective efforts and greater solidarity to preserve shared memory, uphold social values, and pass them on to future generations.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: ¡A la Huelga!
content:
A Full Report on Spain’s General Strike from Vallekas, Madrid, and Barcelona


from the

CrimethInc.

 collective, 20/11/2026


In response to the violent eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, people around Spain poured into the streets and set up

encampments

 in the plazas in a movement against evictions and gentrification. On November 11, a general strike took place throughout the country—the first in

fourteen years

. Here, we present accounts of the events from the vantage points of

Madrid

 and

Barcelona

.


This is a valuable document for all who seek to build the power to defend our communities.


The View from Madrid


We sit in a loosely arranged circle in a local social center run by a trade union. It’s just past midnight. When the clock strikes 12, marking the beginning of Wednesday, November 11, we erupt into cheers. Spain’s first general strike in 14 years is underway.


4.5 million people mobilized


1340 committees across the Spanish state


108 cities mobilized


4 million+ leaflets distributed


600,000+ posters put up


“General Strike for Housing” website


The building opened at 8 pm on Tuesday; it will stay open until 8 pm on Wednesday, with a room designated for strikers to take naps. People mill about, preparing food for our late dinner, drying wet clothing with a hairdryer that someone thought to bring from home. Some catch up with old friends, as the social center has become a gathering place for all in the area who need it. Others sign up to take shifts making coffee, preparing food, and protecting the space over the hours ahead.


We are

Vallekanos

, some by birth, others more recent transplants. Vallecas, known as Vallekas to many, is an urban area of Madrid so large that it was divided into two districts (Puente de Vallecas and Villa de Vallecas). The area is an epicenter of anti-fascist working-class resistance in Spain’s capital. After

Maricarmen was evicted

 in September and the general strike was announced in October, local organizations and social movements in the districts came together to help organize for the strike. Similar convergences have taken place in thousands of localities around Spain.


“It’s syndicalist terrorism.”


—Isabel Díaz Ayuso, right-wing President of the “Madrid Community”


The enthusiasm that fills this social center on the eve of the general strike flows from the same energy that erupted in millions of Spaniards on the day that Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman, was evicted from her home of 70 years in Madrid. Something clicked in the collective consciousness of the country at that moment. The percentage of Spain’s population that lives as tenants has risen steadily over the last few decades, reaching 25%, and recently, rents have skyrocketed.


All of us have heard the horror stories. A coworker who lives in a village a hundred kilometers away because they couldn’t afford housing near the office. Families with children who are forced to live in a single sub-letted room. Residents of protected housing who were evicted after their homes were sold to ruthless investment funds.


A memorial to Maricarmen a few steps away from her home.


Thanks to years of hard work by grassroots housing movements across the country, a voice has emerged to connect these struggles. The

Sindicato de Inquilinas

 (“Tenant’s Union”) has become a household name, appearing day after day in the news and on social media. The Union has shown the country that it is neither normal nor right that decent, stable housing has become increasingly impossible to find in this country, and the opportunity to become a homeowner even more so. The Union has exposed these struggles as the product of a deliberate political and financial strategy perpetrated by the wealthy. The Union has developed a powerful architecture of local assemblies, which made it possible to channel this collective outrage into a call for a general strike.


What follows is a local report and analysis from the districts of Vallekas and the city of Madrid as a whole, tracing the efforts leading up to the strike and the events of the day itself.


It Was About Time for a Strike!


As

we reported last month

, the current housing crisis in Spain had been approaching a breaking point in the months leading up to Maricarmen’s eviction. In Madrid, rental prices have risen 50% over the past five years, and many in the city find themselves forced to spend upwards of 70% of their monthly …

author: Julius Gavroche
title: For Christian Ferrer (1960-2026)
content:
At the sad news of Christian Ferrer’s death, we feel that we can do no better than to publish Tomás Ibáñez obituary, along with a short piece by Ferrer himself.


Farewell to our comrade and anarchist thinker Christian Ferrer


by Tomás Ibáñez


Redes Libertarias

, 18/11/2026


The unexpected death in Buenos Aires, at the age of 66, of Christian Ferrer on Monday 16 November has surprised, shocked and saddened all of us comrades who held him in high regard as a person, as an anarchist and as the author of unrivalled writings. It seemed to me that the best way to convey what Christian was like is to reproduce here the words he wrote years ago in memory of his friend and fellow activist Carlos Torres, who died in 2005. Much of what he writes about his friend could be said of Christian himself; it’s just that he expresses it far better than anyone else, so letting him speak for himself is undoubtedly the most appropriate course of action – all the more so because, when we read his words, they give us a direct sense of what our dear, much-missed and admired Christian Ferrer was like.


Pan de Dios


Christian Ferrer


He was barely older than me; he was half a year older. He was taller—by about ten centimetres—and for some reason he seemed immense compared to my build. His muscles were more powerful than mine; he weighed twenty or thirty kilos more. He was much quicker, could shoot his tongue out in an instant and, if necessary, would tear to shreds anyone who dared to stand up to him. The booming voice that made him so distinctive seemed to come from some fiery depths within him; I, on the other hand, speak to myself. His liver could handle several—many—bottles of alcohol, whilst mine would give out after just one litre of red wine. He, Carlos, had a steel-like spirit, and I, Christian, am weak—perhaps less so than I suppose, but weak by comparison—so he outstripped me by at least a thousand kilowatts of willpower. We were mismatched, and we were friends.


If I were the Pope or the Chief Rabbi, or indeed a prominent heresiarch, I would issue an inviolable decree prohibiting the use of the verb form “we were”. “We were” is a word that should never have been uttered on earth because in paradise no one ever said it. One simply was, in every eternal moment. When someone says “we were”, they are probably referring to a religious conversion that cast them out of their faith, or an abandonment that separated them from their political ideology, or a break-up that distanced them from their partner forever. But what tore me away from my friend was no decision, no disappointment, no betrayal. If we were inseparable, it pains me to speak of us in the past tense. What am I without him now?


The first time I saw him, we were both twenty years old, and that was during the presidency of Lieutenant-General Jorge Rafael Videla; the meeting took place at the

Federación Obrera Regional Argentina

 [Argentine Regional Workers’ Federation], the former anarchist trade union, whose ramshackle premises lay languishing in the Buenos Aires neighbourhood of Barracas. I’m not giving these details because I have a good memory, but because we remember the places where miracles happen in great detail, and also because that day I knew we were going to be friends with a certainty more typical of children than of the fledgling adults we barely were. That night I returned to my flat intoxicated by that kind of happiness which holds both comfort and promise. Our age, the times, the place and the neighbourhood were precarious. And although I recall our friendship under the shadow of that iron beam, I realise that our lives were always under threat: from repression during the dictatorship, from the torment inflicted by drugs, and from the now unverifiable promise of an old age we would share in neighbouring houses.


We met in the midst of a brawl incomprehensible to outsiders—a pathetic fight pitting a dozen old, almost senile anarchists against five or six young hotheads who were trying to breathe new life into a political movement that had died half a century earlier. It was in the midst of that scuffle that I heard my friend shout at a frail old man who opposed our demands: “Go and throw streamers at the burial niche” [or “”drop dead,” “get lost,” or “go celebrate your own funeral”, from the Argentine Spanish “Andá a tirar serpentinas al nicho”]. The phrase deserves a place in a repertoire of surrealist obscenities, for blasphemous and surrealist he …

author: Mitchell Plitnick
title: Following ICJ Ruling on Myanmar Genocide, Is Israel Next?
content:
The reasons the International Court of Justice gives for its ruling all echo Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice announced its landmark ruling in the case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya people.

For the first time in the ICJ’s history, it found a state directly guilty of genocide.

It is hard to overstate the significance of this case. Supporters of Palestine are immediately, and correctly, going to draw parallels to South Africa’s case against Israel. But the ruling also has deeper, more global implications.

“Genocide” is a highly contested term. Defenders of Israel’s actions in Gaza often say that it is a legal term, and they’re not wrong. But it is not only a legal term; it has colloquial meanings as well.

The term was coined relatively recently, in 1944 by Raphael Lemkin. He was spurred to create the word in his book, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe by the Holocaust of World War II but did not intend for that horror to stand as the definition of the term. In fact, he noted himself that he would apply it to the Ottoman Empire’s atrocities against the Armenian people three decades prior.

The argument that genocide is a purely legal term is dangerous. With no court to rule, would that exclude the obvious genocide of the Indigenous Peoples of the Western Hemisphere? Perhaps more to the point, would the fact that no state has, before today, been found guilty of genocide by the ICJ mean that it has not happened since the agreement on the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide of 1948?

That would certainly be disputed in the cases of Rwanda, Darfur, Cambodia, Bosnia, the Yazidis in Iraq and Syria, and a depressing number of other cases, just in the past seventy-eight years.

These facts are important to note because the argument that the ICJ has not declared genocide in Gaza does not mean there is no genocide in Gaza. That will remain so even if the ICJ does not hold Israel responsible for the crime of genocide in Gaza.

But it is obvious that the outcome of South Africa’s case against Israel carries monumental weight, and the case against Myanmar holds many parallels.

The Rohingya lived under a brutal junta in Myanmar which severely restricted their rights. Myanmar claims that their actions against the Rohingya community were a response to Rohingya violence. Myanmar, like Israel, argued that the refugee crisis and the sizable number of civilian deaths were part of security operations.

Yet it was never certain what the ICJ ruling would turn out to be, and as much as the case has many similarities to Gaza, the ruling does not by any means guarantee that the case of Gaza will be decided in the same way. But it does offer a strong ray of hope in that direction.

Only two accusations of genocide had ever come before the ICJ prior to this one. One was a cross-accusation between Serbia and Croatia which the Court summarily dismissed. The other was the Srebrenica massacre of 1993, where Bosnia and Herzegovina accused Serbia and Montenegro of genocide.

In that case (which, it should be noted, took fourteen years between when it was filed and when it was decided), the ICJ decided that genocide had been committed, but that the states were not responsible for the genocide. The ICJ ruled only that Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide.

That was worrisome because the case clarified that conviction for genocide has an extremely high bar. The ICJ ruled that, to prove genocidal intent, the circumstances must lead to only one conclusion: that genocide was the goal of the state’s actions. If any other motive is possible, then intent cannot be legally established.

Proving intent is already difficult, since genocidal states do not generally announce, as the Nazis did, that they intended to wipe entire groups of people out of a specific place. Saying that such proof requires that no other conclusion is even possible was seen by many as a bar so high that no state could ever be held responsible for genocide.

The ruling against Myanmar shows that, although the bar is high, it can be reached. That is an enormous development for those who hope to see Israel held accountable for genocide.

author: Randi Beers
title: News quiz Nov. 21 | Old traditions and new beginnings
content:
The holidays are again approaching and there’s lots to remember: gifts, Christmas parties, cards, holiday concerts, family visits — and don’t forget the turkey. But do you remember the events of last week? Let’s find out.


1.

 The public got a chance to see inside Nunavut’s new Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre during an open house on Nov. 14. The centre will offer various services to assist residents recovering from addiction. Which amenity is not included at the facility?


A.

 A daycare


B.

 A country food processing area


C.

 An Olympic-sized swimming pool


2.

 The Qikiqtani Inuit Association opposes a finding by the Nunavut Impact Review Board that a planned hydro project for Iqaluit does not need a full public review. Which company is behind the project?


A.

 Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp.


B.

 Arctic Fresh Projects Ltd.


C.

 Qulliq Energy Corp.


3.

 Iqaluit-born artist Aija Komangapik helped paint a new mural at the University of Ottawa. What did she illustrate?


A.

 A number of sea creatures, real and mythical, including narwhal, a grey seal and Sedna.


B.

 Traditional practices being passed down through generations.


C.

 A map of Inuit Nunangat that shows how all the regions are culturally connected.


4.

 What new powers would proposed Bill S-8 give police?


A.

 The authority to search people’s luggage before boarding regional northern flights.


B.

 The authority to intercept mail.


C.

 The authority to open anybody’s Christmas presents without a search warrant.


5.

 Speaking of police, an investigation in Ottawa led to the seizure of five kilograms of cocaine alleged to be destined to Nunavut. How many doses of cocaine did police estimate they kept off the streets?


A.

 5,000


B.

 50,000


C.

 500,000


Nunavut Justice Minister George Hickes, left, and Nunavut RCMP commanding officer Chief Supt. Kent Pike discuss drug-trafficking routes into Nunavut during a news conference in Iqaluit on April 15. (File photo by Arty Sarkisian)


Answers:


1.

 C — The $83.7-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre

will have a little something

 for everybody — a sewing room, daycare, area for processing country food and a group therapy room. But there is no pool.


2.

 A — Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp. is behind the $500-million proposal to build a hydro plant for Iqaluit. The company is owned by Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is owned by QIA. This means QIA is

requesting

 a full public review of its own project.


3.

 B — Artist Aija Komangapik’s portion of the mural includes a seal, narhwhal, blue whale and walrus. “The creation for all the animals starts in the ocean, and for Inuit, it starts with Sedna,” she said to Nunatsiaq News

in an interview

.


4.

 B — Don’t worry, nobody is going through your presents without a search warrant. But if passed, Bill S-8 would give police the

power to intercept mail

 if they believe a package holds illicit items such as alcohol or drugs. (They would still need a search warrant.)


5.

B — Police

estimate

 a cocaine seizure they executed in August kept 50,000 doses of cocaine out of the territory. No charges have been announced in relation to the seizure.

author: Ayden Runnels
title: Texas Drops Lawsuits Against Out-of-State Abortion Providers
content:
”These cases were baseless from the start and designed to intimidate doctors nationwide,” said one abortion advocate.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton on Friday dropped two lawsuits that were filed against out-of-state doctors for sending abortion medication to Texas — a practice his successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed not to upkeep.

In January and February, Paxton sued two doctors in California and nurse practitioner Debra Lynch in Delaware for mailing abortion pills to Texas residents and operating services that help do so. But on Friday, Paxton filed notices of nonsuit in both cases, part of a wave of withdrawals his office has filed as he prepares to leave office in January.

It is illegal for Texas doctors to mail abortion medication within the state — but Paxton has also sued doctors in other states who prescribe the medication. Other states’ “shield laws,” which protect physicians who send abortion medications, have complicated Paxton’s efforts to seek damages against the doctors.

The end of the two suits was celebrated by abortion advocates, including Nancy Northup, president and CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, who also highlighted Attorney General-elect Johnson’s pledge to not to sue out-of-state doctors who mail abortion pills to Texas.

“The incoming Attorney General agrees with most Americans that doctors shouldn’t be treated like criminals,” Northup said. ”These cases were baseless from the start and designed to intimidate doctors nationwide.”

Less than a day after winning his election, Johnson told The Texas Tribune he would “cease using Texas abortion laws as an instrument of persecution and intimidation” and described challenges to other states’ shield laws as “judicially absurd.”

One of the California doctors, Dr. Remy Coeytaux, is also being sued by a Galveston County man who accused Coeytaux of providing his girlfriend with abortion pills at the direction of her ex-husband.

That suit and Paxton’s suit against Coeytaux and Dr. Rebecca Gomperts were brought under House Bill 7, described by opponents as a “bounty hunter law” which allows private citizens to sue those who distribute or mail abortion medication to or from Texas.

Disclosure: Center for Reproductive Rights has been a financial supporter of The Texas Tribune within the past five years. The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that is funded in part by donations from members, foundations and corporate sponsors. Financial supporters play no role in our journalism. Find a complete list of them and more information about our financial and disclosure policies here.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Randi Beers
title: Blubber for bibles
content:
Greenlanders were the first Inuit to have the Christian Bible translated into their language.


Between 1750 and 1850, Danish and Norwegian ministers of the Lutheran Church and German Moravians worked to translate the scriptures into Kalaallisut. They were aided by the Danish Bible Society and the London-based British and Foreign Bible Society.


By 1850, there were at least 20 versions of the Bible in existence. Some were more accurate than others. As missionaries’ knowledge of the language progressed, the translations became better.


The writing systems used also posed a problem. The Greenlandic orthography had not yet been standardized. It would remain for Samuel Kleinschmidt, son of a Moravian missionary, to undertake that task in the 1850s.


The Qallunaat ministers could not, of course, have taken on the monumental task of translating into a language new to them without the assistance of Inuit converts to Christianity who were willing, and usually eager, to help them.


Before 1800, the New Testament and some psalms had been translated by Paul Egede, son of Hans Egede, who had established the first mission in Greenland in 1721. Paul Egede had the advantage of having grown up in Greenland and therefore spoke Greenlandic much better than his father did.


Paul Egede did not mention the names of his Greenlandic assistants when his first translations were published in 1744. We only learn their names through his journal, published more than four decades later, in 1788.


His main assistants were a woman, Arnarsak, baptized in 1737, and a man, Pungiok, who took the Christian name of Hans.


The two made an unusual request of Egede. They did not want the translations, for which they were in part responsible, to be shared widely among the Kalaallit.


Egede explained their reasoning: “It would not be useful for their unbelieving compatriots to be made aware, for example, that Cain, one of God’s first rational creations, was so wicked, or of Jacob’s deception of his father and brother, [or] the polygamy of the patriarchs.”


The two Greenlanders suggested that, instead, only certain selections from the translations should be distributed and that the more lurid parts be omitted. Nonetheless, the translations were published in their entirety.


The Moravians in Greenland were off to a slower start with biblical translations. In the late 1700s, they expended their mission efforts to Labrador where they built on the strengths of missionaries to that coast who brought with them the knowledge they had acquired in Greenland.


In 1804, the British and Foreign Bible Society was formed, with a daunting mandate to translate the Bible into all the languages of the world. Within a century, their publications were available in over 1,000 languages.


In Labrador, the Inuit Moravian converts eagerly accepted the British and Foreign Bible Society’s publications of the Gospel, as translated by their missionaries, who usually worked by revising Greenlandic publications into their understanding of the local dialect.


Grateful Inuit wrote letters of thanks to the society. Brother Benjamin Kohlmeister sent some of these letters from Nain to Rev. C. J. Latrobe, who provided them to the society.


The Labrador Inuit, unprompted, decided to make a collection of seal blubber to send to the society to help in the costs of its work. They knew that blubber was a valuable trade commodity at the Moravian stores — the Moravians supported the costs of their missions through trade with the Inuit.


Kohlmeister wrote: “Some brought whole seals, others half a seal or pieces, as they could spare it. Some brought pieces of blubber in the name of their children, requesting that their poor gifts might be accepted.”


The Inuit had learned that the society’s work was supported through donations from pious people, who were often poor.


They explained, through Kohlmeister: “We have indeed spoken together, and observed, that these many books, given to us without pay, must be very dear somewhere, but we never have known before now, that even poor people bring their money, out of pure love, that we may get these comfortable words of God. We are indeed poor, but we might bring now and then some blubber as a contribution.”


The blubber yielded 30 gallons of oil. Kohlmeister went on: “They now begged me to send this collection of blubber to those generous friends who printed the Bibles for them, that more heathen might be presented with that book.”


A careful …

author: Corey Larocque
title: Pirutsiagutiit ends Inuit Child First Initiative uncertainty
content:
It’s welcome news the federal government has finally ended the uncertainty around its Inuit Child First Initiative that has existed for two years. But there’s still a lot of work to be done to see how its $115-million-a-year replacement will work as Ottawa transfers responsibility to four Inuit treaty organizations.


On Wednesday, Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed unveiled details about the new

Pirutsiagutiit

 program the federal government unveiled in its recent budget.


The government created it to provide health, social and education products, services and supports to address what Obed called the “profound inequities” Inuit children face. It has been nearly a year since Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty pledged to

retool the old program

.


The Liberals had stumbled along since 2025 when funding for the Inuit Child First Initiative dried up. Ottawa provided two temporary

extensions

 to keep the program going while it worked on a long-term replacement.


Pirutsiagutiit, which means “resources for growing well” in Inuktut, hands the responsibility for managing the five-year, $575-million funding to Inuit treaty organizations — Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., Makivvik, Inuvialuit Regional Corp., and the Nunatsiavut government.


It’s rooted in the idea that community-based decisions are better than Ottawa-based decisions.


“Inuit are best-placed to understand the needs of our children,” Obed said.


Many Nunavummiut will remember Inuit Child First Initiative as the program that funded universal food vouchers in most of the territory’s communities in 2024 and 2025. It helped feed

15,000

 Inuit children over the two years it was in place.


In most communities, Inuit families were eligible for a $500 grocery store voucher for each child under the age of 18 and an additional $250 a month for each child under four.


But Ottawa ended that universal program, plunging thousands of families who had come to rely on the vouchers into

financial uncertainty

. The government replaced it with a scheme that required families to make individual applications for money to pay for groceries.


A return to a universal food voucher program “is not the path we have chosen,” Gull-Masty said during Wednesday’s news conference. It will be up to each treaty organization to determine the terms and conditions for all the supports it will provide.


Pirutsiagutiit should provide more certainty about what supports will be eligible for funding. There had been what Obed called “real frustration” caused by the federal Indigenous Services Department’s changing terms and conditions about what was previously eligible.


Pirutsiagutiit will take effect on April 1, 2027 — the start of the government’s next fiscal year. Even then, the Inuit Child First Initiative will remain in place until each treaty organization works out terms and conditions of the new program with Ottawa.


With each treaty organization responsible for making decisions about how to use its share of the money, it sounds like the supports that will be eligible for funding might vary from one part of Inuit Nunangat to another.


One of the problems with the Inuit Child First Initiative was the lack of clarity about what was eligible for funding. To make Pirutsiagutiit more effective in helping Inuit children, the important task will be to make it clear what health, education and social supports are eligible to be funded.

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Floods add to severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza
content:
Palestinians in the Gaza strip continue to live in precarious conditions, accommodated in makeshift, overcrowded shelters and tents brought about by a war waged with catastrophic consequences.

Israeli authorities are resisting efforts to improve living conditions in Gaza, even as they advance the demarcated Yellow Line that is shrinking the already diminished territory.

Heavy rainfall since November 6 has added to the misery for Gazans, 65% of whom live in tents or rudimentary shelters. Just under 1 million people live in areas prone to flooding, with 400,000 living in areas determined by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as “extremely high risk”.

Tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians have been flooded.

Instances of respiratory illnesses are on the rise. “The numbers already show the pressure,” Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said. “Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the rains “damaged displacement sites, shelter and humanitarian facilities, and disrupted services across all five governorates”.

The damage caused within 24 hours was formidable, affecting 26,000 households. (That number has since risen to 46,000.) More than 6000 family shelters were destroyed in that time, with 17,400 damaged. Damaged buildings have collapsed, and the rains have added to existing structural and environmental risks.

Adding to this are the problems of exposed ordnance buried under the debris or shifted to other areas, endangering the lives of residents and humanitarian personnel.

The November 13 humanitarian situation report from OCHA is evenly grim. Between November 3–9, Israeli airstrikes, shooting and shelling continued, killing 22 Palestinians and injuring 90.

This brought the total number of reported deaths since the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement to 1613, with 5833 suffering injuries. The Ministry of Health in Gaza retroactively added 12 fatalities once their identification details were verified.

But there has not been a rise in humanitarian supplies to cope with the rain-borne crisis — rather the opposite. Between November 2–8, 228 of the 262 United Nations and partner trucks intended for entry into Gaza were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom; 128 from Ashdod, 25 from Egypt, 44 from Israel, 12 from the West Bank and 18 from Jordan.

The OCHA reported that the number of trucks offloaded constituted a fall of 42% from the previous week. Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor, citing concerns over smuggling. Between November 3–8, no trucks were offloaded.

The overall figures also fell due to, in the UN agency’s words, “reduced aid volumes available to partners amid funding constraints”.

The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), responsible for coordinating aid, says otherwise. The crisis is being addressed; poor sanitary conditions were being improved prior to the rain, an effort coordinated with international bodies. More than 93,000 tents and over 8600 trucks holding tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the winterization plan was launched by the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs.

But the Haaretz newspaper obtained data which revealed a growing decline in food deliveries to Gaza, to add to severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair crippled infrastructure.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel had pledged that it would permit 4200 vehicles carrying essential humanitarian aid and commercial items, including food, fuel, vital medical equipment and supplies, shelter materials and equipment for repairing essential infrastructure into Gaza each week.

COGAT’s own figures supplied to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show totals well short of the promised monthly rate of 18,200 vehicles allowed into the Strip: 4700 in March, 5300 in April and over 9600 in May.

In June, the number rose to 12,000, only to fall again to 10,000 for the months of July and August. September proved to be the high point with 13,000, while in October only 6500 vehicles were allowed in. (Seemingly caught out by this unusual affliction of verisimilitude, COGAT called its own figures “inaccurate”, saying that Israel had met and even exceeded its humanitarian commitments.)
