title: Iraqi army takes control of Jurf al-Sakhar, stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah
content:
The Iraqi central government has taken control of security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region, which has been dominated by the pro-Iranian militia Kataib Hezbollah for more than a decade. On Friday, army units and other security forces entered the town, located approximately 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad. The deployment followed an agreement that temporarily averted an armed confrontation between government forces and the influential militia.


Jurf al-Sakhar, renamed Jurf al-Nasr by Shiite militias after its recapture from the Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014, is considered one of Kataib Hezbollah’s most important strongholds. The Iran-aligned militia has spent years establishing military structures there largely independently of the Iraqi central government. Baghdad’s attempt to regain control is therefore seen as a major test for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.


Joint security command assumes responsibilities


According to Iraqi security officials, a joint command comprising units of the army, federal police, Popular Mobilization Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi), and police responsible for energy infrastructure began operating on Friday morning. The new command structure is expected to gradually assume responsibility for security and coordinate the withdrawal of the militia units previously stationed in the area. According to Iraqi government spokesperson Saad Maan, security forces have already begun monitoring the oil pipelines running through the region.


A major road link toward Karbala is also scheduled to reopen on Saturday. Units of the Iraqi army and federal police are expected to secure the route. The agreement stipulates that Kataib Hezbollah groups will leave the area and make way for state security forces. However, it remains unclear whether the militia will actually lose its longstanding influence over the region. The handover is expected to take place over an extended period.


Press conference by Iraqi officials


Iraqi officials held a press conference on the security situation in the Jurf al-Sakhar region on Friday.


Speaking here, Ahmed Hatim Hamid, commander of the Main Control Base, announced that a base had been established for the Iraqi army and police forces. He also reported that the Chief of Staff of the Iraqi Army had visited the region to monitor the deployment of military forces and inspect the measures taken.


The spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces stated that all administrative and management responsibilities in the Jurf al-Sakhar region had been transferred to the control base.


Meanwhile, the head of the Security Media Cell announced that a commando battalion had been deployed to the region to protect its oil pipelines. Stating that handover procedures were underway between the forces in the area, the head of the Security Media Cell said that security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region would now be under the control of federal forces.


Oil smuggling triggered power struggle


The latest confrontation was sparked by investigations into an alleged network involved in the illegal trade of Iraqi oil. According to an investigation by the Reuters news agency, members of Kataib Hezbollah, together with individuals from state security agencies and oil authorities, are suspected of having diverted crude oil from pipelines and smuggled it for years. Investigators reportedly discovered tampered pipelines, concealed pumping facilities, and a small refinery. The financial losses could amount to several hundred million dollars. Kataib Hezbollah denies the allegations and views the government’s actions as an attempt to force the militia to surrender its weapons.


In connection with the investigations, Prime Minister al-Zaidi ordered the dismissal of nine senior officials from security agencies and the oil sector. At the same time, government troops were placed on alert and prepared for a possible operation against the militia. The escalating tensions eventually led to negotiations involving influential Shiite politicians. Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, also reportedly traveled to Baghdad to mediate between the parties. The handover now underway is seen as the outcome of these talks.


Closed off to the local population since 2014

title: Solidarity reception for Rojava at New South Wales parliament
content:
The Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia (FDKS-A), the Sydney Democratic Kurdish Community Centre, and the Sydney Kurdish Youth Association organized a solidarity reception for Rojava at the Parliament of New South Wales (NSW), Australia.


Speaking at the event, members of parliament expressed their support for the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom, peace, and democracy. Representatives of political parties, civil society organizations, and members of the Kurdish community attended the reception.


Greens MP Abigail Boyd described the resistance in Kobanê as a symbol of international solidarity and the right of peoples to self-defense, affirming her party’s solidarity with the Kurdish people.


Labor Party MP Charishma Kaliyanda emphasized that Kobanê had become a symbol of courage, resistance, and, in particular, women’s struggle for freedom.


Liberal Party MP Justin Clancy also highlighted the significance of the Kurds’ struggle against ISIS for Australia and the wider world.


FDKS-A (Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia) Co-Chair Gülfer Olan stated that the resistance in Kobanê was a struggle that concerned not only the Kurdish people but all of humanity, stressing that protecting the achievements of Rojava was a shared responsibility.


Baran Söğüt, spokesperson for the Federation’s Diplomacy Commission, commemorated Australian YPG volunteers

Reece Harding

,

Ashley Johnson

, and Jamie Bright, who lost their lives in the fight against ISIS in Rojava.


Michelle Harding, the mother of YPG internationalist Reece Harding (Bagok Serhed) who fell in Rojava in 2015, praised the Kurdish fighters for putting up remarkable resistance despite their limited resources. “I have enormous respect for them. Despite everything they went through, they managed to find solutions with the limited resources available to them,” she said.


The event also addressed the significance of the traditional floral-patterned headscarf symbolizing the resistance of Kurdish women, the Yazidi community’s solidarity with the resistance in Kobanê, and the Kurdish people’s struggle.


Speaking on behalf of the Reverend Bill Crews Foundation, Dr. Anjalika Wijesurendra reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining solidarity with the Kurdish people and their struggle for freedom.


The reception concluded with chants of “Bijî Kobanê” and “Bijî Berxwedana Rojava” and a musical performance.

title: COP31: Women’s organizations criticize inequitable distribution of climate finance
content:
Criticism of international climate finance is mounting at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya. Women’s rights and environmental organizations accuse industrialized countries of failing to adequately meet their financial commitments and disadvantaging the populations most affected by the climate crisis in the allocation of funds. They say the focus is not only on the amount of funding pledged, but also on who decides how it is used and which initiatives actually gain access to international climate funds.


On Thursday, the Women and Gender Constituency (WGC), a coalition of women’s rights and gender organizations involved in the UN climate negotiations, highlighted significant shortcomings in funding for climate adaptation measures, the participation of local communities, and a socially just energy transition. Together with other civil society organizations, it is calling for public climate finance to be directed specifically toward the people and communities most severely affected by the consequences of global warming.


Little funding reaches women-led initiatives


Figures from the Dutch environmental and development organization Both ENDS illustrate how unequally international climate finance is distributed. According to the organization, only around 0.1 percent of global climate finance goes to initiatives supporting women and the environment. Women’s organizations and local communities developing their own solutions to the impacts of the climate crisis thus receive only a tiny fraction of the available funding.


The Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action (GAGGA) points to another figure: Just 0.22 percent of climate-related official development finance reaches women’s rights organizations. Although the two figures are based on different definitions and scopes, the organizations argue that both highlight the structural barriers faced particularly by smaller initiatives.


International climate funds are largely administered through governments, development banks, and major institutions. For local women’s organizations, complicated application procedures, demanding administrative requirements, and short funding periods often pose significant obstacles. Daan Robben, who is responsible for locally led climate finance at Both ENDS, criticizes the notion that merely promising public participation is sufficient. Instead, women’s organizations and local communities need direct access to flexible, long-term funding.


Adaptation Fund falls far short of funding target


The funding gap is also evident in the international Adaptation Fund, which supports developing countries in addressing the impacts of climate change that have already occurred or are anticipated. Among other things, the fund supports projects aimed at protecting communities from droughts and floods, securing water supplies, and strengthening local livelihoods. At a high-level funding meeting on November 17, only Spain, Germany, and Ireland announced new contributions. Together with earlier pledges from Estonia, Portugal, and the Belgian region of Brussels, the announced contributions totaled US$50 million by the following day.


This means that only one-sixth of the annual minimum target of $300 million has been met. In a joint statement issued on November 18, the WGC and other civil society coalitions described the contributions as wholly inadequate. They called on industrialized countries to provide additional funding before the climate conference concludes.


The scale of the funding gap becomes clear when compared with actual needs. According to calculations by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), developing countries will require approximately $305 billion annually by 2035 to adapt to climate change. Taking inflation into account, this figure could rise to around $420 billion. The organizations emphasize that additional funding must not lead to further indebtedness among the affected countries. Instead of loans, they are calling for grants that do not have to be repaid and can be used as directly as possible for local adaptation measures.


Public responsibility instead of dependence on investors


Underlying the dispute over funding is a fundamental question of international climate policy. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement obliges industrialized countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. title: “Tree of Remembrance” created for murdered women in Amed
content:
Since Friday, a “Tree of Remembrance” in Sümer Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) has commemorated women who were murdered in the city over the past two years. The Women’s Council of the Metropolitan Municipality attached the names of the murdered women to the branches of a tree to preserve their life stories in collective memory. The initiative was organized as part of events marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.


At the unveiling of the memorial tree, Rojda Çeçen from the Women’s Council Secretariat stated that violence against women was not limited to acts of violence themselves. “Looking the other way is also part of the violence. Confronting violence is therefore a shared responsibility of society as a whole," she emphasized.


Çeçen particularly commemorated two women who have been murdered in Sümer Park only recently. She said the pain of their deaths was still deeply felt. "The names attached to the tree represent not only individual victims of femicide but also lives cut short, voices silenced, and women whose memory must not be erased," she stated.


“Remembrance also means responsibility”


Özden Gürbüz Sümer, head of the Metropolitan Municipality’s Department of Women’s Policies, explained that the project had been jointly developed and implemented by the Women’s Council. She said the tree was intended not only to create a place of remembrance but also to encourage people to reflect on their own responsibilities.


“Sometimes we find it difficult to remember what we cannot see. With this Tree of Remembrance, we want not only to make these women visible but also to encourage people to take responsibility for what they see,” Sümer explained.


“May its roots strengthen collective memory”


Sümer continued: "In this way, the life stories of the murdered women are intended to become a lasting part of collective memory and the history of the women’s struggle. Remembrance must give rise to a sense of responsibility that strengthens solidarity and advances the struggle for a life of equality, freedom, and freedom from violence."


In closing, Sümer drew on the symbolism of the tree: “May its roots strengthen collective memory, while its branches reach toward a future free from violence.” She also pledged to continue the struggle against violence against women so that no more names would have to be added to the tree.

title: Kurdish women discuss shared political perspectives in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan gathered in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. Organized by the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women, the meeting also serves as preparation for the third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women. The central question is how women’s organizations can develop common positions amid political upheavals and strengthen their participation in decision-making processes.


In addition to representatives of women’s organizations, the gathering is attended by women politicians, activists, and other prominent figures from Kurdistan. In her opening speech, Şîrîn Tahir described the meeting as an important and decisive step in shaping the platform’s future work.


Tahir outlined three main priorities: assessing political developments in Kurdistan and the Middle East and their impact on women’s rights, critically reviewing the work carried out so far, and making organizational preparations for the third women’s conference. The aim, she said, was to bring Kurdish women’s collective strength and capacity for action into closer alignment across the borders of all four parts of Kurdistan.


https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/w9XHyjDvqAHxEhNecCQM_20_5c6c0282c82d8f10f993c5ab1d3a7e1e_video_1080p_converted.mp4


Prioritizing national unity over party-political interests


During the first session, participants discussed the political challenges facing the Kurdish people and the impact of regional shifts in power on women’s rights and political status. It was emphasized that Kurdish women are internationally recognized as members of a single people, regardless of which part of Kurdistan they come from. “This shared identity must be matched by stronger political cooperation.”


The participants stressed that the national unity of Kurdish women must not be subordinated to party-political interests. Instead, they underlined, autonomous women’s organizing must take a leading role in developing shared political perspectives.


At the same time, participants warned against leaving the current transformations solely in the hands of existing, predominantly male-dominated power structures. They pointed put that, without women taking an active leadership role, there was a risk that political decisions would continue to be shaped by patriarchal attitudes. “The Kurds are not powerless in the face of the changes taking place in the Middle East. Through democratic struggle and collective political action, they can strengthen their rights and political status,” participants emphasized during the discussions.


Southern Kurdistan: Warning against political division


The political situation in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) featured prominently in the discussions. The participants strongly opposed any division of the region or weakening of its political status. In their assessment, such developments would primarily serve the interests of Turkey, Iran, and the Syrian transitional government, leaving the people of Southern Kurdistan more vulnerable to external interference.


The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) were therefore urged not to pursue their political differences at the expense of existing achievements. “Preserving the region’s political status must take precedence over party-political disputes,” the participants demanded.


The participants identified democracy, social unity, and political freedom as fundamental prerequisites for safeguarding these achievements. In this context, they also discussed a message from Abdullah Öcalan to the political forces of Southern Kurdistan, in which he had emphasized the formation of a democratic government and women’s participation in leadership as important steps toward overcoming the current situation.


The participants criticized the widespread exclusion of women from political decision-making processes. As a concrete initiative, they proposed forming a women’s delegation to hold talks with political parties and other political actors. The delegation, they said, would advocate for the protection of the political status of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and the effective participation of women.

title: Bakırhan: The goal of the peace process is democracy and equal citizenship
content:
Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the Turkish government’s budget policies and outlined the objectives of the ongoing peace process at a meeting with civil society organizations in Mersin. The event was held as part of the DEM Party’s campaign, "Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice.” Bakırhan began by highlighting the social diversity of Mersin, where people of different backgrounds and faiths live together. He said the city, with its strong tradition of social and trade union struggles, could serve as an example for the whole of Turkey.


Budget not being used to meet the people’s needs


Referring to the budget deliberations, Bakırhan accused the government of spending tax revenues primarily on armaments, conflict-driven policies, interest payments, and companies with close ties to the government, rather than on the needs of the people. By contrast, he said, the DEM Party sought to prioritize the interests of workers, pensioners, women, young people, and low-income groups.


The DEM Party Co-Chair was particularly critical of rising child poverty, stating that many students could no longer afford their education expenses or were having to contribute to their families’ income. He described the rejection of proposals for free school meals in parliament as shameful: “One of the most shameful things in this world is being unable to provide even a single meal to children who go to school hungry.”


Bakırhan also addressed the current fund crisis. He demanded a full investigation into the irregularities, disclosure of who had received the funds, and reimbursement of the losses suffered by the affected workers, including interest.


“Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles”


Regarding the ongoing peace and democratic society process, Bakırhan stated: “Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles. The process must not be reduced solely to ending the armed conflict. What matters is establishing a democratic order in which Kurds, Alevis, and other ethnic and religious communities can freely express their identities and enjoy equal rights."


He appealed to political forces that have remained distant from the process, calling in particular on Yeni Party Chair Özgür Özel to reconsider his position. “A genuine and strong opposition is not one that runs away from peace, but one that moves toward it.”


Bakırhan also rejected the notion that the process would be complete once the armed conflict ended: “We will continue this struggle until democracy and equal citizenship are achieved. No one should therefore imagine any other outcome. Anyone who believes that the Kurds can be deceived at the negotiating table or turned into an instrument of another political agenda, or who thinks this is merely about a peace process, is mistaken. The goal is democracy and equal citizenship.”


Call for an end to government-appointed trusteeships


Bakırhan identified ending the state-imposed trusteeships of elected municipalities and safeguarding the rights of political prisoners as necessary steps. He called for the reinstatement of the dismissed co-mayors of Akdeniz district, the release of imprisoned politicians pending trial, and adequate medical care for prisoners suffering from illness. According to the DEM Party’s assessment, a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question could save up to US$50 billion annually. The party states that these funds should benefit workers, pensioners, students, low-income families, and small business owners.


In closing, Bakırhan praised the public support for peace and democratization: “Repression and undemocratic practices come and go. But this hall, the will of the people gathered here, and their diversity will remain.”

title: Resistance against solar power project in Arzoxlî on day 30
content:
The resistance against the construction of a solar power plant in Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır), has entered its second month. For 30 days, residents have been protesting against the energy project, which threatens their agricultural land and, consequently, their livelihoods. On Friday, numerous people once again gathered at the protest tent to continue the mobilization, which has been led primarily by women.


In addition to villagers, representatives of political parties, activists from the Peace Mothers Council, and members of civil society and environmental organizations took part in the protest. Chanting slogans including “We will prevail through resistance” and “Em axa xwe nadin” (“We will not give up our land”), the demonstrators marched from the village square to the protest tent.


“We will not bow to these companies”


Peace Mother Nezahat Teke, who also joined the protest, was particularly critical of the support the company was receiving from uniformed state personnel. “We will not bow to these companies. The women and men here must not be left alone in the rain,” Teke declared. She said the company could rely on military support in carrying out its activities. “This is not a matter for the soldiers, but for the company owner. Yet soldiers and police are supporting him. We mothers will resist until the end.”


Villager Güler Çiftçi also reaffirmed that the residents would not give up despite increasingly difficult weather conditions. “We wish the whole world had come out to support us today. We are fighting for our own land and our own water, through rain and drought, enduring hardship and difficult conditions. We will not surrender our land to anyone.”


Çiftçi accused the state security forces of siding with the company, saying: “The company has the state behind it. We do not want to see soldiers and the gendarmerie as our adversaries. We wish they would stand behind us. But unfortunately, today they are standing behind the company rather than us.” Çiftçi stressed that residents would continue to defend their living environment and the future of their children.


“Women are defending their livelihoods”


Halide Türkoğlu, spokesperson for the Women’s Council of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), praised the leading role of women in the resistance in Arzoxlî. Their struggle, she said, was directed not merely against a single construction project, but against the loss of the economic and ecological foundations of village life.


“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated.


She stated that the government has deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site rather than taking the concerns of the people seriously.


Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.


“While the alliance between capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights: Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them,” the DEM Party politician said.


Criticism of environmental policy amid the ongoing peace process

author: Daron Letts
title: Lack of security guard rules could expose GN, professor says
content:
The Government of Nunavut could be sued if unregulated private security guards in the territory break the law, says a criminologist, who studies surveillance and security regulation.


That’s because Nunavut has no legislation that governs the training and certification of security guards.


“What are they waiting for? I don’t understand the rationale for not pursuing it and passing it into law,” University of Windsor professor Randy Lippert said in a phone interview.


The government does not appear to share that sense of urgency.


It has received calls to enact regulation during sessions of the legislative assembly in 2018, 2023 and 2025.


The latest call for regulation came from current Justice Minister George Hickes during the winter 2025 sitting of the legislative assembly, about 10 months before he joined cabinet.


He also highlighted the need for Nunavummiut to be hired in security roles.


“I want to encourage all entities of the government to consider working together on setting the stage of bringing forward legislation in the next government,” Hickes said as a regular MLA on Feb. 26, 2025, about nine months before he became a cabinet minister.


Last week, however, he declined to comment on the issue.


Justice Department spokesperson Stephen Shaddock said in an email earlier this month that the department

“is monitoring regulatory approaches in other Canadian jurisdictions.”


“However, there is no specific timeline for considering similar legislation in Nunavut.”


The Northwest Territories is the only other jurisdiction in Canada that does not regulate the private security industry.


But in Ontario, for example, the Private Security and Investigative Services Act requires companies to ensure guards have and maintain a valid agency licence. If security guards employed by the agency are charged for working without a valid licence, their employer may also face charges.


The licencing process includes a criminal records check and completion of mandatory basic training, which is at least 40 hours.


Ontario’s law allows people to submit complaints in instances where they believe a guard violated the act. The solicitor general’s office reviews those complaints.


Iqaluit’s Northern store recently

ramped up

 its security to include guards in tactical uniforms equipped with body cameras and what appear to be retractable batons.


The North West Co., the Winnipeg-based parent company of Northern, contracts the guards through Iqaluit-based Canadian Arctic Protective Services.


In an email earlier this month, the security company’s regional director, Paul Hunter,

 

declined to say whether the device that the guards carry is a baton.


A supervisor with Canadian Arctic Protective Services stands at the exit of Iqaluit’s Northern store with a body-worn camera in October. A University of Windsor professor warns the Government of Nunavut could be civilly liable if a security guard breaks the law because the territory is one of two Canadian jurisdictions without a law regulating the private security industry. (File phot Daron Letts)


Retractable batons and other instruments that may be used as weapons are regulated under the Criminal Code, said Shaddock.


“Organizations should ensure that equipment carried by employees complies with the law, as non-compliance may result in criminal charges and potential civil liability,” he said.


Lippert said that liability could extend to the government itself.


“If something bad happens, it seems like a lot of people are going to get sued, and it may well include the government,” he said.


When asked about Lippert’s warning, the Justice Department’s spokesperson said the department would not comment on “a hypothetical scenario.”


“In all instances where the Government of Nunavut is served with a lawsuit, the government will review the matter on its merits and respond accordingly,” Shaddock said in an email.

title: Amazon Workers Say: We Won’t Build It. A Better Future is Possible (No Tech for Apartheid)
content:
WE WON’T BUILD IT—A BETTER FUTURE IS POSSIBLE: Amazon workers with #NoTechForApartheid are outraged by the news that Amazon executives enabled the Israeli military to use the company’s proprietary AI facial recognition program to surveil and target Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal onslaught of Gaza, as confirmed by The Guardian this week.

We stand in unwavering solidarity with the people of Palestine who have endured over three years of Israel’s atrocity crimes made possible by Amazon’s weaponized dual-use technology. And we believe Amazon workers have a responsibility to speak out, to organize, and to act.

Are you an Amazon worker ready to build a better world with your coworkers? Attend a worker forum on December 1st to process this news, connect with your coworkers, and chart out our next steps together: nota.sbs/s/amzworkermasscall

We’ve long warned that Project Nimbus – Amazon and Google’s joint $1B cloud computing contract with the Israeli military and government – has been a military program from the start. Now, we know that our bosses have knowingly played an active role to aid and abet Israel’s crimes since day 1 of this genocide.

There is a staggering amount of public evidence detailing the harms Amazon technology has helped inflict on the Palestinian people. The revelation that Amazon executives knew about the illegal and violent uses of the technology means that these executives must be held personally accountable for their knowing and intentional violations of international law.

We understand that, under Project Nimbus’ contract terms, Amazon signed away all authority and ability to restrict how Israel uses its facial recognition technology or any of the other technology Amazon provides them.

The path forward is clear: Amazon workers must continue organizing to ensure Amazon commits to not renewing Project Nimbus when it expires in 2028.

And if our bosses won’t take action, workers will.

author: Amy Goodman
title: COP31 Declared a Failure as Declaration Text Excludes Mention of Fossil Fuels
content:
“I do not bear good news,” Panama’s environment minister said. “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.

“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.

“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from Turkey on the final scheduled day of the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.

Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: I do not bear good news. We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.

AMY GOODMAN: And this is Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s environment minister, speaking just before we went to air, flanked by representatives from Finland and Vanuatu, Belgium, Ivory Coast, France, Guatemala and other countries.

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: We have come together because we feel that the COP can still be saved if we focus on six key issues for our final declaration that clarifies for the world where we must go.

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.

Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly. We must transition away from fossil fuels in an orderly manner, if we are to confront climate change.

The third point for us, which is very important, is that fair contributions to climate finance must come from those with greatest responsibility. You pollute, you pay. It’s actually rather simple. You cause the problem, you must help to fix it. If you are the biggest emitter of CO2, if you are the biggest producers or consumers of petroleum, then you must contribute to solve this problem and these issues.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, in a packed room for the press, the Climate Action Network, which encompasses over 2,500 civil society groups worldwide, as speakers detailed the failures of the COP, there were activists in the room, journalists and many others representing this COP31. The activists on the stage called out the European Union and other developed nations for their obstruction. The room repeatedly broke out into chants of “shame.” The moderator of CAN called the draft text a “disgrace” and introduced speakers.

DANNI TAAFFE: Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International.

TASNEEM ESSOP: There is nothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. … This COP has had the highest number of lobbyists — fossil fuel lobbyists, AI lobbyists, CCUS lobbyists, CDR …

author: Bianca Blell
title: Trump Administration Proposes Cuts to Pregnancy-Related Work Protections
content:
The Trump administration is preparing to narrow federal workplace protections for pregnant workers, potentially limiting access to accommodations for a range of reproductive health conditions.

On November 2nd , the New York Times reported that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) is considering revisions to regulations implementing the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), spearheaded by President Donald Trump. The PWFA was passed by Congress in 2022, initially implemented during the Biden administration.

The original law was meant to fill a gap in disability and discrimination protections that employees are guaranteed in the workplace. Under current regulations, employees are generally required to make reasonable adjustments for qualified employees experiencing pregnancy-related limitations. Examples of such accommodations include additional bathroom breaks, schedule changes, lighter duties, temporary reassignment, and time off for prenatal appointments, including more.

The proposed revisions aim to narrow workplace protections under the PWFA, potentially shrinking the types of accommodations employers are required to provide. One of the changes being considered is a modification to how the EEOC interprets the phrase “pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.” This agency, under the President’s advisory, could present reversals that affect accommodations related to abortion and fertility treatments.

The potential rollback extends beyond abortion access. Under the current regulations, employers may be required to provide accommodations for employees seeking abortion, including time off for the procedure and related travel. While voluntary abortions have already been removed from this scope by a 2025 federal court ruling, medically necessary procedures currently remain covered.

The potential rollback extends beyond abortion access. Employees undergoing fertility treatments may need time off for medical appointments, medication schedules, or procedures. Workers experiencing miscarriages or postpartum depression may also require temporary adjustments to their schedules or responsibilities. Without clear federal protections, employees could face greater difficulty securing accommodations for these conditions, particularly in workplaces where employers are unwilling to provide flexibility.

Research also demonstrates the importance of workplace accommodations for maternal health. A 2025 study found that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was associated with a 3.2% increase in births in states newly covered by the law. The original 2022 law has contributed to a nearly 10% decrease in miscarriages.

The current administration strives for a pro-natalist agenda, encouraging American women to marry and increase births per family. In May 2026, the White House announced new initiatives aimed at expanding fertility benefits and supporting mothers. Yet the administration’s consideration of narrower workplace protections could make it more difficult for workers to access the reproductive health care and employment accommodations that help them build and support families.

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was an important bipartisan achievement that recognized workers should not have to choose between maintaining their employment and protecting their health. Although the law itself remains in effect, weakening its implementing regulations could leave workers with fewer protections during some of the most vulnerable periods of their lives. The federal government should strengthen protections, not undermine the progress that workers and advocates fought to achieve.
